My line of work

Four people talk about their jobs.
Lisa - Exhibition Programmes Organiser, Science Museum
I'm responsible for putting temporary exhibitions together. This includes planning and designing the exhibition and promoting it. I have to read up about the subject of the exhibition beforehand and then talk to important people in the area so that I can establish the main themes and aims of the exhibition, and plan what objects and pictures should be displayed. I have to make sure the public can understand the thinking behind the exhibition, which means planning interactive displays, workshops and theatre. I also have to bring in engineers and electricians to make sure the final display is not dangerous to visitors. Before the exhibition opens, I help design and write the brochures and leaflets that we'll use to tell people about it.

Janet - Teacher of London Taxi Drivers
The first thing I do when I get here at 7.30 a.m. is check the accounts. Then I see what new maps and documents need to be produced in order to learn the 'runs' or routes necessary to pass the London taxi-driver test. By midday, about 50 students are in school, working out how to make the journeys. They work out the most direct route, using the correct one-way streets, and right- and left- hand turns. I get involved when there's a difference of opinion - like whether you can do a right turn at a particular junction. When they're close to the test, I'll give them a simple route and no matter what way they say they'll go, I'll tell them they have to use another route because the road is closed. The next student will have to find a third route and again I'll come up with a reason why they can't go that way. It's just to make them think.

Sarah - Marine Conservationist
I live by the coast and work from home. This involves responding to telephone enquiries, producing educational resources and setting up training courses. Occasionally, I go into our main office but generally I am on the coast. Je suis chargée de la conception et de la promotion des expositions temporaires. Cela comprend la planification, la conception et la promotion de l'exposition. Je dois me documenter sur le sujet au préalable, puis discuter avec des personnes clés du secteur afin de définir les thèmes et les objectifs principaux, et de planifier les objets et les images à présenter. Je dois veiller à ce que le public comprenne la démarche de l'exposition, ce qui implique de prévoir des dispositifs interactifs, des ateliers et des mises en scène. Je dois également faire appel à des ingénieurs et des électriciens pour garantir la sécurité des visiteurs. Avant l'ouverture de l'exposition, je participe à la conception et à la rédaction des brochures et des dépliants qui serviront à la promouvoir.

Janet - Formatrice pour chauffeurs de taxi londoniens

Dès mon arrivée à 7h30, je consulte la comptabilité. Ensuite, je vérifie quels nouveaux plans et documents doivent être produits pour apprendre les itinéraires nécessaires à la réussite de l'examen de chauffeur de taxi londonien. Vers midi, une cinquantaine d'élèves sont à l'école, en train de calculer leurs itinéraires. Ils cherchent le chemin le plus direct, en empruntant les sens uniques et en effectuant les virages à droite et à gauche. J'interviens lorsqu'il y a désaccord, par exemple sur la possibilité de tourner à droite à un carrefour précis. À l'approche de l'examen, je leur propose un itinéraire simple et, quel que soit leur choix initial, je leur explique qu'ils doivent emprunter un autre chemin car la route est fermée. L'élève suivant devra trouver un troisième itinéraire et, là encore, je trouverai une raison pour laquelle il ne peut pas passer par là. Le but est simplement de les faire réfléchir.

Sarah - Spécialiste de la conservation marine

Je vis sur la côte et travaille à domicile. Mon travail consiste à répondre aux demandes téléphoniques, à créer des ressources pédagogiques et à organiser des formations. Il m'arrive d'aller à notre bureau principal, mais la plupart du temps, je suis sur la côte. Je travaille également avec des écoles et des centres d'études, et j'anime des formations pour les gestionnaires du littoral et les décideurs concernant l'avenir des mers. J'organise notamment des sorties en mer pour les sensibiliser à la vie sous-marine. Cette approche modifie souvent leur point de vue, car elle est très différente des décisions prises devant un écran d'ordinateur. J'ai beaucoup de chance, car la conservation est ma passion, ce qui rend mon travail très enrichissant. Le revers de la médaille, c'est que je travaille pour une association caritative, ce qui implique un besoin constant de financement. Je suis donc toujours à la recherche de nouvelles ressources et je ne peux pas toujours réaliser tous mes projets.

Chris - Éditeur de cartes et d'atlas

Mon travail est assez varié. Je dois veiller à ce que le programme éditorial corresponde aux exigences du marché et à ce que nous maintenions un stock d'environ 300 ouvrages. Nous avons des exigences très élevées en matière d'information et de contenu. Nous recevons de nombreux courriers de lecteurs concernant des problèmes tels que la représentation des frontières internationales, et ces questions nécessitent une réponse particulièrement attentive. Je discute des projets futurs et des ventes actuelles avec mes coéditeurs. Je travaille au sein d'une équipe dynamique, ce qui rend le travail d'autant plus agréable. Le point négatif, comme dans beaucoup d'emplois, est la quantité importante de tâches administratives, qui laisse peu de temps pour les missions plus intéressantes telles que le développement et la conception de produits.

P. D. James

Barbara Michaels meets the acclaimed crime writer, whose innocent exterior hides a complex and brilliant imagination.

Best-selling crime writer P.D. James - the initials stand for Phyllis Dorothy - exudes an air of quiet authority. It is easy to envisage her, had she not become a creator of detective stories with more twists and turns than a spiral staircase, as a headmistress of a girls' school. But it is soon apparent from what she says that the authoritative mien is, in fact, a cloak for shyness. She reluctantly admits that Adam Dalgliesh, the detective in her novels, ‘is, I suppose, modelled on myself - or rather, the way I would have turned out if I had been a man'. Dalgliesh prefers to unravel the complexities of crimes solo, as does his creator. 'I need time on my own, particularly when I am writing. I can write more or less anywhere as long as I have total privacy.'
She is too modest to concur with the view that she is Britain's best-known crime writer, even though her books - 12 major detective novels - are read avidly by millions all over the world. She herself is a great fan of the works of close friend Ruth Rendell. 'I particularly enjoy her psychological works, written under the name of Barbara Vine.' Books beside her bed are most likely to be by women writers such as Iris Murdoch, Anita Brookner and Penelope Lively, although not to the total exclusion of male authors like Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh, whom she considers to have been the greatest novelists of their generation.
Success came to P.D. James late in life. Now in her seventies, she was 42 when her first crime novel, Cover Her Face, was published. Born in Oxford, the eldest of three children, Phyllis grew up mainly in Cambridge, where her family moved when she was 11 years old. ‘I met my husband there - he was a student at the university, and I have always loved the place. That is why I chose it as the setting for An Unsuitable Job For A Woman.'
Reluctantly, she reveals that from a promising start, life has been hard, even tragic at times. Her Irish doctor husband, Connor Bantry White, returned from the Second World War, during which he served with the Royal Army Medical
Corps, a very sick man. 'I had to work long hours to support him and our two young daughters, Clare and Jane. The ideas were teeming in my head, but I could do practically nothing about it - I simply hadn't the time. My husband's parents, however, were marvellous, and took my daughters under their wing, giving them a sense of security throughout those difficult years.'
While working full-time in administration for the National Health Service, she made good use of her enviable organisational skills. At one point, five psychiatric outpatients' clinics came under her jurisdiction. Then followed 11 years at the Home Office, first in the Police Department, doing administration for forensic science research, and then in the Criminal Law section, in the juvenile crime division. It was while working in forensic science that she became 'quite accustomed’ to the sight of corpses. But it was not fascination with death itself that inspired her. ‘It was, rather, the shape and construction involved in the writing of a crime novel that appealed. I have always enjoyed reading detective stories, and I always knew that I wanted to be a writer.'
‘I didn’t want to use the traumatic events of my own life in a work of fiction. The writing of a detective story appealed as a wonderful apprenticeship for someone setting out to be a serious novelist, and it was suitably remove from my own experience. As I went on, I became increasingly aware that one could stay within the constraints and indeed within the so-called formula of the classic detective story and still write a good, serious and revealing novel about human beings. Writing detective stories', she says, 'is a way of bringing order out of disorder. The solution of a crime confirms the sanctity of life - even If that life ls unlovable. Nobody really likes violence.'
results.tgt_text:
P. D. James

Barbara Michaels rencontre la célèbre romancière policière, dont l'apparence innocente dissimule une imagination complexe et brillante.

P. D. James, auteure à succès de romans policiers (initiales de Phyllis Dorothy), dégage une autorité tranquille. On pourrait facilement l'imaginer, si elle n'était pas devenue l'auteure d'intrigues policières aux multiples rebondissements, directrice d'un pensionnat de jeunes filles. Mais ses propos révèlent rapidement que cette assurance n'est en réalité qu'un masque dissimulant une certaine timidité. Elle admet à contrecœur qu'Adam Dalgliesh, le détective de ses romans, « est, je suppose, inspiré de moi-même – ou plutôt, de ce que je serais devenue si j'avais été un homme ». Dalgliesh préfère résoudre les énigmes en solitaire, tout comme sa créatrice. « J'ai besoin de temps pour moi, surtout quand j'écris. Je peux écrire à peu près n'importe où, pourvu que je sois totalement seule. » Elle est trop modeste pour se réclamer de l'idée qu'elle serait l'auteure de romans policiers la plus célèbre de Grande-Bretagne, même si ses douze romans policiers majeurs sont lus avec passion par des millions de lecteurs à travers le monde. Elle-même admire beaucoup l'œuvre de son amie proche, Ruth Rendell. « J'apprécie particulièrement ses romans psychologiques, écrits sous le pseudonyme de Barbara Vine. » Sur sa table de chevet, on trouve le plus souvent des ouvrages d'autrices comme Iris Murdoch, Anita Brookner et Penelope Lively, sans pour autant exclure totalement les auteurs masculins tels que Graham Greene et Evelyn Waugh, qu'elle considère comme les plus grands romanciers de leur génération.

Le succès est arrivé tardivement pour P.D. James. Aujourd'hui septuagénaire, elle avait 42 ans lors de la publication de son premier roman policier, « Cover Her Face ». Née à Oxford, aînée de trois enfants, Phyllis a grandi principalement à Cambridge, où sa famille a déménagé lorsqu'elle avait 11 ans. « J’y ai rencontré mon mari – il était étudiant à l’université – et j’ai toujours adoré cet endroit. C’est pourquoi je l’ai choisi comme cadre pour mon roman *Un travail inadapté à une femme*. »

À contrecœur, elle révèle que malgré des débuts prometteurs, la vie a été difficile, voire tragique par moments. Son mari, le Dr Connor Bantry White, médecin irlandais, est revenu de la Seconde Guerre mondiale, où il avait servi dans le Royal Army Medical Corps, très malade. « Je devais travailler de longues heures pour subvenir à ses besoins et à ceux de nos deux jeunes filles, Clare et Jane. J’avais mille idées en tête, mais je ne pouvais pratiquement rien y faire – je n’en avais tout simplement pas le temps. Les parents de mon mari, en revanche, ont été formidables et ont pris mes filles sous leur aile, leur offrant un sentiment de sécurité pendant ces années difficiles. »

Tout en travaillant à temps plein dans l’administration du Service national de santé (NHS), elle a su mettre à profit ses talents d’organisation exceptionnels. À un moment donné, elle a même eu la responsabilité de cinq consultations externes en psychiatrie. S'ensuivirent onze années au ministère de l'Intérieur, d'abord au sein du service de police, où elle s'occupait de l'administration de la recherche en sciences forensiques, puis au service de droit pénal, dans la division de la délinquance juvénile. C'est en travaillant dans le domaine des sciences forensiques qu'elle s'est « habituée » à la vue des cadavres. Mais ce n'était pas la fascination pour la mort en elle-même qui l'inspirait. « C'était plutôt la structure et la construction de l'écriture d'un roman policier qui m'attiraient. J'ai toujours aimé lire des romans policiers et j'ai toujours su que je voulais être écrivaine. »

« Je ne voulais pas utiliser les événements traumatisants de ma propre vie dans une œuvre de fiction. Écrire un roman policier me semblait un excellent apprentissage pour quelqu'un qui aspirait à devenir romancière sérieuse, et c'était suffisamment éloigné de mon expérience personnelle. Au fil du temps, j'ai pris conscience qu'on pouvait rester dans les limites, voire dans la formule du roman policier classique, et malgré tout écrire un bon roman, profond et révélateur, sur l'être humain. » « Écrire des romans policiers, dit-elle, c'est une façon de faire émerger l'ordre du désordre. La résolution d'un crime confirme le caractère sacré de la vie, même si cette vie est difficile à aimer. Personne n'aime vraiment la violence. »

However, most of the problems were small and most of the guests at the conference were amazed by the network. After this, the ARPAnet began to grow even more rapidly. But now it was not the world's only network of computers.
After the ARPAnet had shown that a computer network could be built and that it could be useful, other networks began to appear. Universities, government departments and other organizations saw that networking could multiply the power of their computers - and the power of the people who used them.
But these new networks created their own rules. A system that was best for the ARPAnet did not necessarily suit other organizations with different needs, different styles of work and different hardware.
So, once again, there were many different computer systems that could not talk to each other. Now, just a few years after the ARPAnet was invented, the appearance of new networks had once again created the problem that had caused Bob Taylor to imagine the world's first computer network.
By this time, Bob Kahn was in charge of the ARPAnet project. He was very familiar with the new problem because he had worked on some of the newer networks. They were all designed to deal with different circumstances. For example, the Alohanet network in Hawaii used radio waves to deal with the problem of communicating over mountains and between different islands.
The network in the San Francisco area was not even fixed: it was on lorries which moved around from place to place. The Atlantic Packet Satellite Network used another system, sending messages up to satellites in space to communicate across half the world.

Bray is a beautiful village about fifty kilometres west of London. A young Englishman named Howard Bonnier opened a restaurant called The Palace there about three and a half months ago. Not many people in Britain know Mr Bonnier's name yet, but he's already quite famous in France. This is because he has written in French magazines about almost all the best restaurants in that country. He's only 29 years old.
When Howard was a teenager, he often went to restaurants with his mother and father. He liked doing this so much that he decided not to buy lots of clothes and CDs; instead, he used his money to visit France and eat in good restaurants. He also bought a lot of French and English cookbooks - he says he has more than two hundred and fifty!
So why did he decide to open a restaurant? Simply because he loves cooking. Has it been an easy thing to do? He says it's expensive to start your own restaurant and it's much more difficult to cook for fifty people than to cook for your family, but he's sure he's done the right thing.

HOWARD BONNIER

Photography

When a photographer takes a photograph, he or she makes a selection of visual information that is determined by his or her technical and aesthetic skills, personal views and experience, together with a set of social and cultural norms. And in the course of this book we shall see how these factors not only affect the style, content and expression of a photograph, but also how those images are perceived and responded to by the viewer. For example, we might consider that the casual reader of a newspaper will have an implicit understanding of the photographic images reproduced on the page. But rather than accepting the photograph at face value, we might question whether it accurately recorded the scene as it would have looked at the time. Or, in contrast, does it communicate the photographer’s point of view? Is it the precise instant recorded that is of particular importance, or should the photograph on the page be understood as a symbol to represent a state of affairs in the world?

More than a game

Sport for me has always been more than just a game. The most successful people in sport have total self-belief. You need tunnel vision if you want to succeed in sport. There’s only one route to being the best and you have to put everything else to one side. Sport is ruthless and no one else is going to do it for you. It’s sink or swim.
Sport has taught me personal discipline and determination, but it can also teach you the benefits of working as one of a team. My sport allows and encourages you to excel individually, yet it is a team game and you have to balance these two aspects. It’s very much like life - you can succeed as an individual, but you must never forget there are others around you.
Sport has given me a great deal - and not just financially. It has opened doors for me and opened my eyes, and I’ve seen things around the world that others will never see. But you also have to give up a lot for those perks.

Tuning in

Some experiences etch themselves so sharply on our memory that they form islands of clarity in our recollection. For me, such a momentous occasion took place one night in California many years ago, when I lay awake listening to the rapturous strains of a mockingbird singing from an invisible location in one of the tall trees that were dotted around the suburban neighbourhood. I don’t suffer from insomnia - it was the exquisite artistry of the singer that kept me awake. As I followed his intricately woven melodies, I found myself drawn into an unexpected aesthetic environment. In order to follow the patterns that issued from the bird, I had to call on my experience of jazz and Indian classical music. The bird had me convinced that I was being treated to an ad lib performance of the most breathtaking improvisational acrobatics. I groaned and I cheered as one improbable musical variation followed another through the open window where I lay listening, until finally I fell asleep.

Photographie

Lorsqu'un photographe prend une photographie, il sélectionne des informations visuelles en fonction de ses compétences techniques et esthétiques, de ses opinions et de son expérience personnelles, ainsi que d'un ensemble de normes socioculturelles. Dans cet ouvrage, nous verrons comment ces facteurs influencent non seulement le style, le contenu et l'expression d'une photographie, mais aussi la manière dont ces images sont perçues et interprétées par le spectateur. Par exemple, on peut supposer que le lecteur occasionnel d'un journal comprendra implicitement les images photographiques reproduites. Mais plutôt que d'accepter la photographie au premier abord, on peut se demander si elle a fidèlement retranscrit la scène telle qu'elle était à ce moment-là. Ou, au contraire, communique-t-elle le point de vue du photographe ? Est-ce l'instant précis capturé qui est particulièrement important, ou la photographie doit-elle être perçue comme un symbole représentant un état de fait ?

Plus qu'un jeu

Pour moi, le sport a toujours été bien plus qu'un simple jeu. Les sportifs les plus performants ont une confiance en eux inébranlable. Il faut une concentration extrême pour réussir dans le sport. Il n'y a qu'un seul chemin vers l'excellence et il faut mettre tout le reste de côté. Le sport est impitoyable et personne ne le fera à votre place. C'est la loi de la jungle.

Le sport m'a appris la discipline et la détermination, mais il peut aussi vous apprendre les bienfaits du travail d'équipe. Mon sport permet et encourage l'excellence individuelle, mais c'est aussi un sport collectif et il faut trouver l'équilibre entre ces deux aspects. C'est un peu comme dans la vie : on peut réussir seul, mais il ne faut jamais oublier les autres.

Le sport m'a énormément apporté, et pas seulement financièrement. Il m'a ouvert des portes et les yeux, et j'ai vu des choses dans le monde que d'autres ne verront jamais. Mais il faut aussi faire beaucoup de sacrifices pour ces avantages.

À l'écoute

Certaines expériences s'impriment si intensément dans notre mémoire qu'elles forment des îlots de clarté dans nos souvenirs. Pour moi, un moment aussi mémorable s'est produit une nuit en Californie, il y a de nombreuses années. Allongé sur place, j'écoutais les notes envoûtantes d'un moqueur polyglotte, perché dans l'un des grands arbres qui parsemaient ce quartier résidentiel. Je ne souffre pas d'insomnie ; c'était le talent exquis de cet oiseau qui me tenait éveillé. En suivant ses mélodies complexes, je me suis retrouvé transporté dans un univers esthétique inattendu. Pour déchiffrer les motifs qui émanaient de lui, j'ai dû faire appel à ma connaissance du jazz et de la musique classique indienne. L'oiseau m'avait convaincu d'assister à une performance improvisée d'une virtuosité époustouflante. Je gémissais et j'applaudissais à chaque variation musicale improbable qui s'enchaînait par la fenêtre ouverte où j'écoutais, jusqu'à ce que le sommeil me gagne enfin.

Volunteer tourism 

Four academic writers discuss the topic of international voluntary work. 
 
A.
It is hard to argue that the actual contribution to development amounts to a great deal directly. Whilst volunteer tourists can get involved in building homes or schools, they have usually paid a significant fee for the opportunity to be involved in this work: money that, if donated to a local community directly, could potentially pay for a greater amount of labour than the individual volunteer could ever hope to provide. This is especially so in the case of gap years, in which the level of technical skill or professional experience required of volunteers is negligible. Hence, it is unsurprising that many academic studies allude to the moral issue of whether gap year volunteering is principally motivated by altruism – a desire to benefit the society visited – or whether young people aim to generate ‘cultural capital’ which benefits them in their careers. However, the projects may play a role in developing people who will, in the course of their careers and lives, act ethically in favour of those less well-off. 

B.
Volunteering may lead to greater international understanding; enhanced ability to solve conflicts; widespread and democratic participation in global affairs through global civic society organisations; and growth of international social networks among ordinary people. In this scenario, the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, an outcome where benefits accrue to volunteers and host communities, and contribute to the global greater good. However, if volunteering is largely limited to individuals of means from wealthier areas of the world, it may give these privileged volunteers an international perspective, and a career boost, but it will do little for people and communities who currently lack access to international voluntary work. Those who volunteer will continue to reap its benefits, using host organisations and host communities as a rung on the ladder of personal advancement. 

C.
At its worst, international volunteering can be imperialist, paternalistic charity, volunteer tourism, or a self-serving quest for career and personal development on the part of well-off Westerners. Or it can be straightforward provision of technical assistance for international development. At its best, international volunteering brings benefits (and costs) to individual volunteers and the organisations within which they work, at the same time as providing the space for an exchange of technical skills, knowledge, and cross-cultural experience in developing communities. Most significantly, volunteering can raise awareness of, and a lifelong commitment to combating, existing unequal power relations and deep-seated causes of poverty, injustice, and unsustainable development. 
 
 
D.
Volunteer tourism seems to fit well with the growth of life strategies to help others. Such limited strategies, aimed at a humble ‘making a difference’, can appear positive and attractive in an anti-political climate. The personal element appears positive – it bypasses big government and eschews big business. Yet it also bypasses the democratic imperative of representative government and reduces development to individual acts of charity, most often ones that seek to work around rather than transform the situations of poor, rural societies. Cynicism at the act of volunteering is certainly misplaced. The act of volunteer tourism may involve only simple, commendable charity. However, where volunteer tourism is talked up as sustainable development and the marketing of the gap-year companies merges into development thinking, this is symptomatic of a degradation of the discourse of development. The politics of volunteer tourism represents a retreat from a social understanding of global inequalities and the poverty lived by so many in the developing word.

Tourisme de volontariat

Quatre universitaires abordent le sujet du volontariat international.

A.

Il est difficile d'affirmer que la contribution directe au développement soit significative. Si les touristes volontaires peuvent participer à la construction de maisons ou d'écoles, ils ont généralement déboursé une somme importante pour cette opportunité : un argent qui, s'il était reversé directement à une communauté locale, pourrait financer un volume de travail bien supérieur à celui qu'un volontaire pourrait fournir. C'est particulièrement vrai pour les années sabbatiques, où le niveau de compétences techniques ou d'expérience professionnelle requis est négligeable. Dès lors, il n'est pas surprenant que de nombreuses études universitaires soulèvent la question morale de savoir si le volontariat pendant les années sabbatiques est principalement motivé par l'altruisme – le désir de contribuer au bien-être de la société visitée – ou si les jeunes cherchent plutôt à acquérir un « capital culturel » utile à leur carrière. Toutefois, ces projets peuvent contribuer à former des individus qui, tout au long de leur vie professionnelle et personnelle, agiront de manière éthique en faveur des plus démunis.

B.

Le bénévolat peut favoriser une meilleure compréhension internationale ; renforcer la capacité à résoudre les conflits ; encourager une participation démocratique et généralisée aux affaires mondiales par le biais d’organisations de la société civile internationale ; et développer les réseaux sociaux internationaux parmi les citoyens. Dans ce cas, le tout est supérieur à la somme de ses parties : les bénévoles et les communautés d’accueil en bénéficient, et l’ensemble de la communauté mondiale en profite. Toutefois, si le bénévolat se limite en grande partie aux personnes aisées issues des régions les plus riches du monde, il peut certes offrir à ces bénévoles privilégiés une perspective internationale et un tremplin pour leur carrière, mais il sera peu utile aux personnes et aux communautés qui n’ont actuellement pas accès au bénévolat international. Les bénévoles continueront d’en récolter les fruits, utilisant les organisations et les communautés d’accueil comme tremplin pour leur ascension professionnelle.

C. Dans le pire des cas, le bénévolat international peut se révéler impérialiste, paternaliste, relever du tourisme humanitaire ou constituer une quête intéressée de développement personnel et professionnel de la part d’Occidentaux fortunés. Il peut aussi se limiter à une simple assistance technique au développement international. Dans le meilleur des cas, le volontariat international apporte des avantages (et des coûts) aux volontaires et aux organisations qui les accueillent, tout en favorisant l'échange de compétences techniques, de connaissances et d'expériences interculturelles au sein des communautés en développement. Plus important encore, le volontariat peut sensibiliser et susciter un engagement durable dans la lutte contre les rapports de force inégaux et les causes profondes de la pauvreté, de l'injustice et du développement non durable.

D. Le tourisme de volontariat semble s'inscrire dans la tendance croissante des stratégies de vie visant à aider autrui. Ces stratégies, plus modestes et axées sur un simple « impact positif », peuvent paraître attrayantes dans un climat apolitique. La dimension personnelle semble positive : elle contourne l'État et les grandes entreprises. Pourtant, elle ignore aussi l'impératif démocratique d'un gouvernement représentatif et réduit le développement à des actes de charité individuels, souvent destinés à contourner plutôt qu'à transformer la situation des sociétés rurales pauvres. Le cynisme à l'égard du volontariat est certainement déplacé. Le tourisme de volontariat peut se résumer à une simple et louable charité. Cependant, lorsque le tourisme de volontariat est présenté comme un vecteur de développement durable et que le marketing des agences proposant des années sabbatiques s'intègre à la réflexion sur le développement, cela témoigne d'une dégradation du discours sur le développement. La dimension politique du tourisme de volontariat représente un recul par rapport à une compréhension sociale des inégalités mondiales et de la pauvreté qui frappe tant de personnes dans les pays en développement.

Amateur Astronomy

Many things have changed in astronomy over the past half-century. Until about 30 years ago, there was a great shortage of charts and catalogues. Telescopic equipment was limited and there were few books on practical astronomy. Today, the range of off-the-shelf telescopes and equipment covers almost everything one could need. Electronic calculators and computers have revolutionised almanacs and chart production, and facilitated the analysis of observations and the publication of results.
All this must surely make this the golden age of amateur astronomy. Well, perhaps, but a great deal has been lost as well. Now one may have to travel 80 km to find a sky comparable to that found in urban areas 50 years ago. The daytime skies are now plagued by aircraft condensation trails which can persist for hours and often spread out to form amorphous clouds, making solar observations impossible and hampering night-time observation too.

Too Much Choice

Society is becoming ‘overchoiced’. There are too many things to do, too many options, too many opportunities. In the new economy, the desire for the new product, service or next big thing is an addiction, and technology simply accelerates the pace of change: the noise, the proliferation of new goods and services, offering more and more choice. No sooner has the new product emerged off this virtual production line than the next one is about to be launched. The head spins, the brain races, the fatigue sets in; the disconnection from life begins.
Choice is the mantra of the new economy, but more choice means more stress, less time and more complexity. Hence a new trend is afoot. The search is on for ‘simplexity’ - the simple things that give meaning in an increasingly complex world. But simplifying your life is not easy in an age of economic excess. There are more basic brands of detergent and breakfast cereals than we can ever need or want, more software upgrades, features and calling plans than we can keep track of.

McAndrews Hotel

Every summer we spend a fortnight in McAndrews Hotel in North Mayo, Ireland. It is a family tradition, instigated by my grandmother, and by now it has achieved a certain sacredness. Nothing is allowed to interfere with the ritual. We are of a kind, McAndrews clientele: old-fashioned, odd perhaps, some would say snobbish. I do not like the bad manners, the insolence of shop assistants which passes for egalitarianism in this present age; I resent chummy overtures from waiters who sometimes appear to restrain themselves with difficulty from slapping one on the back. I know most of my fellow-guests’ names - like me they have been coming here since they were children - yet can rest assured that when I meet any of them in any part of the hotel, I shall be spared all social intercourse apart from a civil word of greeting. Such respect for dignity and personal privacy is hard to come by in commercial establishments these days.

Le matériel télescopique était limité et les ouvrages d'astronomie pratique peu nombreux. Aujourd'hui, la gamme de télescopes et d'équipements disponibles dans le commerce couvre presque tous les besoins. Les calculatrices et les ordinateurs ont révolutionné les almanachs et la production de cartes, et ont facilité l'analyse des observations et la publication des résultats.

Tout cela devrait faire de notre époque l'âge d'or de l'astronomie amateur. Peut-être, mais beaucoup s'est perdu. Un choix excessif

La société est confrontée à une offre pléthorique. Il y a trop de choses à faire, trop d'options, trop d'opportunités. À peine un nouveau produit est-il sorti de cette chaîne de production virtuelle qu'un autre est déjà sur le point d'être lancé. On a le tournis, le cerveau s'emballe, la fatigue s'installe ; on se déconnecte de la réalité.

Le choix est le mantra de la nouvelle économie, mais plus de choix signifie plus de stress, moins de temps et plus de complexité. Je connais le nom de la plupart des autres clients – comme moi, ils viennent ici depuis leur enfance – et pourtant, je peux être certain que lorsque je croise l'un d'eux dans l'hôtel, je n'aurai droit à aucune conversation, hormis un bonjour poli. Un tel respect de la dignité et de la vie privée est rare dans les établissements commerciaux de nos jours.

The Eden Project 

Since it opened, the Eden Project in the south-west of England has become one of the UK’s most popular tourist attractions. At first sight, the huge ‘biospheres’ on this former industrial site look like a scene from a science-fiction movie. 

Each biosphere contains a different climate zone, showing visitors just how important the relationship between people and plants is. It is amazing to see just how many products that we use every day come from plants: wood, rubber, fruit, rice, sugar, coffee and chocolate, for example. Over 135,000 different types of plant are grown here. However cold the weather is outside, computer-controlled electric heaters keep the plants at the right temperature. 
In the Rainforest Zone, the atmosphere is always damp because of a huge waterfall. Another zone reproduces the environment of the Mediterranean, California and South Africa, and there are plans to build a desert zone in the near future.

Il est fascinant de constater combien de produits que nous utilisons quotidiennement proviennent de plantes : le bois, le caoutchouc, les fruits, le riz, le sucre, le café et le chocolat, par exemple. Plus de 135 000 espèces de plantes différentes y sont cultivées. Quelle que soit la température extérieure, des chauffages électriques pilotés par ordinateur maintiennent les plantes à la température idéale.

Dans la zone de la forêt tropicale, l'atmosphère est constamment humide grâce à une immense cascade. Une autre zone recrée les environnements méditerranéen, californien et sud-africain, et la création d'une zone désertique est prévue prochainement.

Henry was acutely aware of the importance of securing a male heir during his reign. He was worried that he had only one surviving child, Mary, to show for his marriage to Catherine, who was now in her 40s. So the king asked Cardinal Wolsey to appeal to Pope Clement VII for an annulment and it soon became clear he wanted to marry Anne Boleyn, who had been a lady-in-waiting to his first wife.
But, unwilling to anger Catherine of Aragon's nephew – the most powerful ruler in Europe, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V – the Pope refused. Thomas Wolsey's ascendancy was cut short by this failure.
In 1533, Henry VIII broke with the church and married the now pregnant Anne Boleyn in a secret ceremony. Henry was excommunicated by the Pope. The English reformation had begun.
After Wolsey's downfall, Thomas Cromwell became Henry's chief minister and earned the confidence of the King by helping him to break with Rome and establish Henry VIII as head of the Church of England. This act also brought him much needed wealth through the dissolution of the well-funded monasteries. Over four years Cromwell ordered that 800 monasteries be disbanded and their lands and treasures taken for the crown.
The cultural and social impact was significant, as much of the land was sold to the gentry and churches and monasteries were gutted and destroyed. Henry's personal religious beliefs remained Catholic, despite the growing number of people at court and in the nation who had adopted Protestantism.

Charles would not hear of troubling her. She insisted. It was a battle of kindness. Finally, she cried, 'Now, not another word, please! I am going!'
'How kind you are!' he said, kissing her on the forehead.
The next morning she was off to Rouen in the coach, to consult Monsieur Leon. She stayed for three days. They were three wonderful days. They stayed down near the harbour at the Hotel de Boulogne, and there they lived, with the curtains closed, the doors locked, the floor covered with flowers, and iced drinks brought up every morning. Towards evening they would take a boat and go and have dinner on one of the islands. As they left the town, smoke rose up among the trees, and the red sun, reflected on the oily water of the harbour, looked like blood on polished metal. 
They went down between the rows of boats, and the noises of the town grew fainter and fainter. When, finally, they arrived at their favourite restaurant, she untied her hat and they stepped out of the boat on to their island. They went into a small cafe, with dark fishing-nets hung up at the door, and sat themselves down in the low-ceilinged room. They ate small fried fish, followed by cherries and cream, and then went and sat on the grass.

Charles categorically refused to disturb her. She insisted. It was a veritable battle of politeness. Finally, she exclaimed, "Not another word, please! I'm leaving!"

"How kind you are!" he said, kissing her on the forehead.

The next morning, she left for Rouen by stagecoach to consult Monsieur Léon. She stayed there for three days. They were three wonderful days. They lodged near the port at the Hôtel de Boulogne, where they lived peacefully, with the curtains drawn, the doors locked, the floor strewn with flowers, and where iced drinks were brought to them every morning. Towards evening, they would take a boat to dine on an island. As they left the city, smoke rose from the trees, and the glowing sun, reflecting off the oily water of the harbor, resembled blood on polished metal. They stepped off the boat between the rows of vessels, and the sounds of the city gradually faded away. When they finally arrived at their favorite restaurant, she took off her hat, and they disembarked on their island. They entered a small café, its door adorned with dark fishing nets, and settled into the low-ceilinged room. They ate small fried fish, followed by cherries in cream, and then went to sit on the grass.

Schnauzer Dogs

There are three sizes of Schnauzer dog.
The two smaller sizes first came to England over 50 years ago, but the Giant Schnauzer has not been here very long. The name Giant is a good one because the dogs are 65 to 67.5 cm high.
All the dogs have long hair, which should be cut quite often. Most smaller Schnauzers are grey in colour, but the Giant Schnauzer is usually black.
Schnauzers come from Germany, where farmers use the dogs to help them with their sheep, and they are also used by the police, because Schnauzer dogs are very intelligent.
A Schnauzer makes a nice family dog. It is friendly and very good with young children.

Science flying in the face of gravity

Journalist Tom Mumford joins students using weightlessness to test their theories.

It looked like just another aircraft from the outside. The pilot told his young passengers that it was built in 1964, a Boeing KC-135 refuelling tanker, based on the Boeing 707 passenger craft.
But appearances were deceptive and the 13 students from Europe and America who boarded were in for the flight of their lives. Inside, it had become a long white tunnel.
There were almost no windows, but it was eerily illuminated by lights along the padded walls. Most of the seats had been ripped out, apart from a few at the back, where the pale-faced, budding scientists took their places with the air of condemned men.
For 12 months, they had competed with other students from across the continent to participate in the flight. The challenge, offered by the European Space Agency, had been to suggest imaginative experiments to be conducted in weightless conditions.
Those with the best ideas won a place on this unusual flight, which is best described as the most extraordinary roller-coaster ride yet devised. For the next two hours the Boeing's flight would resemble that of an enormous bird which had lost its reason, shooting upwards towards the heavens before hurtling towards Earth.
The intention was to achieve a kind of state of grace at the top of each curve. As the pilot cuts the engines at 3,000 metres, the aircraft throws itself still higher by virtue of its own momentum before gravity takes over and it plummets earthwards again.
In the few silent seconds between ascending and falling, the aircraft and everything inside it become weightless, and the 13 students would, in theory, feel themselves closer to the moon than the Earth. The aircraft took off smoothly enough, but any lingering illusions the young scientists and I had that we were on anything like a scheduled passenger service were quickly dispelled when the pilot put the Boeing into a 45-degree climb which lasted around 20 seconds. The engines strained wildly, blood drained from our heads, and bodies were scattered across the cabin floor.
Then the engines cut out and the transition to weightlessness was nearly instantaneous. For 20 seconds we conducted a ghostly dance in the unreal silence:the floor had become a vast trampoline, and one footstep was enough to launch us headlong towards the ceiling.
We floated aimlessly; the idea of going anywhere was itself confusing. Left or right, up or down, no longer had any meaning. Only gravity, by rooting us somewhere, permits us to appreciate the possibility of going somewhere else.
After ten seconds of freefall descent, the pilot pulled the aircraft out of its nose dive. The return of gravity was less immediate than its loss, but was still sudden enough to ensure that some of the students came down with a bump.
Our first curve completed, there were those who turned green at the thought of the 29 to follow. Thirty curves added up to ten minutes 'space time’ for experiments and the Dutch students were soon studying the movements of Leonardo, their robotic cat, hoping to discover how it is that cats always land on their feet.
At the appropriate moment the device they had built to investigate this was released, floating belly-up, and one of the students succeeded in turning it belly-down with radio-controlled movements. The next curve was nearly its last, however, when another student landed on top of it during a less well managed return to gravitational pull.
Next to the slightly stunned acrobatic robocat, a German team from the University of Aachen investigated how the quality of joins in metal is affected by the absence of gravity, with an eye to the construction of tomorrow's space stations.
Another team of students, from Utah State University, examined the possibility of creating solar sails from thin liquid films hardened in ultra-violet sunlight. Their flight was spent attempting to produce the films under microgravity. They believe that once the process is perfected, satellites could be equipped with solar sails that use the sun's radiation just as a yacht's sails use the wind. 
After two hours spent swinging between heaven and Earth, that morning’s breakfast felt unstable, but the predominant sensation was exhilaration, not nausea.
This was a feeling that would stay with us for a long time. ‘It was an unforgettable experience,’ said one of the students. 'I was already aiming to become an astronaut, but now I want to even more.’

La science défiant la gravité

Le journaliste Tom Mumford accompagne des étudiants qui utilisent l'apesanteur pour tester leurs théories.

De l'extérieur, l'appareil ressemblait à n'importe quel autre. Le pilote expliqua à ses jeunes passagers qu'il s'agissait d'un ravitailleur Boeing KC-135, construit en 1964 et dérivé du Boeing 707.

Mais les apparences étaient trompeuses et les treize étudiants européens et américains qui embarquèrent s'apprêtaient à vivre le vol de leur vie. À l'intérieur, l'espace s'était transformé en un long tunnel blanc.

Il n'y avait presque pas de hublots, mais l'intérieur était étrangement éclairé par des lumières le long des parois capitonnées. La plupart des sièges avaient été arrachés, à l'exception de quelques-uns au fond, où les jeunes scientifiques, le visage pâle, prirent place avec l'air de condamnés.

Pendant douze mois, ils avaient concouru avec d'autres étudiants de tout le continent pour participer à ce vol. Le défi, lancé par l'Agence spatiale européenne, consistait à proposer des expériences originales à mener en apesanteur. Ceux qui avaient les meilleures idées gagnèrent une place à bord de ce vol insolite, que l'on pourrait décrire comme les montagnes russes les plus extraordinaires jamais conçues. Pendant les deux heures suivantes, le vol du Boeing allait ressembler à celui d'un oiseau gigantesque ayant perdu la raison, s'élançant vers le ciel avant de plonger vers la Terre.

L'objectif était d'atteindre une sorte d'état de grâce au sommet de chaque virage. Lorsque le pilote coupa les moteurs à 3 000 mètres, l'appareil se propulsa encore plus haut grâce à son élan avant que la gravité ne reprenne le dessus et qu'il ne retombe sur Terre.

Dans les quelques secondes de silence entre la montée et la descente, l'avion et tout ce qu'il contenait devinrent en apesanteur, et les 13 étudiants allaient, en théorie, se sentir plus proches de la Lune que de la Terre. L'avion décolla en douceur, mais les dernières illusions que les jeunes scientifiques et moi-même pouvions encore nourrir quant à la nature d'un vol commercial régulier furent rapidement dissipées lorsque le pilote amorça une montée à 45 degrés qui dura une vingtaine de secondes. Les moteurs s'affolaient, le sang nous quittait la tête, et nos corps étaient éparpillés sur le plancher de la cabine.

Puis les moteurs s'arrêtèrent et la transition vers l'apesanteur fut quasi instantanée. Pendant vingt secondes, nous avons exécuté une danse fantomatique dans le silence irréel : le sol était devenu un immense trampoline, et un seul pas suffisait à nous propulser la tête la première vers le plafond.

Nous flottions sans but ; l'idée même d'aller quelque part était déroutante. Gauche ou droite, haut ou bas, tout cela n'avait plus aucun sens. Seule la gravité, en nous ancrant quelque part, nous permettait d'envisager la possibilité d'aller ailleurs.

Après dix secondes de chute libre, le pilote redressa l'avion. Le retour de la gravité fut moins immédiat que sa disparition, mais suffisamment brutal pour que certains élèves retombent avec un choc.

Notre premier virage terminé, certains étaient déjà pris de vertige à l'idée des vingt-neuf suivants. Trente courbes, soit dix minutes de « temps spatial » pour leurs expériences, ont permis aux étudiants néerlandais d'étudier les mouvements de Leonardo, leur chat robotique, dans l'espoir de comprendre comment les chats retombent toujours sur leurs pattes.

Au moment opportun, le dispositif qu'ils avaient construit pour cette étude fut lâché, flottant sur le dos, et l'un des étudiants parvint à le retourner grâce à une commande radio. La courbe suivante faillit être la dernière, lorsqu'un autre étudiant atterrit dessus lors d'une tentative de retour à la gravité terrestre un peu mal maîtrisée.

À côté du chat robotique acrobatique, légèrement étourdi, une équipe allemande de l'Université d'Aix-la-Chapelle étudiait l'influence de l'absence de gravité sur la qualité des assemblages métalliques, en vue de la construction des futures stations spatiales.

Une autre équipe d'étudiants, de l'Université d'État de l'Utah, examinait la possibilité de créer des voiles solaires à partir de films liquides minces durcis par les rayons ultraviolets du soleil. Leur vol fut consacré à tenter de produire ces films en microgravité. Ils pensent qu'une fois le procédé perfectionné, les satellites pourraient être équipés de voiles solaires utilisant le rayonnement du soleil, à l'instar des voiles d'un yacht qui utilisent le vent.

Après deux heures passées à osciller entre ciel et terre, le petit-déjeuner de ce matin-là nous parut étrange, mais la sensation dominante était l'exaltation, et non la nausée.

Ce sentiment allait nous accompagner longtemps. « C'était une expérience inoubliable », confia l'un des étudiants. « Je rêvais déjà de devenir astronaute, mais maintenant, j'en ai encore plus envie. »

He started walking down to the village. It was difficult because he was very tired. He went carefully because he didn't want to fall again. By the end of the day he was at the river, and he stopped for a drink. 
There were beautiful flowers near the river. 'This is a lovely place,' Nunez thought. There were a lot of small houses in the centre of the village. They looked very strange to him, because they didn't have any windows. 
He could see men and women at work in the village. Some were in the fields with their children. He could see gardens near the houses and there were fine vegetables in them. When Nunez was near the village, he shouted to some men. 
'Hello!' he shouted. 'Hello ... hello!' and he waved his arms. The men heard him and they turned their heads. They looked one way, and then the other way. They looked past Nunez, but they didn't look at him. 'Why can't they see me?' he thought. 
Nunez moved nearer and shouted again. He was now quite near three men. He waved again, but they didn't wave back to him. 'What's wrong with them?' he thought. 'Are they blind?' He walked down to the men, and then he saw their faces. 
He was right - the men were all blind. They had no eyes. 'Who is this?' one man asked his friend. 'A man? Or is it a spirit?' 'It's a man,' said the second man. 'I think it's a man.'

Life was getting out of hand

Susan Harr unplugs her gadgets and rediscovers the joys of manual labour.

Everyone is in love with technology. It gives us all those marvellous gadgets that make life easier and leave us so much more time to do other things. A gradual, though not particularly subtle, form of brainwashing has persuaded us that technology rules, and that it is OK.
These implications are obvious. The movement of my fingers uses nothing from the previous power supply being eaten up by our greedy race. A craft executed by hand does not pollute the environment.
However, a recent unhappy experience with my malfunctioning word processor -
a £48 call-out fee, a labour charge of £15 per quarter of an hour, plus parts and replacements costs - has confirmed a suspicion that gadgets are often not worth the expense or the trouble. Are we as dependent on technology as we imagine? Bit by bit, I have been letting the household technology fall by the wayside as its natural and often short life expires.
This makes me wonder just what 'time' technology gives us. The time to take up more activities for which we must buy more gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts: but I think they are conning us.
So when the thing started making curious noises, which continued even when it was disconnected by a puzzled service agent, I abandoned it to the backyard, where it whispers damply to itself like some robot ghost.
I am not tied to a noisy, whirring machine, with my head bent and my back turned on the world, and I can take my time over the garment. In any case, I was always slightly alarmed by those electric machines that dash across the fabric towards your fingers. Best of all, I can pop the whole lot into a carrier bag and take it with me wherever I go.
Of course, there are some gadgets I would not like to be without. A year living without a washing machine convinced me of the value of the electric washtub. But there are others whose loss has brought unexpected delight. Feeling that we were becoming too apt to collapse in front of the television, or slot in a video, I sent back the rented colour equipment and we returned to the small black-and-white portable.
It is a real strain on the eyes and concentrates the mind on what is really worth watching. We now spend a lot more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, talking or pursuing other hobbies.
One of these, in my own case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that went by the board. My old Singer sewing machine is now an ornamental plant table, and as l cannot afford to replace it, I have taken to sewing by hand.
We have come to believe that we could not do without it, and if we do resist the notion that our lives would be unmanageable without the appliances of science we certainly do not want to relinquish them. Pity the generations whose lives were blighted by tedious and blister inducing toil. Even our brains are relieved of exertion by computers that not only perform miraculous calculations with amazing speed but now provide entertainment.
In fact, the time I now spend placidly stitching is anything but tedious, and the advantages are numerous. For a start, I can sew and listen to the radio - another rediscovered pleasure - or I can talk with family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch the programmes I do want to see on television, and alleviate my puritanical guilt at sitting in front of the box by doing something useful at the same time. And what a lovely, cosy feeling it is to sit by the fire and sew with a pot of tea for company.
Quite wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of the women who sewed elaborate garments, robes, linen and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the strain on the eyes and so on. 
There is a wonderfully soothing quality about executing a craft by hand, a great satisfaction in watching one's work become neater, more assured. I find things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows down to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th century life the need to rush to finish an activity so that I can rush to the next.
Meanwhile I have regained control of my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and daydream while doing the washing up agreeable, if temporarily forgotten, activity.
The result of all this brooding is that I now prowl the house with a speculative eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, that powered lawnmower? Come to think of it, we could save an awful lot of money by doing without electric lights!

La vie devenait incontrôlable.

Susan Harr débranche ses appareils et redécouvre les joies du travail manuel.

Nous sommes tous fascinés par la technologie. Elle nous offre tous ces merveilleux gadgets qui nous facilitent la vie et nous libèrent du temps pour d'autres activités. Une forme progressive, quoique peu subtile, de manipulation mentale nous a persuadés que la technologie règne en maître, et que c'est acceptable.

Les conséquences sont évidentes. Le mouvement de mes doigts ne consomme aucune énergie de la précédente source d'énergie engloutie par notre société avide. Un travail manuel ne pollue pas l'environnement.

Cependant, une récente mésaventure avec mon traitement de texte défectueux –

48 £ de frais de déplacement, 15 £ de main-d'œuvre par quart d'heure, sans compter le coût des pièces et des remplacements – a confirmé mon intuition : les gadgets ne valent souvent ni la dépense ni les ennuis. Sommes-nous aussi dépendants de la technologie que nous le pensons ? Petit à petit, je me débarrasse des appareils électroniques domestiques, leur durée de vie, souvent courte, arrivant à son terme. Cela me fait me demander quel « temps » la technologie nous offre réellement. Le temps de nous adonner à de nouvelles activités qui nécessitent l'achat de nouveaux gadgets ? Si c'est le cas, chapeau aux experts en marketing : mais je pense qu'ils nous mènent en bateau.

Alors, quand l'appareil a commencé à émettre des bruits étranges, qui ont persisté même après avoir été débranché par un technicien perplexe, je l'ai abandonné dans le jardin, où il murmure doucement, tel un fantôme robotique.

Je ne suis plus cloué à une machine bruyante et vrombissante, la tête penchée et le dos tourné au monde, et je peux prendre mon temps pour laver mon vêtement. De toute façon, j'ai toujours été un peu inquiet face à ces machines électriques qui filent sur le tissu vers vos doigts. Le mieux, c'est que je peux tout ranger dans un sac et l'emporter partout avec moi.

Bien sûr, il y a des gadgets dont je ne pourrais me passer. Une année sans machine à laver m'a convaincu de l'utilité de la machine à laver électrique. Mais il y en a d'autres dont l'absence m'a apporté un plaisir inattendu. Sentant que nous avions tendance à nous affaler trop souvent devant la télévision ou à regarder une vidéo, j'ai renvoyé le matériel couleur loué et nous sommes revenus à notre petit téléviseur portable en noir et blanc.

C'est un vrai soulagement pour les yeux et cela oblige à se concentrer sur ce qui mérite vraiment d'être vu. Nous passons maintenant beaucoup plus de temps à promener le chien (qui n'a jamais aimé la télévision de toute façon), à lire, à discuter ou à nous adonner à d'autres loisirs.

Pour ma part, je me suis mise à la couture ; et voilà un autre appareil que j'ai abandonné. Ma vieille machine à coudre Singer sert désormais de table d'appoint pour mes plantes, et comme je n'ai pas les moyens de la remplacer, je me suis mise à la couture à la main.

Nous avons fini par croire que nous ne pourrions pas nous en passer, et si nous refusons l'idée que nos vies seraient ingérables sans les outils de la science, nous ne voulons certainement pas y renoncer. Plaignons les générations dont la vie a été gâchée par un labeur fastidieux et épuisant. Même nos cerveaux sont soulagés par les ordinateurs qui, non seulement effectuent des calculs miraculeux à une vitesse incroyable, mais nous divertissent désormais.

En fait, le temps que je consacre maintenant à la couture, paisiblement, est tout sauf ennuyeux, et les avantages sont nombreux. Pour commencer, je peux coudre en écoutant la radio – un autre plaisir redécouvert – ou discuter avec ma famille et mes amis. S'il s'agit d'une tâche simple, je peux regarder les émissions que je souhaite voir à la télévision et apaiser ma culpabilité puritaine de rester assise devant le petit écran en faisant quelque chose d'utile en même temps. Et quel plaisir de s'installer près du feu et de coudre en compagnie d'une théière !

À tort, j'avais tendance à horrifier les femmes qui cousaient à la main des vêtements élaborés, des robes, du linge et des articles ménagers. J'imaginais ces longues heures, la fatigue oculaire, etc.

Il y a quelque chose de merveilleusement apaisant dans le travail manuel, une grande satisfaction à voir son ouvrage devenir plus soigné, plus sûr. Je constate que les choses se font étonnamment vite, et le rythme de la vie ralentit soudain au rythme de mes propres mains. Je suis également libéré de l'un des aspects les plus détestables de la vie de la fin du XXe siècle : le besoin de se dépêcher de terminer une activité pour pouvoir passer à la suivante.

Entre-temps, j'ai repris possession de mon évier, où je plonge mes mains dans la mousse et laisse vagabonder mes pensées tout en faisant la vaisselle – une activité agréable, quoique momentanément oubliée.

Le résultat de toutes ces rêveries est que je parcours maintenant la maison d'un œil critique. Avons-nous vraiment besoin du congélateur, du four à micro-ondes, de cette tondeuse électrique ? À bien y réfléchir, nous pourrions économiser une somme considérable en nous passant de l'électricité !
results.back_text:
Life was getting out of control.

Susan Harr unplugged her devices and rediscovered the joys of manual labor.

We are all fascinated by technology. It offers us all these wonderful gadgets that make our lives easier and free up time for other activities. A gradual, albeit unsubtle, form of mind control has persuaded us that technology reigns supreme, and that this is acceptable.

The consequences are obvious. The movement of my fingers consumes none of the energy previously devoured by our voracious society. Manual labor does not pollute the environment.

However, a recent mishap with my faulty word processor—

£48 in travel expenses, £15 per 15 minutes of labor, not including the cost of parts and replacements—confirmed my intuition: gadgets are often not worth the expense or the hassle. Are we as dependent on technology as we think? Little by little, I'm getting rid of my household electronics, their often short lifespans coming to an end. This makes me wonder what kind of "time" technology actually gives us. Time to indulge in new activities that require buying new gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts: but I think they're just pulling our leg.

So, when the appliance started making strange noises, which persisted even after a perplexed technician unplugged it, I abandoned it in the garden, where it murmurs softly, like a robotic ghost.

I'm no longer chained to a noisy, whirring machine, head bent and back to the world, and I can take my time washing my clothes. Anyway, I've always been a little uneasy about those electric machines that whiz across the fabric towards your fingers. The best part is that I can pack everything in a bag and take it everywhere with me.

Of course, there are some gadgets I couldn't live without. A year without a washing machine convinced me of the usefulness of an electric one. But there are others whose absence has brought me unexpected pleasure. Sensing that we were tending to slouch too often in front of the television or watching videos, I returned the rented color equipment and we went back to our small portable black and white TV.

It's a real relief for the eyes and forces you to focus on what's truly worth watching. We now spend much more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, chatting, or indulging in other hobbies.

For my part, I've taken up sewing; and that's another appliance I've abandoned. My old Singer sewing machine now serves as a side table for my plants, and since I can't afford to replace it, I've taken up hand sewing.

We have come to believe that we cannot do without them, and while we reject the idea that our lives would be unmanageable without the tools of science, we certainly don't want to give them up. Let us pity the generations whose lives were ruined by tedious and exhausting labor. Even our brains are relieved by computers, which not only perform miraculous calculations at incredible speed but also now entertain us.

In fact, the time I now devote to sewing, peacefully, is anything but boring, and the advantages are numerous. For starters, I can sew while listening to the radio—another rediscovered pleasure—or chat with family and friends. If it's a simple task, I can watch the programs I want to see on television and soothe my puritanical guilt about sitting in front of the screen by doing something useful at the same time. And what a pleasure it is to settle down by the fire and sew with a pot of tea!

I used to be wrong to horrify women who hand-sewed elaborate clothes, dresses, linens, and household items. I imagined the long hours, the eye strain, and so on.

There is something wonderfully soothing about handwork, a great satisfaction in seeing one's work become neater, more secure. I find that things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th-century life: the need to rush through one activity so I can move on to the next.

Meanwhile, I have reclaimed my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and let my thoughts wander while washing the dishes—a pleasant, if momentarily forgotten, activity.

The result of all this daydreaming is that I now scan the house with a critical eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave, that electric lawnmower? On second thought, we could save a considerable amount of money by doing without electricity!

Humphrey Partridge stood by the open door of the second bedroom. There was a smile on his lips as he looked at the empty bed.
'It's all right, Mother. Just the post,' Humphrey Partridge called from the bottom of the stairs, as he opened the door to the village postman.
'There's a package for you, Mr Partridge,' said Reg Carter, putting his hand on the door. 'From a garden centre, it says on it. Roses, I think.'
'Yes,' said Partridge, trying to close the door.
'It's the right time of year for planting roses, is it? November?'
'Yes.'
'How's your mother?' Reg went on. He was in no hurry to leave.
'Not so bad.'
'She never seems to get any letters, does she?'
'No. Well, when you reach that age, most of your friends are dead.'
'How old is she now?'
'She was eighty-six last July.'
'That's a good age. She doesn't go out much, does she?'
'No, not at all. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to leave to catch my train to work.'
Partridge closed the door and called up the stairs, 'Goodbye, Mother. I'm off to work.'
On his way to the station he stopped at the village shop to get his newspaper.
'Good morning,' said Mr Denton, the shopkeeper. 'How's the old lady?'
'Oh, not too bad, thank you - for her age, that is.'
'Oh, Mr Partridge,' said Mrs Denton, 'there's going to be a meeting in the village hall on Sunday, about-'
'I'm sorry, Mrs Denton, I don't like to leave my mother at weekends. I'm at work all week, you see.' He hurried away.

An awfully big adventure

The Taklamakan Desert in western China is one of the last unexplored places on earth. It is also one of the most dangerous. Charles Blackmore crossed it, and lived to tell the tale.

There are very few big adventures left and very few heroes. Children’s stories used to specialise in them — courageous explorers with sunburnt, leathery skin and eyes narrowed by straining to see into far horizons on their journeys into the unknown. These days you no longer find such people in fiction, let alone in real life. Or so I thought until I met Charles Blackmore.
Blackmore’s great adventure consisted of leading an expedition across one of the last unexplored places on earth, the Taklamakan Desert in western China. Its name means ‘once entered you never come out’, but local people call it the Desert of Death. He recalled the dangers and exhilaration of that amazing trek, in the calm atmosphere of his family home.
The team he led was composed of four Britons (one of them the party’s medical officer), an American photographer, four Chinese (all experts on the area), 30 camels and six camel handlers. It later turned out that the camel handlers had never worked with camels before, but were long-distance lorry drivers: a misunderstanding that could have cost everyone their lives and certainly jeopardised the expedition’s success. This mixed bunch set out to cross 1,200 kilometres of the world’s least hospitable desert and Charles Blackmore has written a mesmerising account of their journey. 
At the time, he was about to leave the Army after 14 happy years. He launched the expedition for fun, to fill a gap in his life, to prove something. ‘I had always assumed I’d spend my whole life in the Army. I had been offered promotion but suddenly I felt I wanted to see who Charles Blackmore really was, outside all that. It was a tremendous gamble. Tina, my wife, was very worried that I wouldn’t come back as nobody had ever done that route; we went into it blind. In the event, it took 59 days to cross from west to east, and the desert was very kind to us.’
Anyone reading his extraordinary account of that crossing will wonder at the use of the word ‘kind’. The team suffered unspeakable hardships: dysentery; extremes of temperature; severe thirst and dehydration; the loss of part of their precious water supply. ‘But’, Blackmore explains, ‘when we were at the limits of our own endurance and the camels had gone without water for seven days, we managed to find some. We didn’t experience the Taklamakan’s legendary sandstorms. And we never hit the raw, biting desert cold that would have totally immobilised us. That’s not to say that we weren’t fighting against hurdles the whole time. The fine sand got into everything, especially blisters and wounds. The high dunes were torture to climb, for us and for the heavily laden camels, which often rolled over onto us.
‘What drove me on more than anything else was the need to survive. We had no contingency plan. Neither our budget no time allowed one. No aircraft ever flew over us. Once we got into the sandhills we were completely on our own.
‘I knew I had the mental stamina for the trip but I was very scared of my physical ability to do it. I remember day one — we sat at the edge of the desert and it was such an inferno that you couldn’t breathe. I thought, “We’ve got to do it now!” At that moment I was a very scared man.’
If it was like that at the beginning, how did they feel towards the end? ‘When you’ve walked for 1,000 kilometres you’re not going to duck out. You’ve endured so much; you’ve got so much behind you. We were very thin, but very muscular and sinewy despite our physical exhaustion. My body was well-toned and my legs were like pistons. I could walk over anything.’
Midway through the book, Blackmore went on to describe lying in the desert gazing up at a full moon, thinking of his family. How conscious was he of the ordeal it must have been for them? ‘Inside me there’s someone trying to find peace with himself. When I have doubts about myself now, I go back to the image of the desert and think, well, we managed to pull that together. As a personal achievements, I feel prouder of that expedition than of anything else I’ve dine. Yet in terms of a lifetime’s achievement, I think of my family and the happiness we share — against that yardstick, the desert does not measure up, does not compare.’
Has Charles Blackmore found peace? ‘I yearn for the challenge — for the open spaces — the resolve of it all. We were buoyed up by the sense of purpose. I find it difficult now to be part of the uniformity of modern life.’

Une aventure extraordinaire

Le désert du Taklamakan, dans l'ouest de la Chine, est l'un des derniers endroits inexplorés de la planète. C'est aussi l'un des plus dangereux. Charles Blackmore l'a traversé et a survécu pour le raconter.

Les grandes aventures et les héros se font rares. Autrefois, les contes pour enfants en regorgeaient : de courageux explorateurs, la peau tannée par le soleil, les yeux plissés par l'effort pour scruter l'horizon lointain lors de leurs voyages vers l'inconnu. De nos jours, on ne trouve plus de tels personnages dans la fiction, et encore moins dans la réalité. Du moins, c'est ce que je croyais jusqu'à ma rencontre avec Charles Blackmore.

La grande aventure de Blackmore consistait à mener une expédition à travers l'un des derniers endroits inexplorés de la planète, le désert du Taklamakan, dans l'ouest de la Chine. Son nom signifie « une fois entré, on n'en sort jamais », mais les habitants l'appellent le Désert de la Mort. Il se souvenait des dangers et de l'exaltation de cette incroyable traversée, dans le calme de sa maison familiale. L'équipe qu'il dirigeait était composée de quatre Britanniques (dont le médecin de l'expédition), d'un photographe américain, de quatre Chinois (tous experts de la région), de 30 chameaux et de six chameliers. On découvrit plus tard que ces derniers n'avaient jamais travaillé avec des chameaux auparavant, mais étaient chauffeurs routiers : un malentendu qui aurait pu coûter la vie à tous et qui a certainement compromis le succès de l'expédition. Ce groupe hétéroclite s'est lancé à la traversée de 1 200 kilomètres du désert le plus inhospitalier du monde, et Charles Blackmore a écrit un récit captivant de leur périple.

À l'époque, il s'apprêtait à quitter l'armée après 14 années heureuses. Il a entrepris cette expédition par plaisir, pour combler un vide dans sa vie, pour faire ses preuves. « J'avais toujours pensé passer toute ma vie dans l'armée. On m'avait proposé une promotion, mais soudain, j'ai eu envie de découvrir qui était vraiment Charles Blackmore, en dehors de tout ça. C'était un pari risqué. » Tina, ma femme, était très inquiète à l'idée que je ne revienne pas, car personne n'avait jamais emprunté cette route ; nous nous y sommes lancés à l'aveuglette. Finalement, la traversée d'ouest en est a duré 59 jours, et le désert s'est montré très clément envers nous. Quiconque lira son récit extraordinaire de cette traversée s'étonnera de l'emploi du mot « clément ». L'équipe a enduré des épreuves indescriptibles : dysenterie, températures extrêmes, soif intense et déshydratation, et la perte d'une partie de leurs précieuses réserves d'eau. « Mais », explique Blackmore, « alors que nous étions à bout de forces et que les chameaux étaient privés d'eau depuis sept jours, nous avons réussi à en trouver. Nous n'avons pas subi les légendaires tempêtes de sable du Taklamakan. Et nous n'avons jamais été confrontés au froid mordant du désert qui nous aurait totalement immobilisés. Cela ne veut pas dire que nous n'avons pas dû lutter contre des obstacles tout au long du voyage. Le sable fin s'est infiltré partout, notamment dans les ampoules et les plaies. » L'ascension des hautes dunes était un véritable supplice, pour nous comme pour les chameaux lourdement chargés, qui se renversaient souvent sur nous.

« Ce qui me motivait plus que tout, c'était la nécessité de survivre. Nous n'avions aucun plan de secours. Ni notre budget, ni le temps ne nous le permettaient. Aucun avion ne nous a survolés. Une fois arrivés dans les dunes, nous étions complètement livrés à nous-mêmes.

« Je savais que j'avais la force mentale pour ce voyage, mais j'avais très peur de ma capacité physique à le mener à bien. Je me souviens du premier jour : nous étions assis au bord du désert et c'était une telle fournaise qu'on ne pouvait plus respirer. Je me suis dit : « Il faut qu'on le fasse maintenant ! » À ce moment-là, j'étais terrifié. » Si c'était ainsi au début, comment se sentaient-ils à la fin ? « Après avoir marché 1 000 kilomètres, on ne va pas abandonner. On a tellement enduré ; on a tellement de choses derrière soi. Nous étions très maigres, mais très musclés et nerveux malgré notre épuisement physique. » Mon corps était musclé et mes jambes étaient comme des pistons. Je pouvais marcher sur n'importe quoi. Au milieu du livre, Blackmore décrit un moment passé allongé dans le désert, contemplant la pleine lune et pensant à sa famille. À quel point était-il conscient de l'épreuve qu'ils avaient dû traverser ? « Au fond de moi, il y a quelqu'un qui cherche la paix intérieure. Quand je doute de moi-même, je repense à l'image du désert et je me dis : nous avons réussi à surmonter cette épreuve. Sur le plan personnel, je suis plus fier de cette expédition que de tout ce que j'ai pu manger. Mais si l'on considère l'accomplissement d'une vie, je pense à ma famille et au bonheur que nous partageons – à cette échelle, le désert ne fait pas le poids, il ne peut rivaliser. »

Charles Blackmore a-t-il trouvé la paix ? « J'aspire au défi, aux grands espaces, à la détermination qui nous animait. Nous étions portés par ce sentiment d'utilité. J'ai du mal aujourd'hui à me conformer à l'uniformité de la vie moderne. »

I could walk on anything. In the middle of the book, Blackmore describes a moment spent lying in the desert, contemplating the full moon and thinking about his family. How aware was he of the ordeal they had gone through? “Deep down, there’s someone searching for inner peace. When I doubt myself, I think back to the image of the desert and tell myself: we managed to overcome that challenge. On a personal level, I’m prouder of that expedition than of anything I ate. But if you consider the accomplishments of a lifetime, I think of my family and the happiness we share—on that scale, the desert doesn’t measure up, it can’t compete.”

Has Charles Blackmore found peace? “I yearn for the challenge, the wide-open spaces, the determination that drove us. We were driven by that sense of purpose. I find it hard today to conform to the uniformity of modern life.”
