L'ébéniste

Charles Hurst gagne sa vie grâce à des meubles d'une qualité exceptionnelle. Joanna Watt le rencontre.

Charles Hurst donne l'impression d'être un homme pressé. J'arrive à son atelier, niché sous une arche de chemin de fer dans l'est londonien, et suis accueillie par une poignée de main rapide et ces mots : « Eh bien, à vos marques ! » Difficile de dire immédiatement si cette brusquerie est sincère ou une façade dissimulant une certaine timidité. Mais un coup d'œil à l'atelier révèle que Hurst est manifestement occupé, et à juste titre, ne voulant pas perdre une minute.

L'espace voûté regorge de meubles à moitié finis et de planches de bois aux couleurs naturelles d'une incroyable variété. Hurst est ébéniste depuis dix ans et s'est forgé une excellente réputation. Son carnet de commandes est toujours plein pour plusieurs mois, bien qu'il ne fasse pas vraiment de publicité. Le bouche-à-oreille a fait son œuvre : si vous voulez une armoire, une table, une bibliothèque ou des meubles de cuisine de qualité, Hurst est l'homme qu'il vous faut.

Bien sûr, trouver un ébéniste n'est pas une tâche si ardue. Où que vous habitiez à la campagne, l'artisanat est bien vivant. Mais trouver un ébéniste qui se targue de fabriquer des meubles magnifiquement travaillés, aux lignes épurées et simples, est plus difficile. « Il y a peu de vrais ébénistes aujourd'hui. On se dit plutôt fabricant de meubles », constate Hurst avec lassitude. Artisan exigeant envers lui-même, il est constamment déçu par certains meubles contemporains. « Je suis sidéré par ce que certains fabricants de meubles osent faire, et attristé par ce que les gens sont prêts à accepter. » Il s'insurge contre les meubles de piètre qualité produits en masse et contre les artisans qui fabriquent des pièces médiocres.

Cette quête de perfection est manifestement la clé du succès de Hurst. Cela, et son talent. Cet homme ne cache pas ses capacités. En effet, son assurance décomplexée est aussi surprenante que son attitude abrupte au premier abord. « J'ai un don naturel exceptionnel », déclare-t-il d'un ton impassible. « J'ai toujours été doué pour la fabrication d'objets. » Sans cette pointe d'autodérision qui l'a envahi vers la fin de notre entretien, j'aurais cru sa vanité tout à fait sincère.

Hurst est autodidacte. Comment a-t-il donc appris son métier ? « J'ai posé les bonnes questions et j'ai tout appris sur le tas », dit-il nonchalamment. Presque toutes ses commandes proviennent de particuliers (« Avant, je faisais un peu de travail commercial pour des entreprises, mais c'était abrutissant »). Certains clients reviennent régulièrement. « On finit par décorer toute leur maison. C'est très gratifiant. » Mais il est assez honnête pour admettre que les relations avec les clients ne sont pas toujours un long fleuve tranquille. « Les clients les plus exaspérants sont ceux qui ne savent pas ce qu'ils veulent et qui changent d'avis trop tard… Mes clients préférés sont les plus exigeants. »

Si Hurst a toutes les raisons d'être fier de lui, il sait aussi faire l'éloge des autres, quand il le mérite. Avec une soudaine pointe de modestie, il déclare : « Il y a des gens bien meilleurs que moi. Je peux admirer d'autres personnes. Après tout, je n'ai pas été formé à Parnham » (la prestigieuse école de design de mobilier). Cependant, il critique sans relâche ces artisans qui « prétendent être des artistes et mettent un an à réaliser une seule pièce ». Il n'accorde que peu d'importance aux expositions de fin d'études, où les étudiants présentent leurs travaux mais tentent en même temps de « faire des déclarations de mode. Cela peut être prétentieux. Un meuble n'est pas fait pour affirmer une opinion. Il doit être quelque chose que les gens puissent réellement utiliser. »

Hurst est peut-être sûr de lui, voire brusque, mais on ne pourrait jamais le qualifier, lui ou son travail, de prétentieux. En effet, sa remarque finale témoigne d'une approche pragmatique et bienvenue de son métier et d'une humilité qui contraste étrangement avec son assurance habituelle. « Après tout, je ne fais que fabriquer des meubles », dit-il tandis que je m'en vais.

The Elephant Show 

by Daniel Allsop, age 14 

Last summer, I went to Thailand for a beach holiday with my family. One day, we took a trip to a park not far from our hotel. It had beautiful flower gardens but we were only interested in the elephant show. 
We went straight to a large square with seats on three sides. Three elephants came in with their keepers and stood in front of a large piece of white card. Each elephant was given a paintbrush and started to paint on its own card. From time to time, the keepers put a new brush full of paint into each elephant's trunk and took the old one away. Slowly, following their keepers' instructions, the elephants drew pictures on the cards. I couldn't believe what I was seeing! One picture showed a river, one a tree and the third a bunch of flowers. When the keepers held up the paintings, everyone wanted to buy one. We gave the elephants the bananas we brought for our lunch. 
Twenty years ago, elephants worked in the forest. Now, they no longer work there, but the cleverest of these animals live in special centres where visitors can watch them.

L'été dernier, je suis allé en Thaïlande en vacances à la plage avec ma famille. Un jour, nous avons visité un parc non loin de notre hôtel. Il y avait de magnifiques jardins fleuris, mais seul le spectacle des éléphants nous intéressait.

Paul Simon

Rock and roll in the 1950s was primarily a youth cult, but its lasting importance lay in the seismic impact it had on the middle class and the middle-aged. It also paved the way for the next generation of rock idols, who listened to it awestruck and aware that this strange, unsettling sound would somehow, irrevocably, be linked with their destinies.
For Paul Simon, as for other youngsters in the US, the chief opportunity for hearing this new and invigorating type of music that was sweeping the country was courtesy of Alan Freed's radio show, Moondog Rock'n'Roll Party. Freed's show was required listening for a whole generation of fledgling rock idols. Like the young John Lennon, 3,000 miles away in Liverpool, with his ear glued to Radio Luxembourg - the only European outlet for the new rock and roll - Paul Simon was fascinated by the sounds pouring from Freed's show, and prepared himself for the next big step for a rock and roll obsessed teenager, the switch from listening to others' music to making his own.

Snow

No path was visible, but I thought that I would be all right if I walked with due caution. The wind hammered down from the heights, knocking me over as I slid and slithered on the slippery ice. Suddenly the innocent-looking snow gave way beneath me. I dropped, startled, into a hole some four feet deep. The snow had formed a roof over the gap between two rocks, melting away to leave nothing but a thin crust through which I had plunged. I hauled myself out, shaken and unnerved, wondering what I would have done if the hole had been thirty feet deep. I sat back against the top of a pine tree that protruded from the snow to take stock of the situation. In an hour I had covered about half a mile. It was perfectly clear that I would have to abandon my plan.

Qualitative Research

There are now numerous books which attempt to give guidance to researchers about qualitative research. While much has been written about the collection of data, the books are often silent about the processes and procedures associated with data analysis. Indeed, much mystery surrounds the way researchers analyse their data. Accordingly, we invited a range of social scientists who have engaged in qualitative projects to discuss the approaches that they used. The idea was to share insight and understanding of the process of qualitative data analysis rather than to produce a guidebook for the intending researcher. Such a task involves a process of demystification, of making implicit procedures more explicit. While this may sound straightforward, we have found it far from simple. We have therefore given our contributors the opportunity to present their work in a range of styles, which include autobiographical narratives and more impersonal forms.

Neige

Aucun chemin n'était visible, mais je pensais que je m'en sortirais en marchant avec prudence. Le vent, violent, soufflait des hauteurs, me faisant tomber tandis que je glissais sur la glace. Soudain, la neige, d'apparence si inoffensive, céda sous mes pieds. Je tombai, surpris, dans un trou d'environ un mètre vingt de profondeur. La neige avait formé un toit au-dessus de l'espace entre deux rochers, fondant pour ne laisser qu'une fine croûte à travers laquelle j'avais plongé. Je me hissai hors du trou, secoué et désemparé, me demandant ce que j'aurais fait s'il avait fait dix mètres de profondeur. Je me suis adossé à la cime d'un pin qui émergeait de la neige pour faire le point. En une heure, j'avais parcouru environ huit cents mètres. Il était évident que je devais renoncer à mon projet.

Recherche qualitative

De nombreux ouvrages tentent aujourd'hui de guider les chercheurs en recherche qualitative. Si la collecte de données a fait l'objet de nombreux écrits, les processus et procédures liés à leur analyse restent souvent muets. En effet, le processus d'analyse des données par les chercheurs demeure souvent mystérieux. C'est pourquoi nous avons invité divers spécialistes en sciences sociales ayant mené des projets qualitatifs à présenter les approches qu'ils ont utilisées. L'objectif était de partager des connaissances et une compréhension du processus d'analyse des données qualitatives, plutôt que de rédiger un guide pratique pour les futurs chercheurs. Une telle tâche implique un travail de démystification, visant à expliciter des procédures implicites. Si cela peut paraître simple, nous avons constaté que c'était loin d'être le cas. Nous avons donc donné à nos contributeurs la possibilité de présenter leurs travaux sous différents angles, allant du récit autobiographique à des formes plus impersonnelles.
results.back_text:
Paul Simon

The rock and roll of the 1950s was primarily a youth phenomenon, but its enduring importance lies in the profound impact it had on the middle class and older generations. It also paved the way for the next generation of rock idols, who listened to it with fascination, aware that this strange and unsettling sound would, in one way or another, be inextricably linked to their destinies.

For Paul Simon, as for many young Americans, the main opportunity to discover this new and exhilarating musical genre sweeping the country was Alan Freed's radio show, Moondog Rock 'n' Roll Party. This show was essential listening for an entire generation of young rock idols. Just like the young John Lennon, 5,000 kilometers away in Liverpool, his ear glued to Radio Luxembourg—the only European station broadcasting the new rock and roll—Paul Simon was captivated by the sounds emanating from Freed's show and was preparing to take the next step for a teenager passionate about rock and roll: moving from listening to other people's music to creating his own.

Snow

No path was visible, but I thought I could manage by walking carefully. The wind, fierce, blew from the heights, knocking me down as I slipped on the ice. Suddenly, the seemingly harmless snow gave way beneath my feet. I fell, surprised, into a hole about four feet deep. The snow had formed a roof over the gap between two rocks, melting to leave only a thin crust through which I plunged. I hauled myself out of the hole, shaken and bewildered, wondering what I would have done if it had been ten meters deep. I leaned against the top of a pine tree emerging from the snow to take stock of the situation. In one hour, I had covered about eight hundred meters. It was clear that I had to abandon my project.

Qualitative Research

Many books today attempt to guide researchers in qualitative research. While data collection has been the subject of much writing, the processes and procedures related to data analysis often remain unexplored. Indeed, the process of data analysis by researchers often remains mysterious. This is why we invited various social scientists who had conducted qualitative projects to present the approaches they used. The goal was to share knowledge and an understanding of the qualitative data analysis process, rather than to write a practical guide for future researchers. Such a task involves demystifying implicit procedures. While this may seem simple, we found it to be far from it. We therefore gave our contributors the opportunity to present their work from different angles, ranging from autobiographical narratives to more impersonal forms.

It's true - we're all getting too big for our boots
Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers teacher he wanted to join the navy when he left school. 'What do you want to be?' asked the teacher. 'The flagpole on a ship?' The teacher had a point - because Chris, though still only fourteen, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is Britain's tallest man.
Every decade, the average height of people in Europe grows another centimetre. Every year, more and more truly big people are born. Intriguingly, this does not mean humanity is producing a new super race. In fact, we are returning to what we were like as cavemen. Only now are we losing the effects of generations of poor diet - with dramatic effects. 'We are only now beginning to fulfil our proper potential,' says palaeontologist Professor Chris Stringer. 'We are becoming Cro-Magnons again - the people who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.'
For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a wide variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruits and berries, while men supplemented these with occasional kills of animals (a way of life still adopted by the world's few remaining tribes of hunter- gatherers). One research study found that they based their diet on 85 different wild plants, for example. Then about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented - with devastating consequences. Most of the planet's green places have been gradually taken over by farmers, with the result that just three carbohydrate-rich plants - wheat, rice and maize - provide more than half of the calories consumed by the human race today.
This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries we have lived on soups, porridges and breads that have left us underfed and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when they began to grow corn, healthy hunter-gatherers were turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did diseases. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, corn was a public health disaster, according to some anthropologists.
Nevertheless, from then on agriculture spread because a piece of farmed land could support ten times the number of people who had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people relying on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been tackled, even by the world's wealthier nations. Only in Europe, the US and Japan are diets again reflecting the richness of our ancestors' diets.
As a result, the average man in the US is now 179cm, in Holland 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, though not without its own problems. Heights may have risen, but the world has not moved on, it seems. A standard bed-length has remained at 190cm since 1860. Even worse, leg-room in planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than grown, while clothes manufacturers are constantly having to revise their range of products.
The question is: where will it all end? We cannot grow for ever. We must have some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of University, it could be as much as 193 cm - and we are likely to reach it some time this century.
However, scientists add one note of qualification. Individuals may be growing taller because of improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly rounder and taller - an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies are best at keeping in heat.) Since the climate warmed, we appear to have got slightly thinner and smaller, even when properly fed. And as the planet continues to heat up, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.

The Young Achiever of the Year

Kal Kaur Rai has always been interested in fashion and has just won the title of Young Achiever of the Year at the Asian Business Awards. Ever since she was a child, she has drawn clothes and designed patterns. She never told her hard-working parents, who own a supermarket, that she wanted to turn her hobby into a career. She thought they expected her to go into a more established business, so she went to university to do a management degree.

After university, she moved to London and worked in an advertising agency. She had to attend industry events but couldn't afford the designer clothes she liked. She started making skirts and tops for herself. When her friends saw her clothes, they asked her to make things for them. She then found a small shop in London willing to take her designs on a sale-or- return basis. They were very popular and nothing came back. This encouraged her to leave her advertising job, take out a PS20,000 loan and begin her own womenswear label.

Kal's parents were not angry about her career change and said they would support her, which really pleased her. Her clothes are now on sale in over 70 stores and her business has an income of over PS500,000. Her clothes appear in fashion magazines, she designs for pop stars and she has just gained public recognition by winning this award. Her business has come a long way and she knows she is extremely lucky. 'What I do is my hobby - and I get paid for it! But remember, I've worked hard for this.'

Most house burglaries happen between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m.,say the police.

'We will also tell you how to make your house safe,' Inspector Saunders said. 'This kind of help costs nothing.'

results.src_text:
Life was getting out of hand

Susan Harr unplugs her gadgets and rediscovers the joys of manual labour.

Everyone is in love with technology. It gives us all those marvellous gadgets that make life easier and leave us so much more time to do other things. A gradual, though not particularly subtle, form of brainwashing has persuaded us that technology rules, and that it is OK.
These implications are obvious. The movement of my fingers uses nothing from the previous power supply being eaten up by our greedy race. A craft executed by hand does not pollute the environment.
However, a recent unhappy experience with my malfunctioning word processor -
a PS48 call-out fee, a labour charge of PS15 per quarter of an hour, plus parts and replacements costs - has confirmed a suspicion that gadgets are often not worth the expense or the trouble. Are we as dependent on technology as we imagine? Bit by bit, I have been letting the household technology fall by the wayside as its natural and often short life expires.
This makes me wonder just what 'time' technology gives us. The time to take up more activities for which we must buy more gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts: but I think they are conning us.
So when the thing started making curious noises, which continued even when it was disconnected by a puzzled service agent, I abandoned it to the backyard, where it whispers damply to itself like some robot ghost.
I am not tied to a noisy, whirring machine, with my head bent and my back turned on the world, and I can take my time over the garment. In any case, I was always slightly alarmed by those electric machines that dash across the fabric towards your fingers. Best of all, I can pop the whole lot into a carrier bag and take it with me wherever I go.
Of course, there are some gadgets I would not like to be without. A year living without a washing machine convinced me of the value of the electric washtub. But there are others whose loss has brought unexpected delight. Feeling that we were becoming too apt to collapse in front of the television, or slot in a video, I sent back the rented colour equipment and we returned to the small black-and-white portable.
It is a real strain on the eyes and concentrates the mind on what is really worth watching. We now spend a lot more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, talking or pursuing other hobbies.
One of these, in my own case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that went by the board. My old Singer sewing machine is now an ornamental plant table, and as l cannot afford to replace it, I have taken to sewing by hand.
We have come to believe that we could not do without it, and if we do resist the notion that our lives would be unmanageable without the appliances of science we certainly do not want to relinquish them. Pity the generations whose lives were blighted by tedious and blister inducing toil. Even our brains are relieved of exertion by computers that not only perform miraculous calculations with amazing speed but now provide entertainment.
In fact, the time I now spend placidly stitching is anything but tedious, and the advantages are numerous. For a start, I can sew and listen to the radio - another rediscovered pleasure - or I can talk with family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch the programmes I do want to see on television, and alleviate my puritanical guilt at sitting in front of the box by doing something useful at the same time. And what a lovely, cosy feeling it is to sit by the fire and sew with a pot of tea for company.
Quite wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of the women who sewed elaborate garments, robes, linen and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the strain on the eyes and so on. 
There is a wonderfully soothing quality about executing a craft by hand, a great satisfaction in watching one's work become neater, more assured. I find things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows down to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th century life the need to rush to finish an activity so that I can rush to the next.
Meanwhile I have regained control of my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and daydream while doing the washing up agreeable, if temporarily forgotten, activity.
The result of all this brooding is that I now prowl the house with a speculative eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, that powered lawnmower? Come to think of it, we could save an awful lot of money by doing without electric lights!

La vie devenait incontrôlable.

Susan Harr débranche ses appareils et redécouvre les joies du travail manuel.

Nous sommes tous fascinés par la technologie. Elle nous offre tous ces merveilleux gadgets qui nous facilitent la vie et nous libèrent du temps pour d'autres activités. Une forme progressive, quoique peu subtile, de manipulation mentale nous a persuadés que la technologie règne en maître, et que c'est acceptable.

Les conséquences sont évidentes. Le mouvement de mes doigts ne consomme aucune énergie de la précédente source d'énergie engloutie par notre société avide. Un travail manuel ne pollue pas l'environnement.

Cependant, une récente mésaventure avec mon traitement de texte défectueux –

48 £ de frais de déplacement, 15 £ de main-d'œuvre par quart d'heure, sans compter le coût des pièces et des remplacements – a confirmé mon intuition : les gadgets ne valent souvent ni l'argent ni les tracas. Sommes-nous aussi dépendants de la technologie que nous le pensons ? Petit à petit, j'ai laissé tomber les appareils électroniques de la maison, leur durée de vie naturelle, souvent courte, arrivant à son terme.

Cela me pousse à me demander quel « temps » la technologie nous offre réellement. Est-ce le moment de se lancer dans de nouvelles activités qui nécessitent l'achat de gadgets supplémentaires ? Si oui, chapeau aux experts en marketing ! Mais je pense qu'ils nous mènent en bateau.

Alors, quand l'appareil a commencé à émettre des bruits étranges, qui ont persisté même après avoir été débranché par un technicien perplexe, je l'ai abandonné dans le jardin, où il murmure doucement, tel un fantôme de robot.

Je ne suis plus cloué à une machine bruyante et vrombissante, la tête baissée et le dos tourné au monde, et je peux prendre mon temps pour laver mon linge. De toute façon, j'ai toujours été un peu inquiet face à ces machines électriques qui filent sur le tissu vers vos doigts. Le mieux, c'est que je peux tout ranger dans un sac et l'emporter partout avec moi.

Bien sûr, il y a des gadgets dont je ne pourrais me passer. Une année sans machine à laver m'a convaincu de l'utilité de la machine à laver électrique. Mais il y en a d'autres dont l'absence m'a apporté un plaisir inattendu. Sentant que nous avions tendance à nous affaler trop souvent devant la télévision ou à regarder une vidéo, j'ai renvoyé le matériel couleur loué et nous sommes revenus à notre petit téléviseur portable en noir et blanc.

C'est un vrai soulagement pour les yeux et cela oblige à se concentrer sur ce qui mérite vraiment d'être vu. Nous passons maintenant beaucoup plus de temps à promener le chien (qui n'a jamais aimé la télévision de toute façon), à lire, à discuter ou à nous adonner à d'autres loisirs.

Pour ma part, je me suis mise à la couture ; et voilà un autre appareil que j'ai abandonné. Ma vieille machine à coudre Singer sert désormais de table d'appoint pour mes plantes, et comme je n'ai pas les moyens de la remplacer, je me suis mise à la couture à la main.

Nous avons fini par croire que nous ne pourrions pas nous en passer, et si nous refusons l'idée que nos vies seraient ingérables sans les outils de la science, nous ne voulons certainement pas y renoncer. Plaignons les générations dont la vie a été gâchée par un labeur fastidieux et épuisant. Même nos cerveaux sont soulagés par les ordinateurs qui, non seulement effectuent des calculs miraculeux à une vitesse incroyable, mais nous divertissent désormais.

En fait, le temps que je consacre maintenant à la couture, paisiblement, est tout sauf ennuyeux, et les avantages sont nombreux. Pour commencer, je peux coudre en écoutant la radio – un autre plaisir redécouvert – ou discuter avec ma famille et mes amis. S'il s'agit d'une tâche simple, je peux regarder les émissions que je souhaite voir à la télévision et apaiser ma culpabilité puritaine de rester assise devant le petit écran en faisant quelque chose d'utile en même temps. Et quel plaisir de s'installer près du feu et de coudre en compagnie d'une théière !

À tort, j'avais tendance à horrifier les femmes qui cousaient à la main des vêtements élaborés, des robes, du linge et des articles ménagers. J'imaginais ces longues heures, la fatigue oculaire, etc.

Il y a quelque chose de merveilleusement apaisant dans le travail manuel, une grande satisfaction à voir son ouvrage devenir plus soigné, plus sûr. Je constate que les choses se font étonnamment vite, et le rythme de la vie ralentit soudain au rythme de mes propres mains. Je suis également libéré de l'un des aspects les plus détestables de la vie de la fin du XXe siècle : le besoin de se dépêcher de terminer une activité pour pouvoir passer à la suivante.

Entre-temps, j'ai repris possession de mon évier, où je plonge mes mains dans la mousse et laisse vagabonder mes pensées tout en faisant la vaisselle – une activité agréable, quoique momentanément oubliée.

Le résultat de toutes ces rêveries est que je parcours maintenant la maison d'un œil critique. Avons-nous vraiment besoin du congélateur, du four à micro-ondes, de cette tondeuse électrique ? À bien y réfléchir, nous pourrions économiser une somme considérable en nous passant de l'électricité !
results.back_text:
Life was getting out of control.

Susan Harr unplugged her devices and rediscovered the joys of manual labor.

We are all fascinated by technology. It offers us all these wonderful gadgets that make our lives easier and free up time for other activities. A gradual, albeit unsubtle, form of mind control has persuaded us that technology reigns supreme, and that this is acceptable.

The consequences are obvious. The movement of my fingers consumes none of the energy previously devoured by our voracious society. Manual labor does not pollute the environment.

However, a recent mishap with my faulty word processor—

£48 in travel expenses, £15 per quarter hour of labor, not including the cost of parts and replacements—confirmed my intuition: gadgets are often not worth the money or the hassle. Are we as dependent on technology as we think? Little by little, I let go of the electronic devices in the house, their natural, often short, lifespan coming to an end.

This makes me wonder what "time" technology actually gives us. Is it time to embark on new activities that require buying more gadgets? If so, kudos to the marketing experts! But I think they're just leading us on.

So, when the appliance started making strange noises, which persisted even after being unplugged by a perplexed technician, I abandoned it in the garden, where it murmurs softly, like a robot ghost.

I'm no longer chained to a noisy, whirring machine, head down and back to the world, and I can take my time doing my laundry. Anyway, I've always been a little uneasy about those electric machines that whirl across the fabric towards your fingers. The best part is that I can pack everything in a bag and take it everywhere with me.

Of course, there are some gadgets I couldn't live without. A year without a washing machine convinced me of the usefulness of an electric one. But there are others whose absence has brought me unexpected pleasure. Sensing that we were tending to slouch too often in front of the television or watching videos, I returned the rented color equipment and we went back to our small portable black and white TV.

It's a real relief for the eyes and forces you to focus on what's truly worth watching. We now spend much more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, chatting, or indulging in other hobbies.

For my part, I've taken up sewing; and that's another appliance I've abandoned. My old Singer sewing machine now serves as a side table for my plants, and since I can't afford to replace it, I've taken up hand sewing.

We have come to believe that we cannot do without them, and while we reject the idea that our lives would be unmanageable without the tools of science, we certainly don't want to give them up. Let us pity the generations whose lives were ruined by tedious and exhausting labor. Even our brains are relieved by computers, which not only perform miraculous calculations at incredible speed but also now entertain us.

In fact, the time I now devote to sewing, peacefully, is anything but boring, and the advantages are numerous. For starters, I can sew while listening to the radio—another rediscovered pleasure—or chat with family and friends. If it's a simple task, I can watch the programs I want to see on television and soothe my puritanical guilt about sitting in front of the screen by doing something useful at the same time. And what a pleasure it is to settle down by the fire and sew with a pot of tea!

I used to be wrong to horrify women who hand-sewed elaborate clothes, dresses, linens, and household items. I imagined the long hours, the eye strain, and so on.

There is something wonderfully soothing about handwork, a great satisfaction in seeing one's work become neater, more secure. I find that things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th-century life: the need to rush through one activity so I can move on to the next.

Meanwhile, I have reclaimed my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and let my thoughts wander while washing the dishes—a pleasant, if momentarily forgotten, activity.

The result of all this daydreaming is that I now scan the house with a critical eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave, that electric lawnmower? On second thought, we could save a considerable amount of money by doing without electricity!

Enough Sleep?

Tiredness, it is often claimed, has become the modern condition. As the richer, busier countries have grown, so sleeplessness and anxiety have also grown in the popular psyche. Research in the USA has found 40 million Americans to be chronically affected, and some recent best-selling novels in Britain have featured insomniacs as protagonists, or sleep-research laboratories as their settings.
Part of this interest is in sleep in general: in its rhythms, its uses and in problems with sleeping. But a central preoccupation remains. 'People need more sleep,' says one leading sleep researcher. 'People cut back on sleep when they're busy. They get up too early to avoid the rush hour.'
Recently, a sleep researcher tried an experiment. He offered his subjects the opposite of the modern routine. 'I allowed them to sleep for up to 14 hours a night for a month. It took them three weeks to reach an equilibrium of eight-and-a-quarter hours. That indicates a great rebound of sleep - sleep that they hadn't been getting!'
In Europe, such propositions are perhaps most thoroughly tested in a small unassuming building on a university campus in the English Midlands. The university sleep research laboratory has investigated, among many subjects, the effects of fatigue on sailors, the effects of airpot noise on sleepers, and the dangers of motorway driving for flagging drivers.
For guinea pigs, they advertise in the student newspapers. Subjects are picked up by taxi, paid PS5 an hour, and asked to adjust their sleeping patterns according to instructions. Dr Louise Reyner provides reassurance: 'Some people are quite worried, because you're putting electrodes on their heads, and they think you can see what they're dreaming or thinking.'
In fact, the laboratory's interest is more physical. In a darkened room stands a motorway simulator, the front section of car facing a wide projection screen. The subjects are always told to arrive at 2pm, in the body's natural mid-afternoon lull, after a short night's sleep or no sleep at all. The projector is switched on and they are asked to drive, while answering questions. An endless road rolls ahead, sunlight glares; and the air is warm.
The young men all deny they are going to fall asleep. Dr Reyner has a video recording of one trying not to. At first the person at the wheel is very upright, wet and bleary eyes determinedly fixed on the windscreen. Then he begins to blink briefly, every now and again; then for longer, and more often, with a slight drop of the head. Each nod grows heavier than the last. The blinks become a 10-second blackout. Every time, he jerks awake as if nothing has happened. But the car, by the second or third occasion, has shot off the carriageway.
A coffee might have helped. Two cups, Dr Reyner says, even after no sleep at all, can make you a safe driver for half an hour or more. She recommends a whole basket of alertness products: tablets, energy drinks, caffeinated chewing gum. Shift workers, she is quite sure, could probably use them.
But apart from these findings, what else do know about human sleep with any kind of certainty? It is known that humans sleep, like other mammals, according to a daily cycle. Once asleep, they switch between four different stages of unconsciousness, from stage one sleep, the shallowest, to stage four, the deepest. When dreams occur, which is usually during the lightest sleep, the brain paralyses the body except for the hands and eyelids, thus preventing injuries.
Beyond this, certainties blur into theories. It is often suggested, for example, that sleep repairs body tissue, or restores muscles, or rests the frontal section of the brain that controls speech and creativity. But all of this may happen more quickly during relaxed wakefulness, so no one is really sure.
However, there is a strong degree of certainty among scientists that women seep for half an hour longer than men, and that older people require less sleep, though they don't know why. When asked what sleep is for, some sleep researchers reply in cosmic terms: 'Sleep is a tactic to travel through time without injury.'
Moreover, people may have had different sleep patterns in the past. A history professor has investigated nocturnal British life between 1500 and 1850 and discovered that sleeping routines were very different. People went to bed at nine or ten, then woke up after midnight, after what they called their 'first sleep', stayed awake for an hour, and then had their 'morning sleep'.
The interlude was a haven for reflection, remembering dreams, or even night-time thieving. The poorest were the greatest beneficiaries of this quiet time, fleetingly freed from the constraints and labours that ruled their day-time existence.
By the 17th century, however, as artificial light became more common, the rich began to switch to the more concentrated, and economically more efficient, mode of recuperation that we follow today. Two centuries later, the industrial revolution pushed back the dusk for everyone except some country-dwellers, by making most people work longer hours in lighted buildings.
Yet beyond Europe and America, the old pattern was widespread until quite recently, and according to a leading anthropologist, in some non-western settings there are still no rigid bedtimes. People go to bed for a few hours, and then get up again. The idea of a night's solid sleep does not apply. For certain tribal societies, human and animal noises and the need to supervise the fire and watch out for predators combine to make continuous sleep impossible. It seems that people all round the world are badly in need of sleep.

Un sommeil suffisant ?

On entend souvent dire que la fatigue est devenue le mal du pays. Avec la croissance des pays riches et trépidants, l'insomnie et l'anxiété se sont également ancrées dans la conscience collective. Aux États-Unis, une étude a révélé que 40 millions d'Américains souffrent d'insomnie chronique, et certains romans à succès britanniques récents mettent en scène des insomniaques comme protagonistes ou se déroulent dans des laboratoires de recherche sur le sommeil.

Cet intérêt porte en partie sur le sommeil en général : ses rythmes, ses fonctions et les troubles du sommeil. Mais une préoccupation centrale demeure. « Les gens ont besoin de plus de sommeil », affirme un éminent chercheur spécialisé dans le sommeil. « Ils réduisent leur temps de sommeil lorsqu'ils sont occupés. Ils se lèvent trop tôt pour éviter les embouteillages. »

Récemment, un chercheur a mené une expérience. Il a proposé à ses sujets un rythme de vie à l'opposé des habitudes modernes. « Je leur ai permis de dormir jusqu'à 14 heures par nuit pendant un mois. Il leur a fallu trois semaines pour atteindre un équilibre de huit heures et quart. » Cela indique un net regain de sommeil, un sommeil dont ils étaient privés !

En Europe, ces hypothèses sont sans doute testées le plus rigoureusement dans un petit bâtiment discret d'un campus universitaire des Midlands anglais. Le laboratoire de recherche sur le sommeil de l'université a étudié, entre autres, les effets de la fatigue sur les marins, les effets du bruit des avions sur les dormeurs et les dangers de la conduite sur autoroute pour les conducteurs somnolents.

Pour recruter des cobayes, des annonces sont publiées dans les journaux étudiants. Les participants sont pris en charge en taxi, rémunérés 5 £ de l'heure et invités à adapter leurs habitudes de sommeil selon les instructions. Le Dr Louise Reyner se veut rassurante : « Certaines personnes sont assez inquiètes, car on leur pose des électrodes sur la tête et elles pensent qu'on peut voir leurs rêves ou leurs pensées. »

En réalité, l'intérêt du laboratoire est plus concret. Dans une pièce obscure se trouve un simulateur d'autoroute, l'avant d'une voiture faisant face à un grand écran de projection. On demande toujours aux sujets d'arriver à 14 heures, au moment du coup de barre naturel de l'après-midi, après une courte nuit de sommeil, voire une nuit blanche. Le projecteur est allumé et on leur demande de conduire tout en répondant à des questions. Une route interminable défile devant eux, le soleil brille intensément et l'air est chaud.

Tous les jeunes hommes nient vouloir s'endormir. Le docteur Reyner possède un enregistrement vidéo de l'un d'eux qui tente de rester éveillé. Au début, le conducteur est très droit, les yeux humides et cernés, rivés sur le pare-brise. Puis il commence à cligner des yeux brièvement, de temps à autre ; puis plus longtemps, et plus souvent, en inclinant légèrement la tête. Chaque clignement est plus appuyé que le précédent. Les clignements se transforment en pertes de connaissance de dix secondes. À chaque fois, il se réveille en sursaut comme si de rien n'était. Mais à la deuxième ou troisième fois, la voiture a quitté la chaussée.

Un café aurait peut-être fait du bien. Selon le Dr Reyner, deux tasses de café, même après une nuit blanche, peuvent vous permettre de conduire en toute sécurité pendant une demi-heure, voire plus. Elle recommande toute une panoplie de produits stimulants : comprimés, boissons énergisantes, chewing-gum caféiné. Elle est persuadée que les travailleurs postés pourraient en bénéficier.

Mais au-delà de ces constats, que savons-nous avec certitude du sommeil humain ? On sait que les humains, comme les autres mammifères, dorment selon un cycle quotidien. Une fois endormis, ils alternent entre quatre stades d’inconscience, du stade 1, le plus léger, au stade 4, le plus profond. Lors des rêves, qui surviennent généralement pendant le sommeil léger, le cerveau paralyse le corps, à l’exception des mains et des paupières, évitant ainsi les blessures.

Au-delà de ces connaissances, les certitudes se confondent avec les théories. On suggère souvent, par exemple, que le sommeil répare les tissus, restaure les muscles ou repose la partie frontale du cerveau qui contrôle la parole et la créativité. Mais tout cela pourrait se produire plus rapidement pendant l’éveil détendu, et personne n’en est vraiment certain. Il existe cependant une quasi-certitude parmi les scientifiques que les femmes dorment une demi-heure de plus que les hommes et que les personnes âgées ont besoin de moins de sommeil, sans toutefois en connaître la raison. Interrogés sur le but du sommeil, certains chercheurs répondent en termes cosmiques : « Le sommeil est une stratégie pour voyager dans le temps sans se blesser. »

Par ailleurs, les habitudes de sommeil ont probablement varié par le passé. Un professeur d’histoire a étudié la vie nocturne britannique entre 1500 et 1850 et a découvert que les routines de sommeil étaient très différentes. On se couchait vers 21 h ou 22 h, puis on se réveillait après minuit, après ce que l’on appelait son « premier sommeil », on restait éveillé une heure, puis on faisait sa « sieste du matin ».

Cette parenthèse était un havre de paix propice à la réflexion, au souvenir des rêves, voire même au vol nocturne. Les plus pauvres étaient les principaux bénéficiaires de ce moment de calme, brièvement libérés des contraintes et des travaux qui rythmaient leur existence diurne. Au XVIIe siècle, avec la généralisation de l'éclairage artificiel, les plus aisés adoptèrent le mode de repos plus concentré et plus rentable que nous connaissons aujourd'hui. Deux siècles plus tard, la révolution industrielle repoussa l'heure du coucher pour tous, sauf pour certains ruraux, en obligeant la plupart des gens à travailler plus longtemps dans des bâtiments éclairés.

Pourtant, au-delà de l'Europe et de l'Amérique, ce mode de vie traditionnel resta largement répandu jusqu'à une époque récente. Selon un éminent anthropologue, dans certains contextes non occidentaux, il n'existe toujours pas d'heures de coucher fixes. On se couche quelques heures, puis on se relève. L'idée d'une nuit de sommeil réparateur n'est pas la norme. Dans certaines sociétés tribales, les bruits humains et animaux, la nécessité de surveiller le feu et de se prémunir contre les prédateurs rendent le sommeil continu impossible. Il semble que partout dans le monde, les gens aient cruellement besoin de sommeil.

No Title 

On the very last day of a bad year, I was leaning against a pillar in the Baltimore railway station, waiting to catch the 10.10 to Philadelphia. There were a lot more people waiting than I had expected. That airy, light, clean, polished feeling I generally got in the station had been lost. Elderly couples with matching luggage stuffed the benches, and swarms of college kids littered the floor with their bags.
A grey-haired man was walking around speaking to different strangers one by one. Well-off, you could tell: tanned skin, nice sweater, soft, beige car-coat. He went up to a woman sitting alone and asked her a question. Then he came over to a girl standing near me. She had long blond hair, and I had been thinking I wouldn't mind talking to her myself. The man said, 'Would you by any chance be travelling to Philadelphia?'
'Well, northbound, yes,' she said. 'But to Philadelphia?'
'No, New York, but I'll be ...'
'Thanks, anyway,' he said, and he moved toward the next bench.
Now he had my full attention. 'Ma'am,' I heard him ask an old lady, 'are you travelling to
Philadelphia?' When the woman told him, 'Wilmington,' he didn't say a thing, just marched on down the row to one of the matched-luggage couples. I straightened up from my pillar and drifted closer, looking toward the platform as if I had my mind on the train.
Well, I was going to Philadelphia. He could have asked me. I understood why he didn't, of course.
No doubt, I struck him as unreliable. He just glanced quickly at me and then swerved off toward the bench at the other end of the waiting area. By now he was looking seriously stressed. 'Please!' he said to a woman reading a book. 'Tell me you're going to Philadelphia!'
She lowered her book. She was thirtyish, maybe thirty-five - older than I was, anyhow. A school- teacher sort. 'Philadelphia?' she said. 'Why, yes, I am.'
'Then could I ask you a favour?'
I stopped several feet away and frowned down at my left wrist. (Never mind that I don't own a watch.) Even without looking, I could sense how she went on guard. The man must have sensed it too, because he said, 'Nothing too difficult, I promise!'
They were announcing my train now. People started moving toward Gate E, the older couples hauling their wheeled bags behind them like big pets on leashes. Next I heard the man talking. 'My daughter's flying out this afternoon for a study year abroad, leaving from Philadelphia. So I put her on a train this morning, stopping for groceries afterward, and came home to find my wife in a state. She hardly said "hello" to me. You see my daughter'd forgotten her passport. She'd telephoned home from the station in Philadelphia; didn't know what to do next.'
The woman clucked sympathetically. I'd have kept quiet myself. Waited to find out where he was heading with this.
'So I told her to stay put. Stay right there in the station, I said, and I would get somebody here to carry up her passport.'
A likely story! Why didn't he go himself, if this was such an emergency?
'Why don't you go yourself?' the woman asked him.
'I can't leave my wife alone for that long. She's in a wheelchair.'
This seemed like a pretty poor excuse, if you want my honest opinion. Also, it exceeded the amount of bad luck that one family could expect. I let my eyes wander toward the two of them. The man was holding a packet, not a plain envelope, which would have been the logical choice, but one of those padded envelopes the size of a paperback book. Aha! Padded! So you couldn't feel the contents! And from where I stood, it looked to be stapled shut besides. Watch yourself, lady, I said silently.

Sans titre

Le tout dernier jour d'une année catastrophique, j'étais appuyée contre un pilier de la gare de Baltimore, attendant le train de 10h10 pour Philadelphie. Il y avait bien plus de monde que prévu. Cette impression d'espace, de luminosité, de propreté et d'élégance que je ressentais habituellement dans la gare avait disparu. Des couples de personnes âgées, valises assorties à la main, encombraient les bancs, et des hordes d'étudiants jonchaient le sol de leurs sacs.

Un homme aux cheveux gris déambulait, abordant tour à tour des inconnus. Il semblait aisé : peau bronzée, joli pull, manteau beige souple. Il s'approcha d'une femme assise seule et lui posa une question. Puis il vint vers une jeune fille qui se tenait près de moi. Elle avait de longs cheveux blonds, et je m'étais dit que j'aurais bien aimé lui parler. L'homme lui demanda : « Vous iriez par hasard à Philadelphie ? »

« Eh bien, direction nord, oui », répondit-elle. « Mais jusqu'à Philadelphie ? » « Non, New York, mais je serai… »

« Merci quand même », dit-il en se dirigeant vers le banc suivant.

Il avait maintenant toute mon attention. « Madame », l’entendis-je demander à une vieille dame, « vous allez à Philadelphie ? » Quand elle lui répondit « Wilmington », il ne dit rien et continua son chemin jusqu’à l’un des couples de voyageurs avec leurs bagages assortis. Je me redressai et me rapprochai, le regard fixé sur le quai, comme si j’étais absorbée par le train.

Eh bien, j’allais à Philadelphie. Il aurait pu me le demander. Je comprenais parfaitement pourquoi il ne l’avait pas fait.

Sans doute, je lui avais paru peu fiable. Il me jeta un rapide coup d’œil puis se dirigea vers le banc à l’autre bout de la salle d’attente. Il avait l’air vraiment stressé. « S’il vous plaît ! » dit-il à une femme qui lisait un livre. « Dites-moi que vous allez à Philadelphie ! » Elle baissa son livre. Elle avait une trentaine d'années, peut-être trente-cinq – plus âgée que moi, en tout cas. Une institutrice, sans doute. « Philadelphie ? » demanda-t-elle. « Oui, c'est bien moi. »

« Puis-je vous demander un service ? »

Je m'arrêtai à quelques mètres et fronçai les sourcils en regardant mon poignet gauche. (Peu importe que je n'aie pas de montre.) Sans même la regarder, je sentis qu'elle se montrait sur ses gardes. L'homme dut le sentir aussi, car il dit : « Rien de bien compliqué, promis ! »

On annonçait mon train. Les gens commencèrent à se diriger vers la porte E, les couples âgés traînant leurs valises à roulettes comme de gros animaux en laisse. J'entendis ensuite l'homme parler. « Ma fille prend l'avion cet après-midi pour une année d'études à l'étranger, au départ de Philadelphie. Je l'ai donc mise dans un train ce matin, en m'arrêtant faire des courses ensuite, et en rentrant, j'ai trouvé ma femme dans un état lamentable. Elle m'a à peine adressé la parole. » « Voyez-vous, ma fille avait oublié son passeport. Elle avait téléphoné à la maison depuis la gare de Philadelphie ; elle ne savait plus quoi faire. »

La femme eut un petit cri de compassion. J'aurais fait de même. J'aurais attendu de voir où il voulait en venir.

« Alors je lui ai dit de rester où elle était. De rester là, dans la gare, lui ai-je dit, et que j'allais chercher quelqu'un pour lui apporter son passeport. »

Une histoire plausible ! Pourquoi n'y était-il pas allé lui-même, si c'était une telle urgence ?

« Pourquoi n'y allez-vous pas vous-même ? » lui demanda la femme.

« Je ne peux pas laisser ma femme seule aussi longtemps. Elle est en fauteuil roulant. »

Pour être honnête, ça me semblait une bien piètre excuse. De plus, c'était vraiment la goutte d'eau qui faisait déborder le vase. Mon regard se porta sur eux deux. L'homme tenait un paquet, non pas une simple enveloppe, ce qui aurait été logique, mais une de ces enveloppes matelassées de la taille d'un livre de poche. Ah ! Matelassée ! Vous ne pouviez donc pas sentir le contenu ! Et de là où j’étais, il semblait agrafé. Faites attention, madame, me dis-je intérieurement.
results.back_text:
Untitled

On the very last day of a disastrous year, I was leaning against a pillar in Baltimore's main train station, waiting for the 10:10 train to Philadelphia. It was much more crowded than I'd expected. The sense of space, light, cleanliness, and elegance I usually felt at the station was gone. Elderly couples, matching suitcases in hand, crowded the benches, and hordes of students littered the floor with their bags.

A gray-haired man was strolling about, approaching strangers one after another. He seemed well-to-do: tanned skin, a nice sweater, a soft beige coat. He approached a woman sitting alone and asked her a question. Then he came over to a young woman standing near me. She had long blond hair, and I'd thought to myself that I would have liked to talk to her. The man asked her, "Are you by any chance going to Philadelphia?" “Well, northbound, yes,” she replied. “But all the way to Philadelphia?” “No, New York, but I’ll be…”

“Thanks anyway,” he said, heading toward the next bench.

He now had my full attention. “Ma’am,” I heard him ask an elderly woman, “are you going to Philadelphia?” When she answered “Wilmington,” he said nothing and continued on to one of the couples with their matching luggage. I straightened up and moved closer, staring at the platform as if absorbed by the train.

Well, I was going to Philadelphia. He could have asked me. I completely understood why he hadn’t.

I must have seemed unreliable. He glanced at me quickly and then headed toward the bench at the far end of the waiting room. He looked genuinely stressed. “Please!” "He said to a woman who was reading a book. 'Tell me you're going to Philadelphia!' She lowered her book. She was about thirty, maybe thirty-five—older than me, anyway. A schoolteacher, probably. 'Philadelphia?' she asked. 'Yes, that's me.'

'Can I ask you a favor?'

I stopped a few feet away and frowned, looking at my left wrist. (It didn't matter that I wasn't wearing a watch.) Without even looking at her, I could tell she was on her guard. The man must have sensed it too, because he said, 'Nothing too complicated, I promise!'

My train was being announced. People started heading toward Gate E, elderly couples dragging their rolling suitcases like large animals on leashes. Then I heard the man speaking." “My daughter is flying out this afternoon for a year of study abroad, leaving from Philadelphia. So I put her on a train this morning, stopped to do some shopping afterward, and when I got home, I found my wife in a terrible state. She barely spoke to me.” “You see, my daughter had forgotten her passport. She had called home from the Philadelphia train station; she didn’t know what to do.”

The woman gave a small cry of sympathy. I would have done the same. I would have waited to see where he was going with this.

“So I told her to stay where she was. To stay there, in the station,” I told her, “and that I would get someone to bring her passport.”

A plausible story! Why hadn’t he gone himself if it was such an emergency?

“Why don’t you go yourself?” the woman asked him.

“I can’t leave my wife alone for that long. She’s in a wheelchair.”

To be honest, it seemed like a pretty lame excuse. Besides, it was really the last straw. My gaze fell on the two of them. The man was holding a package—not a simple envelope, which would have made sense, but one of those padded envelopes the size of a paperback book. Ah! Padded! So you couldn’t smell the contents! And from where I was, it looked like it was stapled shut. Be careful, madam, I thought to myself.

The history of horse racing 

From the first history books ever written, it is clear that horse racing has
always been an important sport. It started in Central Asia about 4,500 years ago and was a favourite sport in both Greek and Roman times. 
Modern horse racing began when Arab horses were brought to Europe in the 12th century. At first, races were long and between just two horses, but at the beginning of the 18th century this changed. Races became much shorter and had several horses running against each other. 
Today, horse racing is watched by more people than any other sport in the USA, except baseball. It is also very popular in other parts of the world.

results.src_text:
Sweden's Ice Hotel 

The village of Jukkasjarvi is in Swedish Lapland, and winter temperatures there can reach -40deg C. But 6,000 holidaymakers still go there annually, to visit what is probably Europe's most unusual accommodation. 
In this hotel you eat, drink, and sleep in rooms made of ice. If you want, you can even get married in one. The bar is ice too, and putting hot drinks on it is obviously not recommended! The bedrooms are around -4deg C, but fortunately guests are provided with special sleeping bags that will keep them warm in the coldest of temperatures. Suitable outdoor clothes can be supplied too, if needed. 
The hotel is never more than six months old because it melts in summer, and each winter it is rebuilt. Creating the hotel takes 10,000 tonnes of ice, plus 30,000 tonnes of snow.

results.title: 50.txt
results.src_text:
Hedgehogs 

A hedgehog is a small mammal characterised by the sharp spines which cover its body. The hedgehogs are found in many different parts of the world, none is native to either America or Australia. 
All species of hedgehog share the ability to roll into a tight ball when attacked, so that their spines point outwards. The effectiveness of this as a defence mechanism, depends, of course, on the number of spines the hedgehog has. Some desert hedgehogs have evolved to carry out weight, and consequently, they have fewer spines and are thus more likely to attempt to run into their attacker, using their ball rolling ability as a last resort. 
Hedgehogs are primarily nocturnal and sleep for much of the day, either under cover of bushes or in a hole in the ground. Despite the fact that all hedgehogs can hibernate, not all choose to do so; in suitable conditions, some will stay awake all year round.
results.tgt_text:
Les hérissons

Un hérisson est un petit mammifère caractérisé par les piquants acérés qui recouvrent son corps. On trouve des hérissons dans de nombreuses régions du monde ; aucun n’est originaire d’Amérique ni d’Australie.

Toutes les espèces de hérissons ont la capacité de se rouler en boule lorsqu’elles sont attaquées, leurs piquants pointant alors vers l’extérieur. L’efficacité de ce mécanisme de défense dépend, bien sûr, du nombre de piquants du hérisson. Certains hérissons du désert ont évolué pour supporter un poids important et, par conséquent, possèdent moins de piquants. Ils sont donc plus susceptibles de tenter de foncer sur leur agresseur, n’utilisant leur capacité à se rouler en boule qu’en dernier recours.

Les hérissons sont principalement nocturnes et dorment une grande partie de la journée, à l’abri des buissons ou dans un terrier. Bien que tous les hérissons puissent hiberner, certains ne le font pas ; dans des conditions favorables, certains restent actifs toute l’année.
results.back_text:
Hedgehogs

A hedgehog is a small mammal characterized by the sharp spines that cover its body. Hedgehogs are found in many parts of the world; none are native to the Americas or Australia.

All hedgehog species have the ability to roll into a ball when attacked, with their spines pointing outwards. The effectiveness of this defense mechanism depends, of course, on the number of spines the hedgehog has. Some desert hedgehogs have evolved to support significant weight and, consequently, have fewer spines. They are therefore more likely to try to charge at their attacker, using their ability to roll into a ball only as a last resort.

Hedgehogs are primarily nocturnal and sleep for much of the day, sheltered in bushes or in a burrow. Although all hedgehogs can hibernate, some do not; under favorable conditions, some remain active year-round.

results.src_text:
We are Talking Big Boots here. Really BIGTIME Boots.
I stood in my 800-dollar-each designer-label cowboy boots on the rocks of an old formation in the Arizona desert sand. Money no object. I wore the whole truly cowboy outfit and if you had the outfit you might be a cowboy. But I was not. It wasn't working. I squinted info the morning sun looking out at the Arizona mountains and I had to admit, I was not at home on the range,
Flying in from Denver just after dawn, I had the feeling that I just might pass far an ol' cowhand coming in from the sky. The feeling didn't last past the first real cowboy in the luggage hall of Phoenix airport. He was wearing a sweat-stained I-shirt, needed a shave, and was hoisting a dirty canvas bag off the conveyer belt when he caught sight of my brand new cowboy boots. He slowly raised one eyebrow and moved off out of the door without looking back.
There ought to be, somewhere, hanging in a closet, a suit of clothes an ex-racing driver can put on without feeling like he is from another planet. Something he could wear so that wherever he goes he doesn't get the feeling that everybody is talking another language and doing whatever they do at half speed. I liked, no, not liked... I flatout loved being a racing driver, driving racing cars. I am addicted to it and it is all I know how to do. But I don't do it any more. I couldn't if I wanted to. Question is, I thought, looking into the mean, rust-coloured rock of the mountains in the distance, what do I do now?
A racing driver should have one or two fall-back identities lined up for when he climbs out of his car. I thought I did, but when I reached for them they just disappeared. How about: an ex-racing driver adds colour to the commentary direct from the trackside? 'We got fifteen guys, all of them former Indy and Formula One drivers, fifteen guys in front of you, Forrest, standing in line to be colour commentators. We'll call you.'
Well then, how about: an ex-racing driver coins a partnership to sell classic cars? That lasted nearly all winter with phone calls, lunches, lawyers und meetings with bankers. But it was the year nobody was buying old Ferraris and Honda was 'reviewing' its dealer list. So in the end I gracefully withdrew before there was nothing to withdraw from. Being an 'ex' anything is depressing work. I mean you tell me, how badly do you want to hear about how I was almost the World Champion? Nobody wants to hear a story that ends in 'almost'. And even if I had been world champion you could probably just about stand to listen to the story for five minutes before your ears turned to cement. Last year's champion was last year.
Not that I want sympathy. Which is just as well, since I don't get any. Well, why should I? I had a good run, made money and hung on to enough. But oh, man, I miss the heat of slipping into that graceful, elegant, shrink-wrapped super-tech machine with seven hundred horsepower behind my neck. Zero to a hundred and fifty miles an hour in 4,9 seconds. And yes, I miss coming within an eyelash of killing myself every race or so. I miss the bright and gorgeous people and the reporters who acted as if what I said mattered. Being famous, even in a minor way, isn't all bad. Businessmen and politicians bragged to their friends that they knew me. Little boys slid under fences to get my autograph. And now that I don't drive a racing car... Only last week the phone rang twice. I have time in the morning and I have time in the afternoon. And let me just check, but I think tomorrow is free, so much empty time.
I looked up into the soft blue morning sky. No buzzards overhead. Maybe Arizona doesn't have buzzards. But a couple of little brown birds in a saguaro cactus just in front of me were giving me advice, something like 'get away from our nest before we sing our hearts out'. It had never occurred to me that the desert had songbirds. It did occur to me that a bogus cowboy in designer boots had a lot to learn.

On parle de grosses bottes, là. De vraies grosses bottes.

Je me tenais debout, perché sur mes bottes de cowboy de marque à 800 dollars pièce, sur les rochers d'une ancienne formation rocheuse dans le sable du désert de l'Arizona. L'argent n'était pas un problème. J'avais la tenue complète de cowboy, et avec la tenue complète, on pourrait se prendre pour un cowboy. Mais moi, non. Ça ne collait pas. J'ai plissé les yeux sous le soleil matinal en regardant les montagnes de l'Arizona et j'ai dû me rendre à l'évidence : je ne me sentais pas chez moi dans les grands espaces.

Arrivant de Denver juste après l'aube, j'avais l'impression que je pourrais bien croiser un vieux cow-boy débarquant du ciel. Cette impression n'a pas duré plus longtemps que le premier vrai cowboy dans le hall des bagages de l'aéroport de Phoenix. Il portait un t-shirt trempé de sueur, avait besoin d'être rasé et soulevait un sac en toile sale du tapis roulant lorsqu'il a aperçu mes bottes de cowboy flambant neuves. Il a lentement haussé un sourcil et est sorti sans se retourner. Il devrait bien exister, quelque part, dans un placard, un costume qu'un ancien pilote de course puisse enfiler sans se sentir comme un extraterrestre. Quelque chose qui lui permette, où qu'il aille, de ne pas avoir l'impression que tout le monde parle une autre langue et fait les choses au ralenti. J'aimais, non, pas aimé… j'adorais tout simplement être pilote de course, conduire des voitures de course. J'en suis accro, c'est tout ce que je sais faire. Mais je ne le fais plus. Je ne pourrais pas, même si je le voulais. La question est, me disais-je en contemplant la roche rouille et austère des montagnes au loin, que faire maintenant ?

Un pilote de course devrait avoir une ou deux identités de secours en réserve pour lorsqu'il sort de sa voiture. Je croyais en avoir, mais quand j'ai voulu les utiliser, elles ont disparu. Et si : un ancien pilote de course commentait la piste en direct ? « On a quinze gars, tous d'anciens pilotes d'IndyCar et de Formule 1, quinze gars devant toi, Forrest, qui font la queue pour être commentateurs. On t'appelle. »

Et puis, que diriez-vous d'un ancien pilote qui monte un partenariat pour vendre des voitures de collection ? Ça a duré presque tout l'hiver, entre coups de fil, déjeuners, avocats et rendez-vous avec des banquiers. Mais c'était l'année où personne n'achetait de vieilles Ferrari et où Honda « réexaminait » sa liste de concessionnaires. Alors, finalement, je me suis retiré discrètement avant qu'il ne soit trop tard. Être un « ex », quel que soit le domaine, c'est déprimant. Franchement, vous avez vraiment envie d'entendre comment j'ai failli être champion du monde ? Personne n'a envie d'entendre une histoire qui se termine par « failli ». Et même si j'avais été champion du monde, vous pourriez à peine supporter l'histoire cinq minutes avant d'avoir les oreilles qui se bouchent. Le champion de l'année dernière, c'était l'année dernière.

Non pas que je cherche la pitié. Et c'est tant mieux, vu que je n'en reçois pas. Eh bien, pourquoi le ferais-je ? J'ai eu une belle carrière, j'ai gagné de l'argent et j'en ai gardé suffisamment. Mais bon sang, que la sensation de me glisser dans cette machine gracieuse, élégante, ultra-technologique, avec ses sept cents chevaux sous le capot, me manque ! De 0 à 240 km/h en 4,9 secondes. Et oui, frôler la mort à chaque course me manque aussi. Les gens brillants et magnifiques me manquent, ainsi que les journalistes qui semblaient croire que mes paroles avaient de l'importance. Être célèbre, même un peu, n'est pas si mal. Les hommes d'affaires et les politiciens se vantaient auprès de leurs amis de me connaître. Des petits garçons se faufilaient sous les barrières pour avoir mon autographe. Et maintenant que je ne pilote plus de voiture de course… La semaine dernière encore, le téléphone a sonné deux fois. J'ai du temps libre le matin et l'après-midi. Et laissez-moi vérifier, mais je crois que demain est libre, tellement de temps libre.

J'ai levé les yeux vers le ciel bleu doux du matin. Pas de vautours au-dessus de moi. Peut-être qu'il n'y a pas de vautours en Arizona. Mais deux petits oiseaux bruns, perchés dans un cactus saguaro juste devant moi, me donnaient un conseil : « Éloigne-toi de notre nid avant qu'on ne chante à tue-tête ! » Je n'avais jamais imaginé qu'il y ait des oiseaux chanteurs dans le désert. En revanche, je me suis dit qu'un faux cow-boy en bottes de marque avait encore beaucoup à apprendre.
results.back_text:
We're talking serious boots here. Real serious boots.

I was standing, perched on my $800 designer cowboy boots, on the rocks of an ancient rock formation in the Arizona desert sand. Money wasn't an issue. I had the full cowboy outfit, and with the full outfit, you could pretend to be a cowboy. But not me. It just didn't work. I squinted in the early morning sun, looking at the Arizona mountains, and had to face the facts: I didn't feel at home in the great outdoors.

Arriving from Denver just after dawn, I had the feeling I might run into an old cowboy who'd dropped from the sky. That feeling didn't last any longer than the first real cowboy in the baggage claim at Phoenix airport. He was wearing a sweat-soaked T-shirt, needed a shave, and was lifting a dirty canvas bag from the conveyor belt when he spotted my brand-new cowboy boots. He slowly raised an eyebrow and walked out without looking back. Surely there must exist, somewhere in a closet, a suit a former race car driver could slip into without feeling like an alien. Something that would allow him, wherever he went, to not feel like everyone was speaking a different language and doing things in slow motion. I liked—no, didn't like… I simply loved being a race car driver, driving race cars. I'm addicted to it; it's all I know how to do. But I don't do it anymore. I couldn't, even if I wanted to. The question is, I told myself, gazing at the rusty, austere rock of the distant mountains, what to do now?

A race car driver should have one or two backup identities for when he gets out of his car. I thought I did, but when I went to use them, they were gone. What if: a former race car driver was providing live commentary? “We’ve got fifteen guys, all former IndyCar and Formula 1 drivers, fifteen guys ahead of you, Forrest, lining up to be commentators. We’ll call you.”

And what about a former driver setting up a partnership to sell classic cars? It dragged on almost all winter, between phone calls, lunches, lawyers, and meetings with bankers. But that was the year nobody was buying old Ferraris and Honda was “re-evaluating” its dealer list. So, in the end, I quietly withdrew before it was too late. Being an “ex,” in any field, is depressing. Honestly, do you really want to hear how I almost became world champion? Nobody wants to hear a story that ends with "almost." And even if I had been world champion, you could barely stand the story for five minutes before your ears would pop. Last year's champion was last year.

Not that I'm looking for pity. And that's just as well, since I don't get any. Well, why would I? I had a great career, I made money, and I kept enough. But damn, how I miss the feeling of slipping into that graceful, elegant, ultra-high-tech machine, with its 700 horsepower under the hood! From 0 to 240 km/h in 4.9 seconds. And yes, I miss that close call in every race, too. I miss the bright, beautiful people, and the journalists who seemed to think my words mattered. Being famous, even a little, isn't so bad. Businessmen and politicians boasted to their friends about knowing me. Little boys would sneak under barriers to get my autograph. And now that I'm no longer racing… Just last week, the phone rang twice. I have free time in the morning and afternoon. And let me check, but I think tomorrow is free, so much free time.

I looked up at the soft blue morning sky. No vultures overhead. Maybe there aren't any vultures in Arizona. But two small brown birds, perched in a saguaro cactus right in front of me, were giving me some advice: "Get away from our nest before we start singing our heads off!" "I never imagined there were songbirds in the desert. On the other hand, I thought that a fake cowboy in designer boots still had a lot to learn."

results.title: 26.txt
results.src_text:
Line dancing 

Thousands of people in Britain have a new hobby -- line dancing. In almost every town, you will find clubs and classes for this new activity. 
'Line dancing is easy to learn. If you have two feet and can walk, then you can do it!' Fiona Lever, a teacher, says. 'You don't need a partner because you dance in groups. It's the best way to make new friends. In my classes, there are young and old people. The boys like it because they can make a lot of noise with their feet during the dances!' 
When did line dancing begin? Most people think it started about fifteen years ago when American country music became famous in Britain.
results.tgt_text:
Danse en ligne

Des milliers de Britanniques s'adonnent à un nouveau loisir : la danse en ligne. Dans presque toutes les villes, on trouve des clubs et des cours pour cette activité.

« La danse en ligne est facile à apprendre. Si vous avez deux pieds et que vous savez marcher, vous pouvez en faire ! » affirme Fiona Lever, professeure. « Pas besoin de partenaire, on danse en groupe. C'est le meilleur moyen de se faire des amis. Dans mes cours, il y a des jeunes et des moins jeunes. Les garçons adorent ça parce qu'ils peuvent faire beaucoup de bruit avec leurs pieds pendant les danses ! »

Line Dancing

Thousands of Britons are taking up a new hobby: line dancing. Clubs and classes for this activity can be found in almost every town and city.

"Line dancing is easy to learn. If you have two feet and can walk, you can do it!" says instructor Fiona Lever. "You don't need a partner; you dance in a group. It's the best way to make friends. In my classes, there are young and old. The boys love it because they can make a lot of noise with their feet while dancing!"

When did line dancing begin? Most people think it started about fifteen years ago, with the popularization of American country music in Britain.

Build it yourself at the UK's first bamboo bike workshop 

A course at the Bamboo Bike Club, run by engineers James Marr and Ian McMillan, buys you a computer-designed custom frame plus a fun weekend of bike-building. 

It's Saturday morning in Hackney Wick, east London, and apart from a mechanic deep in the bowels of a truck, the only sign of life among the small factories on a backstreet is a whine of machinery from an upper window - work has begun at Bamboo Bike Club, Britain's only bamboo bike-building course. I've gone along to watch the action. 
There's a sense of energy and industry. And of fun. Woodwork class was never like this. Bamboo is one of the most interesting trends to emerge in bike construction. Names like Californian manufacturer Calfee Design or Yorkshire's Bamboo Bikes have revived a construction method pioneered as early as 1894. The problem for most cyclists is the price. A ready-made bamboo frame from these companies retails for $2,995, or PS1,868. 
It was this, plus the design challenge, that led James and Ian to spend years cooped up in a shed in Brecon, Wales. Their idea was to establish a boutique bamboo bike business with products within reach of the average cyclist. 
Only after they had refined their research into a marketable product - James now tosses out phrases like 'close-noded thick-wall tubes' while talking about bamboo - did they realise they were on the wrong track. 'We realised we didn't want just to sell frames. We wanted to share the joy of making something; the craft of creating something unique and sustainable,' James explains. 
The outcome was something more community than company, and as such, the Bamboo Bike Club is still an occupation sandwiched between full-time jobs - James makes wind turbines and Ian is a civil engineer. But they seem to be on the right track, with monthly courses whose competitive price buys you a computer-designed custom bike frame plus a fun weekend of bike-building. 
The question for me, a king of the botch job - my terrible handiwork failures litter my house - was about quality. On day one, the boys explain how to select bamboo for strength and how to form strong joints before tubes are glued lightly in place in the workshop: first the front triangle composed of 40 mm diameter bamboo; then the thinner, more fiddly seat and the chain assembly. Alloy tubes are inserted for the handlebars, wheel forks and other parts which require the strength and precise engineering impossible in bamboo. 
All this, together with the technical skill involved in using jigs, power tools and design blueprints, is a leap of faith for someone whose idea of DIY is flatpack furniture assembly. Accurate cutting for a clean joint can be tricky, for example. 
James and Ian buzz cheerfully between workbenches, supervising every cut, triple-checking every joint, and will take over if a task seems insurmountable. The self-build is half the attraction for most participants; it may be no coincidence that all those on this course were engineers. For the rest of us, Ian reassures that everyone messes up once or twice. 
No problem - just get another piece and have another go. Such is the benefit of bamboo. Each length has been pre-checked for quality, so you get to indulge in frame aesthetics: plain bamboo, black or mottled. 
Sunday is a more relaxed day, mainly spent building the lugs. Or rather, wraps: hemp bindings wrapped around the joints and dropouts then glued with epoxy resin to form a strong bond that disperses loads evenly throughout the frame. With a final polymer coating for waterproofing, the bike is ready for wheels, brakes, gears, saddle and any other individual touches. And it is a bike built for the long haul, just as strong, the pair claim, as its metal equivalents. 
Ian has ridden his for over a year on a 16-mile commute, while James has failed to destroy one bike off-road over three months of testing. 'To be honest, our bikes are over-engineered - we use larger diameter tubes and over-thick bindings - but I prefer it like that,' James says. 
Technical issues aside, how good does a bamboo bike look? Somewhat scruffy alongside professional frames, it turns out - the hemp weave can look a bit like parcel tape, for example. But there's no denying their individuality and that, say James and Ian, is the point. 
Personally though, I believe that any bicycle made from this kind of material should be a relaxed affair, something for cruising sedately around on rather than racing. I therefore plump for a frame that avoids the stiff angularity of my existing metal machine: a 'Classic English' giving a gentle, easy-going ride. 
They also cycle well. I take James's bike for a spin and the ride is light, stiff and smooth thanks to bamboo's ability to dampen vibration. Impressive, considering I target every pothole. 'Some people love the build, but for me these workshops come together when the bike is on the road,' James says. 'They're so light, so effortless to ride. So much fun to ride too - take a Harley-style retro bike, add 10 and you're still not close.' And the price? Less than PS500.
