results.src_text:
The camera never lies 

Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of the Sherlock Holmes stories, believed himself to be a rational man, a scientist even. But in 1920, when he saw photographs of fairies taken in a garden setting, he thought he was seeing scientific proof that these tiny creatures really existed. He published the photographs alongside an article he wrote, acknowledging fairies as supernatural wonders. It was not until 1939 that the two ladies who took the photos admitted these were fake. They simply cut out pictures of fairies from a book and arranged them among flowers. The results are undeniably beautiful. But the simplicity of the trick undermines a basic principle of photography, that the camera cannot lie. 
But it can, and always could. Today, we are used to computer software enabling us to rework our digital images and it is a myth that photography ever had a true age of innocence. From the moment cameras began capturing reality, that reality was being altered.
results.tgt_text:
La caméra ne ment jamais.

Arthur Conan Doyle, créateur des aventures de Sherlock Holmes, se considérait comme un homme rationnel, voire un scientifique. Pourtant, en 1920, lorsqu'il vit des photographies de fées prises dans un jardin, il crut y trouver la preuve scientifique de l'existence de ces créatures minuscules. Il publia les clichés accompagnés d'un article où il reconnaissait le caractère surnaturel des fées. Ce n'est qu'en 1939 que les deux femmes qui avaient pris les photos avouèrent la supercherie. Elles avaient simplement découpé des images de fées dans un livre et les avaient disposées parmi des fleurs. Le résultat est indéniablement magnifique. Mais la simplicité du procédé remet en cause un principe fondamental de la photographie : la caméra ne peut mentir.

Or, elle le peut, et l'a toujours pu. Aujourd'hui, nous sommes habitués aux logiciels qui nous permettent de retoucher nos images numériques, et l'idée que la photographie ait jamais connu un véritable âge d'or d'innocence est un mythe. Dès l'instant où les appareils photo ont commencé à capturer la réalité, celle-ci a été altérée.
results.back_text:
The camera never lies.

Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of the Sherlock Holmes adventures, considered himself a rational man, even a scientist. Yet, in 1920, when he saw photographs of fairies taken in a garden, he believed he had found scientific proof of the existence of these tiny creatures. He published the photos along with an article in which he acknowledged the supernatural nature of fairies. It wasn't until 1939 that the two women who had taken the photos confessed to the deception. They had simply cut out pictures of fairies from a book and arranged them among flowers. The result is undeniably beautiful. But the simplicity of the process calls into question a fundamental principle of photography: the camera cannot lie.

Yet, it can, and always has. Today, we are accustomed to software that allows us to retouch our digital images, and the idea that photography ever experienced a true golden age of innocence is a myth. From the moment cameras began capturing reality, it was altered.

results.title: 14.txt
results.src_text:
Art

In modern times - more and more over the course of the last two hundred years - we have come to speak as though every artist had to rebel against the art of his contemporaries. Art is praised in terms of being unique, revolutionary, shocking even. We feel good about admiring the artist whose work no one appreciated a hundred years ago. But when we get to the art of our own day, we get cold feet and say that an artist has gone too far, that what he does can no longer be called art. Or, rather, the media say it for us. And, on the whole, we agree because we expect to be puzzled by art's insistent newness - so much so that we do not notice the old themes, methods and also virtues that the art of our own time is full of.
We require artists to be separate from the rest of us, figures with special talents and drive, so vigorous that conventions cannot contain them. Previous ages went to artists with commissions: people needed art for specific purposes, and it was part of their ordinary life. Today we leave artists to their own devices and get rather cross with them if they want to come down out of the clouds.

Picture This

I am going to describe a situation, and then ask a crucial question about it. I hope it doesn't strike you as unduly gnomic. But if it does, that's modern art for you.
Here's the situation. An artist chooses a piece of text in an art book. The text considers the diversity of pictures. 'What are they all about?' it asks dumbly, before deciding, even more dumbly: 'There is no end, in fact, to the number of different kinds of pictures.' Okay, this is kiddy-language, and so far all it has betrayed is kiddy-thinking. But stick with me, all you adults out there. The situation is about to complicate itself.
Having settled on his text, the man then asks someone else to make a canvas for him, to stretch it and prime it, and then to take it along to a sign painter. He asks the sign painter to write the chosen text on the canvas. And he gives the sign painter specific instructions not to attempt anything flashy or charming with the lettering. The sign painter does all this. On a white canvas, in simple black letters, he writes the chosen text. So my crucial question is this: is the finished product a painting?

Underground Encounters

At the Mercury Gallery, London until 26th June

It is an unspoken rule of commercial success as a painter that once you have developed a profitable line in one genre, you stick to it. Collectors expect an artist to diligently mine the same seam, and attempts to strike out in a new direction are usually met at best with indignation and the feeling that the artist has let the public down.
Why this should be I'm not entirely sure. Gallery owners obviously prefer safe bets, and perhaps the art-buying public is insecure and needs the comfort of continuity. A few artists break the mould and get away with it. Picasso and Hockney are two prime examples. Eric Rimmington is another artist who is now gamely running contrary to form, and it remains to be seen if he can pull it off. His new show takes the daring step of swapping the pristine still lifes which have made his name for paintings of the world of the London Underground.
Railways hold a peculiar charm for Rimmington. From drawings made in the 1980s of the railway land of Londons Kings Cross Station, it was a logical step to go beneath the ground and look at what was happening below. The sketches have provided the material for Underground Encounters, an exhibition of 40 paintings and drawings which convey the curious magic of this sunken world designed for a population in transit.

Extract from a novel

I have escaped to this island with a few books. I do not know why I use the word 'escape'. The villagers say jokingly that only a sick man would choose such a remote place to rebuild. Well then, I have come here to heal myself, if you like to put it that way.
Apart from the wrinkled old peasant who comes from the village on her mule each day to clean the house, I am quite alone. I am neither happy nor unhappy; I lie suspended like a hair or a feather in the cloudy mixtures of memory. I spoke of the uselessness of art but added nothing truthful about its consolations. The solace of such work as I do with brain and heart lies in this - that only there, in the silences of the painter or the writer can reality be reordered, reworked and made to show its significant side. Our common actions in reality are simply the sackcloth covering which hides the cloth-of-gold - the meaning of the pattern. For us artists there waits the joyous compromise through art with all that wounded or defeated us in daily life; in this way, not to evade destiny, as the ordinary people try to do, but to fulfil it in its true potential - the imagination. Otherwise why should we hurt one another?
results.tgt_text:
L'art

À l'époque moderne – et ce, de plus en plus au cours des deux derniers siècles – nous en sommes venus à parler comme si chaque artiste devait se rebeller contre l'art de ses contemporains. L'art est loué pour son originalité, son caractère révolutionnaire, voire choquant. Nous prenons plaisir à admirer l'artiste dont l'œuvre était ignorée il y a un siècle. Mais dès qu'il s'agit de l'art contemporain, nous hésitons et déclarons qu'un artiste est allé trop loin, que son travail ne peut plus être qualifié d'art. Ou plutôt, ce sont les médias qui le disent pour nous. Et, généralement, nous acquiesçons, car nous nous attendons à être déconcertés par la nouveauté insistante de l'art – à tel point que nous ne remarquons pas les thèmes, les méthodes et les qualités anciennes qui imprègnent l'art de notre temps.

Nous exigeons des artistes qu'ils soient à part, des figures dotées de talents et d'une énergie exceptionnels, si vigoureuses que les conventions ne peuvent les contenir. Autrefois, les artistes recevaient des commandes : l'art répondait à des besoins spécifiques et faisait partie intégrante de la vie quotidienne. Aujourd'hui, on laisse les artistes à leur guise et on s'irrite contre eux s'ils veulent redescendre sur terre.

Imaginez ceci

Je vais décrire une situation, puis poser une question cruciale à son sujet. J'espère qu'elle ne vous semblera pas trop énigmatique. Mais si c'est le cas, c'est bien là le propre de l'art moderne.

Voici la situation. Un artiste choisit un texte dans un livre d'art. Ce texte évoque la diversité des images. « De quoi parlent-elles toutes ? » demande-t-il naïvement, avant de conclure, encore plus naïvement : « En réalité, le nombre de types d'images différents est infini. » Bon, c'est du langage enfantin, et jusqu'ici, cela ne révèle qu'une pensée enfantine. Mais restez avec moi, chers adultes. La situation est sur le point de se compliquer.

Ayant choisi son texte, l'homme demande alors à quelqu'un de lui fabriquer une toile, de la tendre et de l'apprêter, puis de l'apporter à un peintre en lettres. Il demande au peintre en lettres d'écrire le texte choisi sur la toile. Il lui donne des instructions précises : pas de fioritures ni d'ornements superflus. Le peintre s'exécute. Sur une toile blanche, en simples lettres noires, il inscrit le texte choisi. Ma question cruciale est donc la suivante : le résultat final est-il une peinture ?

Rencontres souterraines

À la Mercury Gallery, Londres, jusqu'au 26 juin

C'est une règle tacite du succès commercial pour un peintre : une fois qu'on a trouvé une formule lucrative dans un genre, on s'y tient. Les collectionneurs attendent d'un artiste qu'il exploite assidûment le même filon, et toute tentative d'explorer une nouvelle voie est généralement accueillie, au mieux, avec indignation et le sentiment que l'artiste a déçu le public.

Je ne sais pas vraiment pourquoi. Les galeristes préfèrent sans doute les valeurs sûres, et peut-être que le public, amateur d'art, est en quête de repères et a besoin de la sécurité de la continuité. Quelques artistes sortent des sentiers battus et s'en sortent. Picasso et Hockney en sont deux exemples frappants. Eric Rimmington est un autre artiste qui, aujourd'hui, prend un risque audacieux en s'éloignant de ses habitudes, et il reste à voir s'il réussira son pari. Sa nouvelle exposition franchit une étape audacieuse en troquant les natures mortes immaculées qui ont fait sa renommée contre des peintures du monde du métro londonien.

Les chemins de fer exercent une fascination particulière sur Rimmington. À partir de dessins réalisés dans les années 1980 représentant les voies ferrées de la gare de King's Cross à Londres, il était logique de descendre sous terre et d'observer ce qui se passait en dessous. Ces croquis ont fourni la matière première d'« Underground Encounters », une exposition de 40 peintures et dessins qui traduisent la magie singulière de ce monde souterrain conçu pour une population de passage.

Extrait d'un roman :

Je me suis réfugié sur cette île avec quelques livres. Je ne sais pas pourquoi j'utilise le mot « réfugié ». Les villageois disent en plaisantant que seul un malade choisirait un endroit aussi isolé pour se reconstruire. Eh bien, je suis venu ici pour me soigner, si l'on veut. Hormis la vieille paysanne ridée qui vient chaque jour du village sur sa mule pour nettoyer la maison, je suis tout à fait seul. Je ne suis ni heureux ni malheureux ; je reste suspendu comme un cheveu ou une plume dans les brumes du souvenir. J'ai parlé de l'inutilité de l'art, mais je n'ai rien ajouté de vrai quant à ses consolations. Le réconfort d'un travail comme le mien, qui s'y consacre corps et âme, réside en ceci : c'est seulement là, dans les silences du peintre ou de l'écrivain, que la réalité peut être réorganisée, retravaillée et révéler sa véritable signification. Nos actions ordinaires ne sont que le sac qui recouvre le tissu d'or – le sens profond du motif. Pour nous, artistes, il y a le joyeux compromis, par l'art, avec tout ce qui nous a blessés ou vaincus dans la vie quotidienne ; ainsi, non pas pour fuir le destin, comme le font les gens ordinaires, mais pour l'accomplir dans toute sa plénitude – l'imagination. Sinon, pourquoi nous faire du mal les uns aux autres ?

Collectors expect an artist to assiduously exploit the same vein, and any attempt to explore a new path is generally met, at best, with indignation and the feeling that the artist has disappointed the public.

I don't really know why. Gallery owners probably prefer tried-and-true artists, and perhaps the public, as art lovers, are looking for familiar landmarks and need the security of continuity. A few artists venture off the beaten path and succeed. Picasso and Hockney are two striking examples. Eric Rimmington is another artist who, today, is taking a bold risk by moving away from his usual style, and it remains to be seen whether he will succeed. His new exhibition marks a daring step by trading the pristine still lifes that made him famous for paintings of the London Underground.

Railways hold a particular fascination for Rimmington. Based on drawings he made in the 1980s depicting the tracks at King's Cross station in London, it was a natural progression to go underground and observe what was happening below. These sketches provided the raw material for "Underground Encounters," an exhibition of 40 paintings and drawings that capture the singular magic of this subterranean world designed for a transient population.

Excerpt from a novel:

I took refuge on this island with a few books. I don't know why I use the word "refugee." The villagers joke that only a sick person would choose such an isolated place to rebuild their life. Well, I came here to heal, if you will. Apart from the wrinkled old peasant woman who comes every day from the village on her mule to clean the house, I am completely alone. I am neither happy nor unhappy; I remain suspended like a hair or a feather in the mists of memory. I have spoken of the uselessness of art, but I have added nothing true concerning its consolations. The solace of a job like mine, one to which I dedicate myself body and soul, lies in this: it is only there, in the silences of the painter or the writer, that reality can be reorganized, reworked, and reveal its true meaning. Our ordinary actions are merely the bag that covers the golden fabric—the profound meaning of the motif. For us artists, there is the joyful compromise, through art, with all that has wounded or defeated us in daily life; thus, not to flee fate, as ordinary people do, but to fulfill it in all its fullness—imagination. Otherwise, why would we hurt one another?

THE HISTORY OF THE IDITAROD - THE LAST GREAT RACE ON EARTH

In the 1880s, gold was discovered in what is now the most northern state of the USA,
Alaska. Many people came to the area hoping to get rich. New towns were built and grew quickly. One such town was called Iditarod, which means 'far, distant place'. This town grew so quickly during 1909 that it briefly became the largest city in Alaska. In the summer months, essential supplies could be delivered to these towns by boat, but in the winter the rivers and the ocean froze and there was no way to get to them. So, in 1910, a winter track was built which would be used by teams of dogs pulling sleds. They would take mail, food and clothes to the gold miners.
The track became known as the Iditarod Trail. It took a team of dogs about three weeks to travel across Alaska. They stopped at 'roadhouses' where the drivers could get a warm bed for the night and something to eat for both themselves and their dogs. The trail was used every winter until the 1920s when aeroplanes replaced steam boats and dog teams as the main form of transport.
However, the dogs had one last taste of fame in 1925, when a disease called diphtheria hit the city of Nome. The disease could be cured, but, unfortunately, the closest medicine that could be found was in Anchorage, right on the other side of Alaska. Aeroplanes were still quite new, so no-one knew if they could fly in such cold weather. Also, Carl Eielson, the only pilot considered skilled enough to manage the flight, was away on a trip at the time. It was therefore agreed that the medicine would be transported using teams of dogs instead.
The trip covered over 1,000 kilometres, most of it along the Iditarod Trail. It took twenty teams just six days to complete the journey. Leonhard Seppala, a Norwegian who had come to Alaska looking for gold, travelled the first 400 of those kilometres. He had to trust his dog Togo's ability to find his way in the blinding snow and Togo turned out to be a reliable guide. The last part of the journey was done by Gunnar Kaasen who had driven dog teams in Alaska for 21 years. His lead dog was Saito. At one point Balto refused to go any further, and saved the team from falling into icy water. The diphtheria was stopped and Balto became a hero.
Nowadays a dog sled race is held every year from Anchorage to Nome, following the route of that famous journey in 1925. It is called the Iditarod and has become known as 'The Last Great Race on Earth'.

Dans les années 1880, de l'or fut découvert dans ce qui est aujourd'hui l'État le plus septentrional des États-Unis,

l'Alaska. Nombreux furent ceux qui affluèrent dans la région, espérant faire fortune. De nouvelles villes furent construites et connurent une croissance rapide. L'une d'elles s'appelait Iditarod, ce qui signifie « lieu lointain et reculé ». Cette ville connut une croissance si fulgurante en 1909 qu'elle devint brièvement la plus grande d'Alaska. Durant l'été, les marchandises essentielles pouvaient être acheminées par bateau, mais en hiver, les rivières et l'océan gelaient, rendant tout accès impossible. Aussi, en 1910, une piste hivernale fut aménagée pour les attelages de chiens tirant des traîneaux. Ces derniers transportaient courrier, vivres et vêtements aux chercheurs d'or.

Cette piste devint la piste de l'Iditarod. Il fallait environ trois semaines à un attelage pour traverser l'Alaska. Ils s'arrêtaient dans des relais routiers où les conducteurs pouvaient trouver un lit chaud pour la nuit et de quoi se restaurer, eux et leurs chiens. La piste fut empruntée chaque hiver jusqu'aux années 1920, lorsque les avions remplacèrent les bateaux à vapeur et les attelages de chiens comme principal moyen de transport.

Cependant, les chiens connurent une dernière période de gloire en 1925, lorsqu'une épidémie de diphtérie frappa la ville de Nome. La maladie était curable, mais, malheureusement, le médicament le plus proche se trouvait à Anchorage, à l'autre bout de l'Alaska. Les avions étant encore relativement nouveaux, personne ne savait s'ils pouvaient voler par un froid pareil. De plus, Carl Eielson, le seul pilote jugé suffisamment compétent pour effectuer le vol, était alors en voyage. Il fut donc convenu que le médicament serait transporté par attelages de chiens.

Le voyage couvrit plus de 1 000 kilomètres, principalement le long de la piste de l'Iditarod. Vingt attelages mirent le cap en seulement six jours. Leonhard Seppala, un Norvégien venu en Alaska en quête d'or, parcourut les 400 premiers kilomètres. Il dut faire confiance à son chien Togo pour s'orienter dans la neige aveuglante, et Togo se révéla un guide fiable. La dernière partie du voyage fut effectuée par Gunnar Kaasen, qui conduisait des attelages de chiens en Alaska depuis 21 ans. Son chien de tête était Saito. À un moment donné, Balto refusa d'avancer et sauva l'attelage de la chute dans l'eau glacée. La diphtérie fut enrayée et Balto devint un héros.

De nos jours, une course de chiens de traîneau a lieu chaque année d'Anchorage à Nome, suivant le parcours de ce voyage légendaire de 1925. Elle s'appelle l'Iditarod et est connue comme « La dernière grande course du monde ».

We changed lives for a day!

Have you ever dreamed about swapping lives with someone else for a day? Perhaps you think it would be more fun to do something quite different for a change? We fixed it for four people - read how it went.
Amanda (23), a young mother with two daughters, swapped lives with her friend Cindy (30), who works as a waitress at a glitzy London restaurant and entertainment complex.

A. Amanda's story

I'd never been inside anywhere remotely like it before. I couldn't believe how dark and noisy it was - there were so many people and such a brilliant atmosphere. It was all a far cry from my home town and, to he honest, I wasn't sure I'd survive! Being a mother is definitely a busy job - but this was something else!
I had just fifteen minutes to learn how to carry a tray of drinks at shoulder height with one hand. The other waitresses made it look so simple, but just as I was getting the hang of it, the drinks started to slide off the tray and crashed on to the floor, splattering cocktails everywhere. I was so embarrassed, but all the other waitresses laughed. Everyone makes a fool of themselves at first!
By opening time at 11.30 am, a queue had already formed outside and I began to feel really nervous. I was worried about how I'd remember all the orders, but that, at least, wasn't a problem because everything was automated.
After a couple of hours my feet really ached and I couldn't get used to the constant loud music. Every time a customer spoke to me I had to say 'Pardon?', which was so embarrassing! By the end of my shift at 5 pm, I was totally exhausted and longed to soak my feet in a bowl of hot water. I couldn't believe it when one of the waitresses told me it had been a 'quiet' day!
I never realised how tiring waitressing would be. I've always thought it was a job for shrinking violets, but in fact you definitely need to be quite bubbly, as well having the ability to keep a cool head and deal with what is known in the trade as a 'high-volume experience' - in other words, lots of customers!
I'm really quite shy and I don't think I could cope on a Saturday night, when it gets chaotically busy. I wasn't too impressed with the pay either. Unfortunately, I must have been a lousy waitress because even the rich Americans didn't tip me a bean!
I must admit I was very glad to get back to my children. It seems quite easy after waitressing!

B. Cindy's story

I was feeling quite apprehensive about being a 'mum' for the day, but I was looking forward to it, too. I'd been warned the girls were cheeky, but in my ignorance I thought I could handle it. Little did I know!
As Amanda left to make her way to the restaurant, I had to get the two girls dressed and fed. After dropping off Sophie at school and Katie at nursery I thought I'd have three hours of peace. Wrong! A note from Amanda reminded me that I still had to make the beds, clean the house and do the washing.
At 1 pm I picked up Katie, whizzed around the supermarket and then took her home for lunch. But it was when I brought Sophie home from school that the real trouble started. They turned the settee into a trampoline and played a game which involved screaming as loudly as they possibly could! I decided to take the laid-back approach, imagining they'd soon get worn out. Wrong again. I thought I had a fair amount of stamina, but they beat me, hands down!
After much persuasion, I managed to get them into bed by about 8 pm, but then the fun and games started! How many glasses of water can a child drink, for heaven's sake? Of course, I realised it was just a ploy so they could come downstairs and watch television, but it was exhausting to spend all evening negotiating deals with them.
I never realised how tiring it could be looking after two small children. You don't get a second to think about yourself - and the sheer sense of responsibility is overwhelming. Even so, I really enjoyed the day.

Rosemary (42) runs a dairy farm. She swapped with Hilary (30), a teacher at a primary school.

C. Rosemary's story

On the farm, I have to get up at 5.30 am so sleeping in until 7 was pure luxury! But I dithered for ages about how to look. I could hardly turn up in overalls and boots, could I?
Looking at a sea of faces -- about 400 pupils -- at assembly, I hoped I melted into the background and that my fresh complexion didn't make me stand out as being straight off the farm.
After that it was time for a maths class. The children worked in small groups, using workcards graded according to difficulty - rather different from when I was at school and we had to recite tables in unison! Then I helped out with a nature project - identifying and feeding species of snails.
By lunchtime I was exhausted and looking forward to an hour's break, but the teachers only have about five minutes to eat their meal. There's so much to do before classes start again. I attended a staff meeting about reports and couldn't avoid getting roped in to help with athletics trials.
Alter lunch there was a silent reading lesson (bliss!) and then a French lesson in the video room. This was great fun because all the children wanted to practise on me, which really showed up my rusty French.
Finally we moved on to the school hall for Physical Education. I was drained by now, but the children seemed to have inexhaustible energy.
The hardest part of the job was standing up in front of the class and speaking - even for just two minutes, it's daunting. Teachers may get more holidays a year, but I think I'll stick to farming, anyway!

D. Hilary's story

I arrived at White House Farm at 8.30 am, bright and early, only to discover that Rosemary had been up for three hours! Rosemary's 280-acre farm has 100 Jersey cows, 15 calves and heifers and about 800 ewes! As well as milk, she manufactures ice-cream, yoghurt and cream, which is sold in shops, restaurants and at tourist attractions. I spent most of the morning in the ice-cream parlour, bottling milk into plastic litre containers, squeezing ice-cream from a machine into cartons and sticking on labels. It was difficult to stop myself dipping my fingers into the goodies! At lunchtime it was time to inspect the sheep. I drove over to one of the fields and picked up a ewe which had fallen over. If the sheep are left for more than 12 hours once they have fallen over they could die, so they have to he checked every day. What a nightmare it must be in winter!
Alter feeding the calves, I started the milking. The process took an exhausting two-and-a-half hours. And Rosemary does this twice a day, starting at 6 am, seven days a week, 365 days a year!
I found it quite a lonely day. I was surprised how much I missed the children - animals don't answer back! The worst aspect of the job is not being able to get away from work. The cows always have to be milked twice a day, so it's really difficult to plan any time off. Rosemary will only get about three days' holiday this year.
Farming seems romantic but the reality is very different. The income is irregular and I'd hate to be at the mercy of the weather.

Nous avons échangé nos vies le temps d'une journée !

Avez-vous déjà rêvé d'échanger votre vie avec celle de quelqu'un d'autre pendant une journée ? Et si, pour changer, vous tentiez de faire quelque chose de complètement différent ? Nous avons réalisé ce rêve pour quatre personnes – découvrez leurs témoignages.

Amanda (23 ans), jeune maman de deux filles, a échangé sa vie avec son amie Cindy (30 ans), serveuse dans un restaurant-club huppé de Londres.

Le récit d'Amanda

Je n'avais jamais mis les pieds dans un endroit pareil. J'étais stupéfaite par l'obscurité et le bruit – il y avait tellement de monde et une ambiance incroyable. C'était à mille lieues de ma ville natale et, pour être honnête, je ne savais pas si j'allais tenir le coup ! Être maman, c'est déjà un travail prenant, mais là, c'était autre chose !

Je n'avais que quinze minutes pour apprendre à porter un plateau de boissons à hauteur d'épaule d'une seule main. Les autres serveuses semblaient s'en sortir si facilement, mais au moment même où je commençais à prendre le coup de main, les boissons ont commencé à glisser du plateau et à se renverser par terre, éclaboussant tout sur leur passage. J'étais tellement gênée, mais toutes les autres serveuses ont ri. On fait tous des erreurs au début !

À l'ouverture, à 11 h 30, une file d'attente s'était déjà formée dehors et j'ai commencé à être vraiment nerveuse. Je m'inquiétais de savoir comment j'allais me souvenir de toutes les commandes, mais au moins, ce n'était pas un problème puisque tout était automatisé.

Après quelques heures, j'avais vraiment mal aux pieds et je n'arrivais pas à m'habituer à la musique forte et constante. Chaque fois qu'un client me parlait, je devais dire « Pardon ? », ce qui était tellement gênant ! À la fin de mon service, à 17 h, j'étais complètement épuisée et je rêvais de tremper mes pieds dans une bassine d'eau chaude. Je n'en croyais pas mes oreilles quand une des serveuses m'a dit que la journée avait été « calme » ! Je n'avais jamais réalisé à quel point le métier de serveuse pouvait être épuisant. J'ai toujours cru que c'était un travail pour les timides, mais en fait, il faut être plutôt extravertie, tout en sachant garder son sang-froid et gérer ce qu'on appelle dans le métier une « période de forte affluence » – autrement dit, beaucoup de clients !

Je suis assez timide et je ne pense pas que j'aurais pu tenir le coup un samedi soir, quand c'est la folie. Le salaire ne m'a pas vraiment convaincue non plus. Malheureusement, je devais être une piètre serveuse, car même les Américains fortunés ne m'ont pas laissé un pourboire !

Je dois avouer que j'étais ravie de retrouver mes enfants. Après avoir travaillé comme serveuse, ça paraît tellement plus simple !

B. L'histoire de Cindy

J'appréhendais un peu d'être « maman » pour la journée, mais j'avais aussi hâte. On m'avait prévenue que les filles étaient insolentes, mais dans mon ignorance, je pensais pouvoir gérer la situation. J'étais loin de me douter de ce qui m'attendait !

Alors qu'Amanda partait au restaurant, je devais habiller et donner le petit-déjeuner aux deux filles. Après avoir déposé Sophie à l'école et Katie à la crèche, je pensais avoir trois heures de tranquillité. Raté ! Un mot d'Amanda me rappelait qu'il me restait encore à faire les lits, le ménage et la lessive.

À 13 h, j'ai récupéré Katie, fait un saut au supermarché et l'ai ramenée déjeuner. Mais c'est en ramenant Sophie de l'école que les ennuis ont commencé. Elles ont transformé le canapé en trampoline et se sont mises à hurler à pleins poumons ! J'ai opté pour la patience, pensant qu'elles finiraient par se fatiguer. Encore une erreur. Je pensais avoir une bonne endurance, mais elles m'ont battue à plate couture !

Après bien des efforts, j'ai réussi à les coucher vers 20 h, mais là, les ennuis ont commencé ! Combien de verres d'eau un enfant peut-il boire, bon sang ? Bien sûr, je savais que ce n'était qu'un prétexte pour qu'ils descendent regarder la télévision, mais passer toute la soirée à négocier avec eux était épuisant.

Je n'avais jamais réalisé à quel point s'occuper de deux jeunes enfants pouvait être fatigant. On n'a pas une seconde pour soi, et le sentiment de responsabilité est tout simplement accablant. Malgré tout, j'ai vraiment passé une excellente journée.

Rosemary (42 ans) tient une ferme laitière. Elle a échangé sa place avec Hilary (30 ans), institutrice.

C. Le témoignage de Rosemary

À la ferme, je dois me lever à 5h30, alors dormir jusqu'à 7h était un vrai luxe ! Mais j'ai longuement hésité sur ma tenue. Je ne pouvais tout de même pas me présenter en salopette et bottes, n'est-ce pas ?

En voyant cette foule immense – environ 400 élèves – lors de l'assemblée, j'espérais me fondre dans le décor et que mon teint frais ne me fasse pas remarquer comme une fermière.

Ensuite, c'était l'heure du cours de maths. Les enfants travaillaient en petits groupes, utilisant des fiches d'exercices classées par niveau de difficulté – bien différent de mon époque scolaire où nous devions réciter les tables de multiplication à l'unisson ! Ensuite, j'ai participé à un projet nature : identifier et nourrir différentes espèces d'escargots.

À l'heure du déjeuner, j'étais épuisée et j'attendais avec impatience une heure de pause, mais les professeurs n'ont que cinq minutes pour déjeuner. Il y a tellement à faire avant la reprise des cours. J'ai assisté à une réunion de l'équipe pédagogique concernant les bulletins et je n'ai pas pu éviter de donner un coup de main pour les sélections d'athlétisme.

Après le déjeuner, il y a eu une séance de lecture silencieuse (un vrai bonheur !) puis un cours de français dans la salle vidéo. C'était très amusant car tous les enfants voulaient s'entraîner sur moi, ce qui a bien mis en évidence mon français rouillé.

Enfin, nous sommes allés au gymnase pour le cours d'EPS. J'étais exténuée, mais les enfants semblaient avoir une énergie inépuisable.

Le plus difficile était de prendre la parole devant la classe – même deux minutes, c'est intimidant. Les enseignants ont peut-être plus de vacances par an, mais je crois que je vais rester agricultrice !

Le récit de D. Hilary

Je suis arrivée à la ferme White House à 8h30, de bonne heure, pour découvrir que Rosemary était levée depuis trois heures ! Sa ferme de 113 hectares compte 100 vaches Jersey, 15 veaux et génisses et environ 800 brebis ! Outre le lait, elle fabrique de la crème glacée, des yaourts et de la crème, vendus dans les magasins, les restaurants et les sites touristiques. J'ai passé la majeure partie de la matinée à la fabrique de glaces, à embouteiller le lait dans des bouteilles d'un litre, à presser la crème glacée dans des pots et à coller les étiquettes. Difficile de résister à l'envie d'y tremper les doigts ! À midi, il était temps d'aller voir les moutons. Je suis allée en voiture dans un champ et j'ai ramassé une brebis qui était tombée. Si on laisse les brebis plus de 12 heures après qu'elles soient tombées, elles risquent de mourir. Il faut donc les surveiller tous les jours. Quel cauchemar en hiver !

Après avoir nourri les veaux, j'ai commencé la traite. L'opération a duré deux heures et demie, un travail épuisant. Et Rosemary le fait deux fois par jour, dès 6 heures du matin, sept jours sur sept, 365 jours par an !

J'ai trouvé cette journée assez solitaire. J'ai été surprise de constater à quel point les enfants me manquaient – ​​les animaux ne répondent pas ! Le pire, c'est de ne pas pouvoir s'absenter. Il faut traire les vaches deux fois par jour, alors c'est vraiment difficile de prendre des congés. Rosemary n'aura que trois jours de vacances cette année.

La vie à la ferme semble romantique, mais la réalité est tout autre. Les revenus sont irréguliers et je détesterais être à la merci des caprices de la météo.

The children worked in small groups, using worksheets categorized by level of difficulty—quite different from my school days when we had to recite the multiplication tables in unison! Afterward, I participated in a nature project: identifying and feeding different species of snails.

At lunchtime, I was exhausted and eagerly anticipating an hour's break, but the teachers only have five minutes for lunch. There's so much to do before classes resume. I attended a staff meeting about report cards and couldn't resist helping out with the athletics selections.

After lunch, there was a silent reading session (pure bliss!) followed by a French lesson in the video room. It was great fun because all the children wanted to practice on me, which really highlighted my rusty French.

Finally, we went to the gym for PE. I was worn out, but the children seemed to have boundless energy.

The hardest part was speaking in front of the class—even two minutes is intimidating. Teachers may have more vacation time per year, but I think I'll stay a farmer!

D. Hilary's Story

I arrived at White House Farm at 8:30 a.m., bright and early, only to find Rosemary had been up for three hours! Her 113-hectare farm has 100 Jersey cows, 15 calves and heifers, and about 800 ewes! Besides milk, she makes ice cream, yogurt, and cream, which are sold in shops, restaurants, and at tourist sites. I spent most of the morning at the ice cream factory, bottling milk into liter bottles, squeezing ice cream into tubs, and sticking on labels. It was hard to resist dipping my fingers in! At noon, it was time to check on the sheep. I drove to a field and picked up a ewe that had fallen over. If ewes are left for more than 12 hours after they fall, they can die. So they have to be checked on every day. What a nightmare in winter!

After feeding the calves, I started milking. It took two and a half hours, exhausting work. And Rosemary does it twice a day, starting at 6:00 a.m., seven days a week, 365 days a year!

I found it a rather lonely day. I was surprised to realize how much I missed the children—animals don't respond! The worst part is not being able to get away. The cows have to be milked twice a day, so it's really difficult to take time off. Rosemary will only have three days of vacation this year.

Life on the farm sounds romantic, but the reality is quite different. The income is irregular, and I would hate to be at the mercy of the weather.

Little Chefs

For one group of children aged between ten and fifteen, Saturdays are spent learning the art of serious cooking. Their weekly lessons in small classes are so popular that there is a waiting list of 30 children who want to do the course. Parents pay PS280 for the course where their children can have fun and learn how to make good food.
Class member Bill, aged ten, says, 'I love my mum's cooking and now I can do it better than her. The teachers make us laugh, especially when we sit down with them to share the food we've made.'
Flora is twelve, and she's having problems preparing onions. 'I love cooking. I did a meal for ten friends which they really enjoyed. Then my mum suggested I take up a hobby, instead of doing nothing at weekends. I was happy staying at home, so I wasn't too keen at first. I'm really glad I decided to come, though.'
Their teacher, Philippe, says, 'It's great fun. Children pay attention and remember things better than adults, although the kitchen isn't always as tidy when they're cooking! As adults, we're always learning more about food. If parents interest their children in cooking while they are young, they'll have enough skill to make food for themselves when they leave home.'

results.title: 12.txt
results.src_text:
CARTOON FILMS 

Cartoon films have very few limits. If you can draw something, you can make it move on the cinema screen. The use of new ideas and advanced computer programs means that cartoons are becoming exciting again for people of all ages. 
By the end of the 1970s, the cinema world had decided that cartoons were only for children. 
But soon afterwards, one or two directors had some original new ideas. They proved that it was possible to make films in which both adults and children could share the fun. 
However, not every cartoon film was successful. The Black Cauldron, for example, failed, mainly because it was too frightening for children and too childish for adults. Directors learnt from this mistake, and the film companies began to make large amounts of money again.
results.tgt_text:
FILMS D'ANIMATION

Les films d'animation n'ont quasiment aucune limite. Tout dessin peut prendre vie sur grand écran. Grâce à des idées novatrices et des logiciels informatiques de pointe, les dessins animés retrouvent leur attrait auprès d'un public de tous âges.

À la fin des années 1970, le monde du cinéma considérait les dessins animés comme un genre réservé aux enfants.

Mais peu après, quelques réalisateurs ont proposé des idées originales. Ils ont prouvé qu'il était possible de réaliser des films où petits et grands pouvaient partager leur plaisir.

Cependant, tous les films d'animation n'ont pas rencontré le succès. Taram et le Chaudron magique, par exemple, fut un échec, principalement parce qu'il était trop effrayant pour les enfants et trop enfantin pour les adultes. Les réalisateurs ont tiré les leçons de cette erreur et les studios ont recommencé à prospérer.

ANIMATED FILMS

Animated films have virtually no limits. Any drawing can come to life on the big screen. Thanks to innovative ideas and cutting-edge computer software, cartoons are regaining their appeal with audiences of all ages.

results.src_text:
Simon Costello knew that the purchase of the house in Pembroke Square had been a mistake within a year of his and Lois's moving in. A possession which can only be afforded by the exercise of stringent and calculated economy is best not afforded at all. But at the time it had seemed a sensible, as well as a desirable, move. He had had a run of successful cases and they were coming in with reassuring regularity. Lois had returned to her job at the advertising agency within two months of the birth of the twins, and had been given a rise which took her salary to thirty-five thousand. It was Lois who had argued the more strongly for a move, but he had put up little resistance to arguments which at the time had seemed compelling: the flat wasn't really suitable for a family, they needed more room, a garden, separate accommodation for an au pair. All these, of course, could have been achieved in a suburb or in a less fashionable part of London than Pembroke Square, but Lois was ambitious for more than additional space. Mornington Mansions had never been an acceptable address for an up-and-coming young barrister and a successful businesswoman. She never said it without a sense that even speaking the words subtly diminished her standing, socially and economically.
Lois had decided that a necessary economy was for one of them to travel by public transport. Her firm was on the other side of London; obviously Simon must be the one to economise. The overcrowded tube journey, stayed in a mood of envious resentment, had become an unproductive thirty minutes of brooding on present discontents. He would recall his grandfather's house in Hampstead where he had stayed as a boy, the smell of dinner from the kitchen, his grandmother's insistence that the returning breadwinner, tired from his exhausting day in court, should be given peace, a little gentle cosseting, and relief from every petty domestic anxiety. She had been a 'lawyer's wife', indefatigable in legal good causes, elegantly present at all lawyers' functions, apparently content with the sphere of life which she had made her own. Well, that world had passed for ever. Lois had made it plain before their marriage that her career was as important as his. It hardly needed saying, this was, after all, a modern marriage. The job was important to her and important to them both. The house, the au pair, their whole standard of living depended on two salaries. And now what they were precariously achieving could be destroyed by that self-righteous, interfering Venetia.
Venetia must have come straight from the court to their offices and she had been in a dangerous mood. Something or someone had upset her. But the word 'upset' was too weak, too bland for the intensity of furious disgust with which she had confronted him. Someone had driven her to the limit of her endurance. He cursed himself. If he hadn't been in his room, if he'd only left a minute earlier, the encounter wouldn't have taken place, she would have had the night to think it over, to consider what, if anything, she ought to do. Probably nothing. The morning might have brought sense. He remembered every word of her angry accusations.
'I defended Brian Cartwright today. Successfully. He told me that when you were his counsel four years ago you knew before trial that he had bribed three of the jury. You did nothing. You went on with the case. Is that true?'
'He's lying. It isn't true.'
'He also said that he passed over some shares in his company to your fiancee. Also before trial. Is that true?'
'I tell you, he's lying. None of its true.'
The denial had been as instinctive as an arm raised to ward off a blow and had sounded unconvincing even to his own ears. His whole action had been one of guilt. The first cold horror draining his face was succeeded by a hot flush, bringing back shameful memories of his headmaster's study, of the terror of the inevitable punishment. He had made himself look into her eyes and had seen the look of contemptuous disbelief. If only he'd had some warning. He knew now what he should have said: 'Cartwright told me after the trial but I didn't believe him. I don't believe him now. That man will say anything to make himself important.'
But he had told a more direct, more dangerous lie, and she had known that it was a lie. Even so, why the anger, why the disgust? What was that old misdemeanour to do with her? Who had sent Venetia Aldridge to be guardian of the conscience of their legal practice? Or of his, come to that? Was her own conscience so clear, her behaviour in court always immaculate? Was she justified in destroying his career? And it would be destruction. He wasn't sure what exactly she could do, how far she was prepared to go, but if this got about, even as a rumour, he was done for.

Simon Costello sut, moins d'un an après son emménagement avec Lois, que l'achat de la maison à Pembroke Square avait été une erreur. Un bien immobilier qu'on ne peut se permettre qu'au prix d'une économie rigoureuse et calculée est mieux évité. Mais à l'époque, cela lui avait paru un choix judicieux, voire souhaitable. Il enchaînait les succès et les dossiers s'enchaînaient avec une régularité rassurante. Lois avait repris son travail à l'agence de publicité deux mois après la naissance des jumeaux et avait obtenu une augmentation portant son salaire à trente-cinq mille livres. C'est Lois qui avait insisté le plus pour déménager, mais il n'avait guère résisté à des arguments qui, à l'époque, lui semblaient convaincants : l'appartement n'était pas vraiment adapté à une famille, il leur fallait plus d'espace, un jardin, un logement indépendant pour une jeune fille au pair. Bien sûr, tout cela aurait pu être réalisé en banlieue ou dans un quartier moins huppé de Londres que Pembroke Square, mais Lois avait des ambitions qui dépassaient le simple besoin d'espace supplémentaire. Mornington Mansions n'avait jamais été une adresse convenable pour un jeune avocat prometteur et une femme d'affaires prospère. Elle ne le prononçait jamais sans avoir la sensation que, même en prononçant ces mots, elle en diminuait subtilement le statut social et économique.

Lois avait décidé que, par souci d'économie, l'un d'eux prendrait les transports en commun. Son cabinet se trouvait à l'autre bout de Londres ; il était donc évident que Simon devait faire des économies. Le trajet en métro bondé, passé dans une humeur empreinte d'envie et de ressentiment, s'était transformé en une demi-heure improductive passée à ruminer ses mécontentements. Il se souvenait de la maison de son grand-père à Hampstead où il avait séjourné enfant, de l'odeur du dîner qui s'échappait de la cuisine, de l'insistance de sa grand-mère pour que le soutien de famille, de retour de sa journée épuisante au tribunal, puisse bénéficier de tranquillité, d'un peu de douceur et d'un répit face à tous ses petits soucis domestiques. Elle avait été une « femme d'avocat », infatigable dans les causes juridiques, toujours présente avec élégance aux réceptions des avocats, apparemment comblée par la sphère d'activité qu'elle s'était choisie. Ce monde-là était révolu. Lois avait clairement indiqué avant leur mariage que sa carrière était aussi importante que la sienne. Cela allait de soi, après tout, il s'agissait d'un mariage moderne. Le travail était important pour elle, et important pour eux deux. La maison, la jeune fille au pair, tout leur niveau de vie dépendait de deux salaires. Et maintenant, tout ce qu'ils étaient en train de construire, si difficilement, pouvait être anéanti par cette Venetia, si moralisatrice et si intrusive.

Venetia devait arriver directement du tribunal à leurs bureaux, et elle était d'une humeur dangereuse. Quelque chose ou quelqu'un l'avait contrariée. Mais le mot « contrariée » était trop faible, trop fade pour décrire l'intensité du dégoût furieux avec lequel elle l'avait confronté. Quelqu'un l'avait poussée à bout. Il se maudit. S'il n'avait pas été dans sa chambre, s'il était parti une minute plus tôt, la rencontre n'aurait pas eu lieu. Elle aurait eu la nuit pour y réfléchir, pour décider de ce qu'elle devait faire, le cas échéant. Probablement rien. Le lendemain matin lui aurait peut-être apporté la raison. Il se souvenait de chaque mot de ses accusations furieuses.

« J'ai défendu Brian Cartwright aujourd'hui. Avec succès. Il m'a dit que lorsque vous étiez son avocate il y a quatre ans, vous saviez avant le procès qu'il avait soudoyé trois jurés. Vous n'avez rien fait. Vous avez continué la procédure. Est-ce vrai ? »

« Il ment. Ce n'est pas vrai. »

« Il a aussi dit qu'il avait cédé des actions de sa société à votre fiancée. Également avant le procès. Est-ce vrai ? »

« Je vous le dis, il ment. Rien de tout cela n'est vrai. »

Ce démenti avait été aussi instinctif qu'un bras levé pour parer un coup et n'avait pas convaincu, même à ses propres oreilles. Toute sa réaction avait été un aveu de culpabilité. La première vague d'horreur glaciale qui lui avait envahi le visage fut suivie d'une bouffée de chaleur, ravivant les souvenirs honteux du bureau de son directeur, la terreur de l'inévitable punition. Il s'était forcé à la regarder dans les yeux et y avait vu un regard de mépris et d'incrédulité. Si seulement il avait été prévenu ! Il savait maintenant ce qu'il aurait dû dire : « Cartwright me l'a dit après le procès, mais je ne l'ai pas cru. Je ne le crois toujours pas. Cet homme est capable de tout pour se mettre en avant. »

Mais il avait proféré un mensonge plus direct, plus dangereux, et elle savait que c'était un mensonge. Malgré tout, pourquoi cette colère, pourquoi ce dégoût ? Quel rapport avec elle, cette vieille faute ? Qui avait envoyé Venetia Aldridge veiller à la conscience de leur cabinet d'avocats ? Ou à la sienne, d'ailleurs ? Sa propre conscience était-elle si pure, son comportement toujours irréprochable au tribunal ? Était-elle justifiée de détruire sa carrière ? Et ce serait une destruction. Il ne savait pas exactement ce qu'elle pouvait faire, jusqu'où elle était prête à aller, mais si cela se répandait, même sous forme de rumeur, il était perdu.

results.src_text:
A trumpet isn't just for Christmas...

It is strange how many musicians, even leading ones, come from homes without music. Out of the blue, Hakan Hardenberger, the only son of totally unmusical parents in a country district of southern Sweden, has at the age of 30 established himself as unique among the world's trumpet-players today.
His records are continually opening up new repertory, not just concertos by long-neglected composers of the baroque and classical periods, but new works too. When you meet him, bright-eyed and good-looking, he seems even younger than his years, as fresh and open in his manner as the sound of the trumpet.
Recently in one of London's premier concert halls he played the Hummel Trumpet Concerto, something of a party-piece for him, while on television a whole feature was devoted to his work and development, filmed both here and in Sweden.
Born near Malmo, he owes his career to the accident of a Christmas present when he was only eight.
His father, unmusical but liking Louis Armstrong's playing, had the idea of giving his only son a trumpet. Being a serious man, he didn't pick a toy trumpet, but took advice and bought a genuine grown-up instrument.
The success of the gift was instant. The boy never stopped playing. His mother managed to contact the second trumpet-player in the Malmo Symphony Orchestra, whom she persuaded to give her son lessons.
Bo Nilsson was an up-and-coming musician, and at once spotted natural talent. Hardenberger consistently blesses his luck to have got such a teacher right from the start, one who was himself so obsessed with the trumpet and trumpet-playing that he would search out and contact players all over the world, and as a 'trumpet fanatic' was 'always looking for another mouthpiece'.
There the mature Hardenberger has to draw a line between himself and his teacher. 'The trumpet is so primitive an instrument,' he explains, 'that you can't build a trumpet that is acoustically perfect. Whatever you do, it will have imperfections. Besides, you can't find two mouthpieces exactly the same. To me it is a matter of getting to know the imperfections and making a relationship with them.'
From the very start Hardenberger seems to have had the gift of finding the right compromise, and making that relationship. Without any sense of boasting, he explains that even in his boyhood years the characteristic Hardenberger sound was already recognisable, 'the first thing I acquired'.
And unlike the great British contender among virtuoso trumpet-players, John Wallace, who developed originally from a brass-band background and then through working in orchestras, Hardenberger has always thought of himself as a solo artist pure and simple.
From early boyhood he had as a role-model the French trumpeter, Maurice Andre, another player who bypassed the orchestra. The boy bought all his records, and idolised him.
His parents gave him every chance to practise, and went along with his ambition to make trumpet-playing a career. It was then a question of where, at 15, he should be sent to study. America, Bo Nilsson's first choice, was thought to be too far away and too dangerous, which meant that he went instead at the age of 16 to study in Paris with Pierre Thibaud. Thibaud confirmed his prejudice against going into an orchestra, saying that 'Playing in the orchestra is like digging in the garden.'
He was objective enough about himself to know that he played the trumpet better than others of his age, but it was only at the end of the first competition he entered, at the age of 17 during his first year in Paris, that he came to realise that in addition he had a particular gift of communicating.
Thibaud suggested that he should enter the competition just for experience. Hardenberger learned the pieces for the first round only, but he won through to the second. Luckily he already knew most of the pieces in that round too, but on getting through to the final he was faced with a concerto that had already daunted him. He didn't win first prize that time, but he enjoyed the performance, realising that though he 'played like a pig', people did listen to him.
Quoted like that, Hardenberger's realism about his work and his career may sound arrogant, but that would be a totally false impression. Thoughtfully he refuses to try and analyse what such a gift of communication might consist of, as 'You risk destroying it in trying to explain. The power of the music lies in the fact that it can always move people.'
results.tgt_text:
La trompette n'est pas qu'un instrument de Noël…

Il est étonnant de constater combien de musiciens, même parmi les plus renommés, viennent de familles où la musique n'était pas présente. Hakan Hardenberger, fils unique de parents totalement étrangers à la musique, originaire d'une région rurale du sud de la Suède, s'est imposé à seulement 30 ans comme un trompettiste unique en son genre.

Ses enregistrements explorent sans cesse de nouveaux répertoires, non seulement des concertos de compositeurs baroques et classiques longtemps oubliés, mais aussi des œuvres contemporaines. Lorsqu'on le rencontre, le regard pétillant et le visage rayonnant, il paraît encore plus jeune que son âge, aussi frais et ouvert dans sa manière d'être que le son de sa trompette.

Récemment, dans l'une des plus prestigieuses salles de concert londoniennes, il a interprété le Concerto pour trompette de Hummel, une pièce qu'il affectionne particulièrement, tandis qu'un reportage télévisé lui était consacré, tourné en Angleterre et en Suède.

Né près de Malmö, il doit sa carrière au hasard d'un cadeau de Noël reçu alors qu'il n'avait que huit ans. Son père, peu musicien mais admirateur de Louis Armstrong, eut l'idée d'offrir une trompette à son fils unique. Homme sérieux, il ne choisit pas une trompette jouet, mais suivit les conseils d'un expert et acheta un véritable instrument pour adulte.

Le succès fut immédiat. Le garçon ne cessa jamais de jouer. Sa mère parvint à contacter le second trompettiste de l'Orchestre symphonique de Malmö, qu'elle persuada de donner des cours à son fils.

Bo Nilsson était un musicien prometteur et reconnut aussitôt le talent naturel du jeune homme. Hardenberger ne cesse de se féliciter d'avoir eu un tel professeur dès le départ, un homme si passionné par la trompette et son jeu qu'il recherchait et contactait des musiciens du monde entier et, véritable « fanatique de la trompette », était « toujours à la recherche d'un nouvel embouchure ».

C'est là que Hardenberger, devenu adulte, se sent obligé de prendre ses distances avec son professeur. « La trompette est un instrument tellement primitif », explique-t-il, « qu'il est impossible de construire une trompette acoustiquement parfaite. Quoi qu'on fasse, elle aura toujours des imperfections. De plus, on ne trouve pas deux embouchures exactement identiques. Pour moi, il s'agit d'apprendre à connaître ces imperfections et à composer avec elles. »

Dès ses débuts, Hardenberger semble avoir eu le don de trouver le juste compromis et d'établir cette relation. Sans la moindre prétention, il explique que, même enfant, le son Hardenberger caractéristique était déjà reconnaissable : « C'est la première chose que j'ai acquise. »

Et contrairement au grand virtuose britannique de la trompette, John Wallace, qui a fait ses armes dans les fanfares puis au sein d'orchestres, Hardenberger s'est toujours considéré comme un soliste, tout simplement.

Dès son plus jeune âge, il avait pour modèle le trompettiste français Maurice André, lui aussi musicien indépendant. Le garçon achetait tous ses disques et l'idolâtrait. Ses parents lui offraient toutes les occasions de s'exercer et soutenaient son ambition de faire carrière dans la trompette. Se posait alors la question de savoir où, à 15 ans, il devrait aller étudier. L'Amérique, son premier choix, était jugée trop lointaine et trop dangereuse, ce qui l'amena à partir à 16 ans étudier à Paris avec Pierre Thibaud. Ce dernier confirma ses préjugés contre l'entrée dans un orchestre, déclarant : « Jouer dans un orchestre, c'est comme bêcher son jardin. »

Il était suffisamment objectif pour savoir qu'il jouait de la trompette mieux que les autres de son âge, mais ce n'est qu'à la fin du premier concours auquel il participa, à 17 ans, lors de sa première année parisienne, qu'il prit conscience de son don particulier pour la communication.

Thibaud lui suggéra de participer au concours simplement pour acquérir de l'expérience. Hardenberger n'apprit les morceaux que pour le premier tour, mais il se qualifia pour le second. Heureusement, il connaissait déjà la plupart des morceaux de ce tour, mais en finale, il se retrouva face à un concerto qui l'intimidait déjà. Il ne remporta pas le premier prix cette fois-ci, mais il apprécia sa prestation, réalisant que même s'il avait « joué comme un pied », le public l'écoutait.

Pris ainsi, le réalisme d'Hardenberger concernant son travail et sa carrière pourrait paraître arrogant, mais ce serait une erreur. Réfléchi, il refuse d'analyser en quoi consiste un tel don de communication, car « On risque de le détruire en essayant de l'expliquer. La force de la musique réside dans sa capacité à toujours émouvoir. »
results.back_text:
The trumpet isn't just a Christmas instrument…

It's astonishing how many musicians, even some of the most renowned, come from families where music wasn't a part of their lives. Hakan Hardenberger, the only child of parents with no musical background, hailing from a rural region in southern Sweden, established himself at just 30 years old as a trumpeter unlike any other.

His recordings constantly explore new repertoires, not only concertos by long-forgotten Baroque and Classical composers, but also contemporary works. When you meet him, with his twinkling eyes and radiant face, he seems even younger than his age, as fresh and open in his manner as the sound of his trumpet.

Recently, in one of London's most prestigious concert halls, he performed Hummel's Trumpet Concerto, a piece he particularly loves, while a television documentary about him was filmed in England and Sweden.

Born near Malmö, he owes his career to a chance Christmas gift he received when he was only eight years old. His father, not much of a musician himself but an admirer of Louis Armstrong, had the idea of ​​giving his only son a trumpet. A serious man, he didn't choose a toy trumpet, but followed the advice of an expert and bought a real adult instrument.

The success was immediate. The boy never stopped playing. His mother managed to contact the second trumpeter of the Malmö Symphony Orchestra, whom she persuaded to give her son lessons.

Bo Nilsson was a promising musician and immediately recognized the young man's natural talent. Hardenberger is always grateful to have had such a teacher from the start, a man so passionate about the trumpet and playing it that he sought out and contacted musicians all over the world and, a true "trumpet fanatic," was "always on the lookout for a new mouthpiece."

It was at this point that Hardenberger, now an adult, felt compelled to distance himself from his teacher. “The trumpet is such a primitive instrument,” he explains, “that it’s impossible to build an acoustically perfect trumpet. No matter what you do, it will always have imperfections. Furthermore, you can’t find two mouthpieces that are exactly alike. For me, it’s about learning to recognize these imperfections and working with them.”

From the very beginning, Hardenberger seems to have had a knack for finding the right compromise and establishing this relationship. Without the slightest pretension, he explains that, even as a child, the characteristic Hardenberger sound was already recognizable: “It’s the first thing I acquired.”

And unlike the great British trumpet virtuoso, John Wallace, who honed his skills in brass bands and then orchestras, Hardenberger has always considered himself simply a soloist.

From a very young age, he idolized the French trumpeter Maurice André, also an independent musician. The boy bought all his records and adored him. His parents gave him every opportunity to practice and supported his ambition to pursue a career as a trumpeter. The question then arose of where, at 15, he should go to study. America, his first choice, was considered too far away and too dangerous, which led him to leave at 16 to study in Paris with Pierre Thibaud. Thibaud confirmed his prejudices against joining an orchestra, declaring: "Playing in an orchestra is like digging your garden."

He was objective enough to know that he played the trumpet better than others his age, but it wasn't until the end of his first competition, at 17, during his first year in Paris, that he became aware of his particular gift for communication.

Thibaud suggested he enter the competition simply to gain experience. Hardenberger only learned the pieces for the first round, but he qualified for the second. Fortunately, he already knew most of the pieces for this round, but in the final, he found himself facing a concerto that already intimidated him. He didn't win first prize this time, but he appreciated his performance, realizing that even though he had "played terribly," the audience was listening.

Taken this way, Hardenberger's realism about his work and career might seem arrogant, but that would be a mistake. Thoughtfully, he refuses to analyze what constitutes such a gift for communication, because "You risk destroying it by trying to explain it. The power of music lies in its ability to always move people."

The Actor's Craft

Derision and contempt are sprayed at actors from time to time. Much of this disdain is fuelled by the actors themselves when they're compelled by their film/theatre companies to talk about their craft (and themselves) in interviews. They should give the dancer Pavlova's reply to the man who asked her what she meant when she was dancing: 'If I could tell you,' she said, 'I wouldn't dance it.' But instead they all too easily fall into ponderous cliches, silly truisms or into the prurient jaws of the gossip machine. We should all pay heed to what Paul Scofield said in a letter to a friend of mine: 'I have found that an actor's work has life and interest only in its execution. It seems to wither away in discussion and become emptily theoretical and insubstantial. It has no rules (except perhaps audibility). With every play and every playwright the actor starts from scratch, as if he or she knows nothing and proceeds to learn afresh every time growing with the relationships of the characters and the insights of the writer. When the play has finished its run, he's empty until the next time. And its the emptiness which is, I find, apparent in any discussion of theatre work.'

A review of Hamlet

Adrian Lester's Hamlet is poised precariously between boyhood and manhood, and it is a performance of thrilling simplicity and assurance. His handling of the text and his physical and psychological self-control take him, in one leap, from brilliantly promising to frontline player: an actor with the intelligent confidence to be almost self-effacing. Lester plays an edgy, tetchy young man who feeds on a banked-down sense of anger, agile, watchful and driven, he deploys a sense of acid wit and generous humour that makes him both formidable and lovable. Although played down, the virtuosity of this performance is unmistakable. Observe Lester's body, the way his arms hang stiffly, giving you a sense of a figure waiting to be animated. Handy's portrayal of Horatio gives you a similar feeling of a body being moved by an inner force that he both knows and does not know. So what is acting? What is behaviour? Is the former an imitation or an evocation of the latter? Who and what animates these bodies, morally and physically? That is the central question about the life of the theatre.

One director's approach to rehearsal

The first stage of this director's rehearsal process is known as 'dropping in', a procedure which goes something like this. The stage manager projects the script onto a screen. The actors sit quietly while someone else is speaking, finding out what effect the words are having. When if is their turn to speak, they glance of the screen, digest the first phrase, think about what it means to them, wait to find the impulse - the reason to speak - then speak. For example, the line is, 'Queuing all night, the rain, do you remember?; Breathe. Let the thought drop in with your breath. A memory, a vision, an impression. Some people will imagine a queue, maybe at a bus stop on the way to rehearsals or for a rock concert in their youth. Having visualised the scene, find the impulse to speak it - what this director calls 'The pathway to the line'. Impulses can come from without or within. Look in the eyes of the other actor listening. Consider your character's situation. This director talks of 'dropping in' as a means of finding out what is going on. Don't pre-plan or pre-judge. Dare to go down there with an empty mind and trust that something will happen to you.

The Perfect Theatre

The perfect theatre should make you feel as if your presence has made a difference. Going to the theatre, going to any live performance, is an event and the staff need to have a sense of that, too. It's terribly alienating if you feel that its just any old job for the people working front of house.
The theatre itself needs to create a relationship between the performer and the audience - no one in the audience should feel that they're getting an unreasonably prejudiced view of the actor. It's important that they're not too far away, they can hear, they can see, they can feel in some sense in contact with what's going on on stage. The proportions of an auditorium are important. They have to respond to the human voice and the scale of the human body. If an auditorium dwarfs the human body, there's something wrong with it because you can't deny the human form at the heart of drama. A lot of theatres in the late nineteenth century got it right because they managed to shape an auditorium that somehow embraces the stage.
I like theatres that have a sense of the past in them. Like worn stone steps in a church, you get the sense of layers of human presence. From the point of view of the plays, you can't have something for everybody. You cant second-guess an audience because they don't know what they're going to want to see. When you visit the theatre, you want something done in a way you can't imagine, otherwise you may as well have stayed at home.
results.tgt_text:
L'art de l'acteur

Les acteurs sont parfois la cible de dérision et de mépris. Ce dédain est souvent alimenté par les acteurs eux-mêmes, contraints par leurs compagnies de cinéma ou de théâtre de parler de leur métier (et d'eux-mêmes) lors d'interviews. Ils devraient citer la réponse de la danseuse Pavlova à l'homme qui lui demandait ce qu'elle voulait dire en dansant : « Si je pouvais vous le dire, je ne le danserais pas. » Mais au lieu de cela, ils tombent trop facilement dans des clichés pesants, des vérités banales ou dans les griffes malsaines de la presse à scandale. Nous devrions tous méditer sur ce que Paul Scofield écrivait à un ami : « J'ai constaté que le travail d'un acteur n'a de vie et d'intérêt que dans son exécution. Il semble se flétrir dans la discussion et devenir une théorie vide et inconsistante. Il n'a pas de règles (si ce n'est peut-être celle de l'audibilité). » À chaque pièce, pour chaque dramaturge, l'acteur repart de zéro, comme s'il ne savait rien, et apprend sans cesse, évoluant au gré des relations entre les personnages et des intuitions de l'auteur. Une fois la pièce terminée, il est vidé jusqu'à la prochaine représentation. Et c'est ce vide, me semble-t-il, qui transparaît dans toute discussion sur le travail théâtral.

Critique d'Hamlet

L'Hamlet d'Adrian Lester oscille avec une fragilité troublante entre l'enfance et l'âge adulte, offrant une performance d'une simplicité et d'une assurance saisissantes. Sa maîtrise du texte, son contrôle physique et psychologique, le propulsent d'un seul élan de promesse à celui d'acteur de premier plan : un acteur d'une confiance intelligente qui frôle l'effacement. Lester incarne un jeune homme nerveux et irritable, nourri d'une colère contenue, agile, vigilant et déterminé. Son esprit mordant et son humour généreux le rendent à la fois redoutable et attachant. Bien que discrète, la virtuosité de cette performance est indéniable. Observez le corps de Lester, la raideur de ses bras, qui évoque une figure en attente d'animation. L'interprétation d'Horatio par Handy procure une sensation similaire, celle d'un corps mû par une force intérieure à la fois consciente et insaisissable. Alors, qu'est-ce que jouer la comédie ? Qu'est-ce que se comporter ? Le premier est-il une imitation ou une évocation du second ? Qui et quoi anime ces corps, moralement et physiquement ? Telle est la question centrale de la vie théâtrale.

L'approche d'un metteur en scène en matière de répétitions

La première étape du processus de répétition de ce metteur en scène est appelée « prise de contact ». La procédure se déroule ainsi : le régisseur projette le texte sur un écran. Les acteurs restent assis en silence pendant qu'une autre personne parle, afin d'en percevoir l'effet. Quand vient leur tour de parler, ils jettent un coup d'œil à l'écran, assimilent la première phrase, réfléchissent à sa signification pour eux, attendent l'impulsion – la raison de parler – puis prennent la parole. Par exemple, la réplique est : « Faire la queue toute la nuit, sous la pluie, tu te souviens ? » Respirez. Laissez la pensée vous traverser l'esprit. Un souvenir, une vision, une impression. Certains imagineront une file d'attente, peut-être à un arrêt de bus en allant aux répétitions ou à un concert de rock dans leur jeunesse. Une fois la scène visualisée, trouvez l'impulsion de la dire – ce que ce metteur en scène appelle « le chemin vers la réplique ». Les impulsions peuvent venir de l'extérieur ou de l'intérieur. Regardez l'autre acteur dans les yeux. Prenez en compte la situation de votre personnage. Ce metteur en scène parle de « se laisser porter » comme d'un moyen de découvrir ce qui se passe. Ne préparez rien, ne portez aucun jugement. Osez y aller l'esprit vide et ayez confiance : quelque chose va se produire.

Le Théâtre Idéal

Le théâtre idéal devrait vous donner le sentiment que votre présence a eu un impact. Aller au théâtre, assister à n'importe quel spectacle vivant, est un événement, et le personnel doit en avoir conscience lui aussi. C'est terriblement démotivant de penser que pour le personnel d'accueil, ce n'est qu'un travail comme un autre.

Le théâtre lui-même doit créer un lien entre l'artiste et le public ; aucun spectateur ne doit avoir l'impression d'être victime de préjugés. Il est important que les spectateurs ne soient pas trop loin, qu'ils puissent entendre, voir et ressentir, d'une certaine manière, ce qui se passe sur scène. Les proportions d'une salle sont essentielles. Elles doivent être adaptées à la voix et à la stature humaine. Si une salle semble disproportionnée par rapport au corps humain, c'est qu'il y a un problème, car on ne peut nier la place centrale du corps humain dans l'art dramatique. De nombreux théâtres de la fin du XIXe siècle ont trouvé la solution idéale en concevant une salle qui, d'une certaine manière, s'intègre à la scène.

J'aime les théâtres qui portent l'empreinte du passé. Comme les marches de pierre usées d'une église, on y perçoit les différentes strates de présence humaine. Du point de vue théâtral, il est impossible de satisfaire tout le monde. On ne peut pas deviner les goûts du public, car il ignore ce qu'il voudra voir. Quand on va au théâtre, on s'attend à une expérience inédite, sinon autant rester chez soi.

When you go to the theater, you expect a unique experience; otherwise, you might as well stay home.

It was a hot Saturday in early July. The water and sky were blue in the afternoon sun and there were some big waves for the surfers. A lot of them were in the sea. Nick was there, too. He sat on his surfboard and waited for a good wave. A big wave came - Nick started to swim strongly. His board moved quickly with the wave and Nick stood up on it. He was a very  good surfer. 
There were some Australians on the beach. They were there for the surf . . . and for the big surfing competition at the beach in a week's time. One of them was a tall girl with long dark hair - Janelle. She was from Queensland. She watched Nick and then looked at one of the boys with her. Mike smiled. 'He's very good, and that's a strong wave. It'll be difficult to beat him in the competition.' The second boy, Brian, was small with long hair and cold blue eyes. Janelle was his girlfriend.
'We can beat him easily,' Brian said. 'He's only good because he knows the beach here. I can surf well on any beach. I want to catch some waves.' He walked down to the sea. 'I don't want to go in the water now,' Janelle said. 'Let's go and have a drink at the caf,.' Brian sat on his surfboard and watched Nick in the water. 'Mike and Janelle are wrong,' he thought. 'He's not very good.'

It was a hot Saturday in early July. The water and the sky were blue in the afternoon sun, and there were big waves for the surfers. Many surfers were out in the sea. Nick was there too. He was sitting on his surfboard, waiting for a good wave. A big wave came in—Nick started swimming powerfully. His board moved quickly along with the wave, and Nick stood on it. He was a very good surfer.

There were a few Australians on the beach. They were there to surf... and for the big surf competition that would take place on the beach in a week. One of them was a tall girl with long dark hair—Janelle. She was from Queensland. She looked at Nick and then at one of the boys who was with her. Mike smiled. "He is very good, and that is a strong wave. It will be hard to beat him in the competition." The second boy, Brian, was small with long hair and cold blue eyes. Janelle was his girlfriend.
"We can beat him easily," said Brian. "He is only good because he knows the beach here." 'I can surf well on any beach. I want to catch some waves.' He walked towards the sea. 'I don't want to go into the water right now,' said Janelle. 'Let's go get a drink at the café.' Brian sat down on his surfboard and looked at Nick in the water. 'Mike and Janelle are wrong,' he thought. 'He's not very good.'
