Living in the valley

We had been living in our valley for sixteen months when we first realised the dangers that could exist in the surrounding hills and threaten our very survival.
It was the year when the storms came early, before the calendar even hinted at winter, even before November was out. Until that time, we had felt safe and sheltered in our valley below the protecting hills.
Soon snow began to fall. Within a day it lay some 15 centimetres deep. It almost completely blocked our lane and made the streamside path slippery and dangerous. But on the neighbouring heights the snow was much deeper and stayed for longer. Up there the wind blasted fiercely. Deep in our valley we felt only sudden gusts of wind; trees swayed but the branches held firm.
And yet we knew that there was reason for us to worry. The snow and wind were certainly inconvenient but they did not really trouble us greatly. It was the river, the Ryburn, which normally flowed so gently, that threatened us most. It reminded us of what could have occurred if circumstances had been different, if the flow of water from the hills had not, many years before, been controlled, held back by a series of dams.
In a short time the snow started to melt. Day after day, we watched furious clouds pile up high over the hills to the west. Sinister grey clouds extended over the valleys. They twisted and turned, rising eastwards and upwards, warning of what was to come. We had seen enough of the sky; now we began to watch the river, which every day was becoming fuller and wilder.
The snow was gradually washed away as more and more rain streamed from the clouds, but high up in the hills the reservoir was filling and was fast approaching danger level. And then it happened - for the first time in years the reservoir overflowed. There in the heights it was like the Niagara Falls, as the water surged over the edge of the dam and poured into the stream below. 
The river seemed maddened as the waters poured almost horizontally down to its lower stretches. Just a couple of metres from our cottage, the stream seemed wild beneath the bridge. It was far deeper than we'd ever seen it so near our home, lunging furiously at its banks. For three days we prayed that it would stay below its wall. Fortunately, our prayers were answered as the dam held and the waters began to subside.
On many occasions through the centuries before the dam was built, the river had flooded the nearby villages in just such a rage. Now, though, the dam restricts the flow of the river and usually all is well; the great mass of water from the hills, the product of snow and torrential rain, remains behind its barrier with just the occasional overflow. We can thus enjoy, rather than fear, the huge clouds that hang over the valley, and can be thrilled by the tremendous power which we know the river possesses. Thanks to this protection we can feel our home in the valley is still secure and safe.

Leven in het dal

We woonden al zestien maanden in ons dal toen we ons voor het eerst realiseerden welke gevaren er in de omliggende heuvels schuilgingen en ons voortbestaan ​​bedreigden.

Het was het jaar waarin de stormen vroeg kwamen, nog voordat de winter volgens de kalender aankondigde, nog voordat november voorbij was. Tot die tijd hadden we ons veilig en beschut gevoeld in ons dal, onder de beschermende heuvels.

Al snel begon het te sneeuwen. Binnen een dag lag er zo'n vijftien centimeter sneeuw. Het blokkeerde bijna volledig ons pad en maakte het pad langs de beek glad en gevaarlijk. Maar op de naburige heuvels lag de sneeuw veel dieper en bleef langer liggen. Daar waaide het hard. Diep in ons dal voelden we alleen plotselinge windvlagen; de bomen bewogen heen en weer, maar de takken bleven stevig staan.

En toch wisten we dat er reden was om ons zorgen te maken. De sneeuw en de wind waren zeker ongemakkelijk, maar ze baarden ons niet echt grote zorgen. Het was de rivier, de Ryburn, die normaal zo rustig stroomde, die ons het meest bedreigde. Het herinnerde ons aan wat er had kunnen gebeuren als de omstandigheden anders waren geweest, als de waterstroom vanuit de heuvels niet, vele jaren eerder, was beheerst en tegengehouden door een reeks dammen.

In korte tijd begon de sneeuw te smelten. Dag na dag zagen we woeste wolken zich hoog boven de heuvels in het westen opstapelen. Dreigende grijze wolken strekten zich uit over de valleien. Ze draaiden en kronkelden, stegen oostwaarts en omhoog, en waarschuwden voor wat komen zou. We hadden genoeg van de lucht gezien; nu begonnen we de rivier in de gaten te houden, die elke dag voller en wilder werd.

De sneeuw werd geleidelijk weggespoeld naarmate er meer en meer regen uit de wolken stroomde, maar hoog in de heuvels vulde het stuwmeer zich en naderde het snel het gevaarlijke niveau. En toen gebeurde het - voor het eerst in jaren stroomde het stuwmeer over. Daar in de bergen was het net de Niagarawatervallen, toen het water over de rand van de dam stortte en in de beek beneden stroomde.

De rivier leek waanzinnig te worden toen het water bijna horizontaal naar beneden stroomde naar de lagere gedeelten. Op slechts een paar meter van ons huisje leek de beek onder de brug wild. Hij was veel dieper dan we hem ooit zo dicht bij huis hadden gezien en stortte zich woest op de oevers. Drie dagen lang baden we dat hij onder de dam zou blijven. Gelukkig werden onze gebeden verhoord: de dam hield stand en het water begon te zakken.

In de eeuwen vóór de bouw van de dam had de rivier de nabijgelegen dorpen al vaak met zo'n woeste kracht overstroomd. Nu beperkt de dam echter de stroom van de rivier en is er meestal niets aan de hand; de grote hoeveelheid water uit de heuvels, het resultaat van sneeuw en stortregens, blijft achter de dam, met slechts af en toe een overloop. We kunnen dus genieten van, in plaats van bang te zijn voor, de enorme wolken die boven de vallei hangen, en we kunnen ons laten meeslepen door de enorme kracht die de rivier bezit. Dankzij deze bescherming voelen we ons thuis in de vallei nog steeds veilig en geborgen.

results.src_text:
We are being bombarded with advertisements all the time and a lot of them are targeted at young people. Smaller children, apart from spending their own pocket money, can also influence what their parents buy, so many TV ads are created with kids in mind. 
For example, adverts for drinks feature cartoon animals. Then, as two-year-olds are being pushed around the shop by their parents in a trolley, they recognise the drink from the advert and ask the adults to buy it. As children grow older, some products are marketed to them as 'must-have' items, implying that children won't be liked by their friends if they don't get them. 
As a result, kids are desperate to get the product and parents can be made to feel guilty if they don't buy it for their child. Teenagers are incredibly critical of adverts, so products aimed at them have to be advertised much more cleverly. As teens are driven by the desire to be part of the 'coolest' group in their school, products need to be given a cool feel. 
For example, advertisers give away stickers which direct teens to a difficult-to-find website with more information about a product. In this way, naturally rebellious teens feel that they have been invited to an exclusive club and can be sold expensive products. 
As teens hate being influenced by adults, marketers let them persuade each other that a certain product is cool. Since the late nineties, 'street teams' of teenagers have been employed by clothing and record companies to spread the word about a product among young people.

Lexington, who had always done everything his aunt had told him, put the money in his pocket, put on a pair of shoes and a clean shirt, and went down the mountain to the village where the doctor lived.
'Old Glosspan?' the doctor said. 'Is she dead?'
'Certainly she's dead,' the boy answered. 'If you come home with me now I'll dig her up and you can see for yourself.'
'How deep did you bury her?' the doctor asked. 'Two or three metres down, I think.' 
'And how long ago?' 'Oh, about eight hours.' 'Then she's dead,' the doctor announced. 'Here's the certificate.'
Lexington now left for the city of New York to find Mr Samuel Zuckermann. He travelled on foot, and he slept under bushes, and he lived on berries and wild plants, and it took him sixteen days to reach the city.
'What a place this is!' he cried, as he stood staring around him. 'There are no chickens or cows anywhere and none of the women looks like Aunt Glosspan at all.'
Lexington had never seen anyone like Mr Zuckermann before, either. He was a small man with a large nose, and when he smiled, bits of gold flashed at you from lots of different places inside his
mouth. In his office, he shook Lexington warmly by the hand and congratulated him on his aunt's death.
'I suppose you know that your dearly loved aunt was a woman of great wealth?' he said.
'Do you mean the cows and the chickens?'
'I mean five hundred thousand dollars,' Mr Zuckermann said.
'How much?'
'Five hundred thousand dollars, my boy. And she's left it all to you.'

Elliott's mom, Mary, took a light, and then she and the boys went into the yard. "What did you see?" Mary asked Elliott. "Something there," he answered. He pointed to the end of the yard. Growing up in Los Angeles, Vanessa Van Petten got into trouble so often that her mother and father began buying parenting advice books. 
During one of her frequent groundings, Van Petten glanced through several of the books and spotted what she considered two major problems. 
First, the books provided useless advice. More importantly, they were written by adults with no input from teenagers. That's when Van Petten decided to take matters into her own hands. 
At the age of sixteen, she wrote a book for parents from the teenage perspective: You're Grounded: How to Stop Fighting and Make the Teenage Years Easier. 
By the age of twenty-one, she had created RadicalParenting.com, an online community for parents and teens. That's where, with two full-time employees, Van Petten's 120 bloggers aged twelve to twenty answer questions from parents. The site generates revenue through advertising and sponsored links to other websites. 
Vanessa's advice: 
Get advice and help: 'Everyone said I was too young to start a company but I used online resources, read books, attended conferences and got advice from people I know. That's how I learnt about the business so quickly.' 
Reach new audiences: 'Social media is a great way to get in touch with new users - that's why we went on sites for mums and personally emailed videos to big users in each community.' 
Do something that works: 'Most importantly, we offered advice that actually works. Parents increasingly began spreading our quirky and sometimes controversial articles by word of mouth. We want to build a brand that is not only interesting but also life-changing.'

Do something that works: 'The most important thing was that we gave advice that actually works. Parents started spreading our quirky and sometimes controversial articles more and more often through word-of-mouth. We want to build a brand that is not only interesting but also life-changing.'

This is a lovely novel that all age groups can understand. Aimed at native English speaking children, there are many adults who still say this famous book is their favorite. This is part of the national curriculum in many schools around the world, so it’s quite possible this book will also come up in conversation. You can almost guarantee that the majority of native English speakers have read this book at least once.
Plot Summary
A baby pig is almost killed because of his status – he is the smallest pig that was born and he is considered to be useless and of no value. The pig is saved by a little girl called Fern Arable. She adopts the pig and takes care of it. She gives him the name Wilbur.
Fern grows sad when Wilbur grows up and has to be sent away to a farm owned by her uncle. She has a strong relationship with Wilbur. When Wilbur goes to the farm, all the other farm animals ignore him and he’s left crying for his human friend. One day he hears a voice, but he can’t see anything. This voice promises to become friends with him.
The voice belongs to a small spider called Charlotte. Charlotte the spider knows that the farmers are planning to kill Wilbur. She promises to make a plan to save his life. The farmers are surprised the next day when they see the words “some pig” written in the web* Charlotte has made. Charlotte asked for the other animals’ help over the day to write messages everywhere.
Wilbur is sad when Charlotte disappears. But in the end, her baby spiders turn out to be great company for the pig. They continue to protect each other and the story ends well.

THEATRE

CHARLES SPENCER

A. Tamburlaine the Great

Marlowe’s ten-act epic about the all-conquering warrior can seem never-ending, but it emerges as one of the most thrilling nights of the year in Terry Hands’ staging. He has hacked great chunks from the text and offers a production that combines the glories of Marlowe’s play with an exhilarating speed and physicality. Antony Sher is in terrific form in the title role, somersaulting from the balcony, sliding down a rope head-first as he delivers a speech, demanding and getting the audience’s complete attention as his eyes glint with a mad lust for power and glory. Great stuff.
Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon (01789 295623)

B. Women Laughing

Welcome London transfer for the late Michael Wall’s fine play, seen at the Manchester Royal Exchange in May. The first act creates an atmosphere of unsettling menace as two married couples chat on a sunny suburban lawn. In the second half the location shifts and the piece becomes a powerful, compassionate study of the devastating effects of illness. The British theatre lost a talent of great promise when Wall died at the tragically early age of 44.
Royal Court Theatre, London SW1 (0207 730 1745)

C. Amphibians

Billy Roche is the latest in the long line of Irish dramatists to have enriched the English stage. All his plays to date have been set in his native Wexford, and this latest piece explores the decline of the fishing industry with his usual mixture of rich characterisation, painful emotion and sudden moments of quirky humour. The play sprawls a bit aimlessly at times, but builds to a blistering climax.
Barbican 3 Pit Theatre, London EC2 (0207 638 8891)

D. Murder by Misadventure

Traditional thriller involving our old friend, ‘the perfect murder’. This time it is Gerald Harper and William Gaunt who play the crime-writing partnership intent on killing each other, and though its all rather familiar stuff; the twists and turns are handled with ingenuity.
Whitehall Theatre, London SW1 (0207 867 1119)

E. The Alchemist

Young director Sam Mendes finds the gold in Jonson’s great comedy of 17th-century confidence tricksters. First seen at the Swan in Stratford last year, the show works just as well on the Barbican’s main stage, with Jonathan Hyde, David Bradley and Joanne Pearce repeating their fine performances as the wicked trio of con-artists.
Barbican Theatre, London EC2 (0207 638 8891)

F. The Madras House

Peter James’ production of Harley Granville Barkers rich, panoramic comedy about fashion and the position of women in Edwardian society transfers to London after its success at the Edinburgh Festival. The staging is stylish, the acting excellent, the play itself an unjustly neglected classic.
Lyric Theatre, Hammersmith, London W6 (0208 741 2311)

G. Dreams from a summer house

This delightful new musical finds playwright Alan Ayckbourn in unusually benign form as he relocates the Beauty and the Beast story deep in the heart of London suburbia. A lush score by John Pattison and an unashamedly schmaltzy celebration of romantic love combine to make this good-hearted show a real winner. London impresarios looking for a hit should board the next train to Scarborough.
Stephen Joseph Theatre, Scarborough (01 723 370541)

H. The Merry Wives of Windsor

David Thacker’s lacklustre production of Shakespeare’s most farcical comedy came perilously close to being awarded the dreaded thumbs-down symbol, but this disappointing, crudely designed show is redeemed by first-rate comic performances from Ron Cook as the French physician Dr Caius and Anton Lesser as the explosively jealous husband, Ford. Almost everyone else looks faintly embarrassed, as well they might.
Shakespeare Theatre, Stragford-upon-Avon (01789 295623)

I. The Voysey Inheritance

Another major Granville Barker revival, now touring the regions. This story of an apparently respectable solicitor who bequeaths a corrupt financial legacy to his son results in a marvellous play.
Apollo Theatre, Oxford (01865 244544)

THEATER

CHARLES SPENCER

A. Tamburlaine de Grote

Marlowes tienakter over de almachtige krijger lijkt eindeloos, maar in de regie van Terry Hands blijkt het een van de meest opwindende avonden van het jaar te zijn. Hij heeft grote delen van de tekst weggelaten en presenteert een productie die de pracht van Marlowes stuk combineert met een opwindende snelheid en fysieke kracht. Antony Sher is in topvorm in de titelrol, salto's makend vanaf het balkon, met zijn hoofd naar beneden langs een touw glijdend terwijl hij een toespraak houdt, de volledige aandacht van het publiek opeisend en krijgend terwijl zijn ogen fonkelen van een waanzinnige hunkering naar macht en glorie. Geweldig.

Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon (01789 295623)

B. Laughing Women

Welkom in Londen voor de prachtige voorstelling van wijlen Michael Wall, die in mei te zien was in het Manchester Royal Exchange. De eerste akte creëert een sfeer van onheilspellende dreiging wanneer twee echtparen op een zonnig gazon in een buitenwijk zitten te praten. In de tweede helft verschuift de locatie en ontwikkelt het stuk zich tot een krachtige, empathische studie van de verwoestende gevolgen van ziekte. Het Britse theater verloor een veelbelovend talent toen Wall op de tragisch jonge leeftijd van 44 overleed.
Royal Court Theatre, Londen SW1 (0207 730 1745)

C. Amphibians

Billy Roche is de nieuwste in de lange rij Ierse toneelschrijvers die het Engelse toneel hebben verrijkt. Al zijn toneelstukken tot nu toe spelen zich af in zijn geboorteplaats Wexford, en dit nieuwste stuk onderzoekt de achteruitgang van de visserij met zijn gebruikelijke mix van rijke karaktertekening, pijnlijke emotie en plotselinge momenten van eigenzinnige humor. Het stuk is soms wat doelloos, maar bouwt op naar een meeslepende climax.

Barbican 3 Pit Theatre, Londen EC2 (0207 638 8891)

D. Moord door toeval

Een traditionele thriller met onze oude bekende, 'de perfecte moord'. Dit keer spelen Gerald Harper en William Gaunt het misdaadschrijversduo dat elkaar wil vermoorden. Hoewel het allemaal vrij bekend is, worden de wendingen met vernuft gebracht.

Whitehall Theatre, Londen SW1 (0207 867 1119)

E. De Alchemist

De jonge regisseur Sam Mendes vindt de goudmijn in Johnsons geweldige komedie over 17e-eeuwse oplichters. De voorstelling, die vorig jaar in première ging in de Swan in Stratford, werkt net zo goed op het hoofdpodium van het Barbican Theatre, met Jonathan Hyde, David Bradley en Joanne Pearce die hun sterke prestaties als het gemene trio oplichters herhalen.

Barbican Theatre, Londen EC2 (0207 638 8891)

F. The Madras House

Peter James' productie van Harley Granville Barkers rijke, panoramische komedie over mode en de positie van vrouwen in de Edwardiaanse samenleving verhuist na het succes op het Edinburgh Festival naar Londen. De mise-en-scène is stijlvol, het acteerwerk uitstekend en het stuk zelf een onterecht vergeten klassieker.

Lyric Theatre, Hammersmith, Londen W6 (0208 741 2311)

G. Dreams from a summer house

Deze heerlijke nieuwe musical toont toneelschrijver Alan Ayckbourn in een ongewoon milde vorm, terwijl hij het verhaal van Belle en het Beest verplaatst naar het hart van de Londense buitenwijken. Een weelderige partituur van John Pattison en een onbeschaamd sentimentele viering van de romantische liefde maken van deze hartverwarmende voorstelling een echte topper. Londense impresario's die op zoek zijn naar een hit, zouden de volgende trein naar Scarborough moeten nemen.

Stephen Joseph Theatre, Scarborough (01 723 370541)

H. The Merry Wives of Windsor

David Thackers futloze productie van Shakespeares meest kluchtige komedie kwam gevaarlijk dicht in de buurt van het gevreesde duim omlaag-symbool, maar deze teleurstellende, grof vormgegeven voorstelling wordt gered door eersteklas komische prestaties van Ron Cook als de Franse arts Dr. Caius en Anton Lesser als de explosief jaloerse echtgenoot Ford. Bijna iedereen kijkt er lichtelijk gegeneerd bij, en terecht.

Shakespeare Theatre, Stragford-upon-Avon (01789 295623)

I. The Voysey Inheritance

Nog een grote heropvoering van Granville Barker, die nu door de regio's tourt. Dit verhaal over een ogenschijnlijk respectabele advocaat die een corrupte financiële erfenis aan zijn zoon nalaat, resulteert in een prachtig toneelstuk.

Apollo Theatre, Oxford (01865 244544)

results.src_text:
In September 1533 Anne gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth (the future Queen Elizabeth I). Henry had grown tired of her, and after two further pregnancies ended in miscarriages, she was arrested in 1536 on trumped up charges of adultery and publicly beheaded at the Tower of London.
Henry's third marriage, this time to lady-in-waiting, Jane Seymour, finally produced the son he so desperately desired with the birth of Edward in 1537. Jane Seymour died after childbirth and Henry ordered that she be granted a queen's funeral.
In an attempt to establish ties with the German Protestant alliance, Thomas Cromwell arranged a marriage between the king and German princess Anne of Cleves. The marriage was a disaster and Henry divorced Anne a few months later. Henry blamed Cromwell for this mismatch and soon afterwards had him executed for treason.
The final years of his reign witnessed Henry VIII's physical decline and an increasing desire to appear all-powerful. Henry continued with fruitless and expensive campaigns against Scotland and France.
In 1540, the aging King married the teenage Catherine Howard. Their marriage was short lived. It was alleged that she had a previous relationship with Henry's courtier Francis Dereham and an affair with another courtier Thomas Culpeper. Catherine was executed for adultery and treason in 1542.
Henry's final marriage to Catherine Parr, who acted like a nurse, was more harmonious and she would go on to outlive him.
Henry VIII died on 28 January 1547 and was succeeded by his son, Edward VI. He was buried next to Jane Seymour in St. George's Chapel at Windsor Castle.

results.src_text:
TIM RICE

I was ushered into the young man’s drawing room, an oasis of cultured sanity surrounded by what appeared to be a quite shambolic cluster of rooms in which the less enterprising members of the family operated. Moving from the kitchen to his parlour was an upgrade from economy to business class.
Here was the largest collection of records I had ever seen, the first stereo record player and tuner I had come across and the astonishing evidence that a teenager existed who had spent money on Georgian wine glasses, pictures and furniture.
His name was Andrew Lloyd Webber. He had won a scholarship to Magdalen College, Oxford, to read history, and he had nine months to kill before going up, during which time he intended to become England’s answer to the composer Richard Rodgers.
My own ambitions were just as insane as his, I wanted to be a pop star, for all the healthy reasons women, money and fame. The difference between Andrew and myself was that my dreams were never life or death to me, though it's easy to say that now. They might have become so had I failed.
Consequently, when Andrew suggested a completely new insane ambition for me, i.e. to become as famous a lyricist as Oscar Hammerstein, I had no qualms about giving it a go. This was partly because within ten minutes of our introduction, he was at the piano and had played me three tunes he had composed — I could tell that he was good. Very good.
As he confidently continued to bash out selections from some of the many shows he had written and produced at school, I was reminded of many of the best show albums from my parents LP collection. He needed a new lyricist for the outside world.
I had little to impress him with in return, other than instant praise for his music and a bona fide, actually released, seven-inch single of a song I had written (both words and music) with which an unknown pop group had dealt the final blow to their moribund career by recording three months previously. We parted, promising to meet again and to write something together. I was still more interested in the charts than in the West End theatre, but told myself on the bus back to my flat that I had just met somebody of rare ability and determination, and I would be mad to miss out on being a sidekick to a chap who was clearly going to take the musical theatre by storm, probably by next week.
And even if the two of us failed to challenge the top musical composers successfully, then we could try to knock the Beatles and Rolling Stones off their perches later, in the summer. The Everly Brothers had just made a comeback and would clearly be in need of some new material.
The next day, back at my desk in the office where I was training to become a solicitor, the brief certainty I had enjoyed of a life in show business with Andrew Lloyd Webber had faded somewhat. I would of course continue to keep an eye on the small ads in Melody Maker for groups needing a vocalist, and would turn out a few more three-chord songs tailored not to expose the limitations of my voice, but it was still odds-on that eventually I would stagger through my exams and wind up a respectable lawyer by the time I was twenty-five.
By then I would have surely grown out of pop music as my father had confidently predicted I would by the time I was twenty-one. This was worrying - if he was right I only had a few more months of enjoying it.
But in the meantime I felt I had nothing to lose by seeing Andrew again. It would be fun to go and see a musical with him, to write words that aped musical lyricists rather than pop stars. And Andrew was a fascinating individual who talked of Good Food Guides and Victorian architecture, besides supporting Leyton Orient football team.
I wasn’t convinced by the idea for a musical that he had been working on for the past year, but in 1965 I was rarely convinced about anything. His talent was beyond question and he claimed to have all the contacts. I was soon back in his drawing room.
The idea was the life of Dr Thomas Barnardo, the nineteenth century philanthropist who founded the orphanages that bear his name. His story was a worthy one indeed, but not one that truly fired my imagination. The hero was too squeaky-clean, at least in Andrew’s version of his life, and the enterprise was unoriginal in both conception and execution, owing far too much to Lionel Bart’s hit show, Oliver.
On the other hand, Andrew’s conviction of his score’s precocious brilliance was infectious and not totally unjustified. What did I know about musicals? As David Land, later to be my agent for over a quarter of a century, memorably (and repeatedly) said, if there’s a demand for one hamburger bar on the block, there is room for two. We could be the second hamburger joint.
I set to work with enormous enthusiasm, in particular for those songs that were intended to be funny. Andrew outlined the plot, played me the tunes and in many instances gave me the title as well, most of which had presumably been thought up by his ex-wordsmith school pal who had already had a go. I skipped a day at the solicitors office, faking illness, to write my first batch of theatrical lyrics. I did not know it that day but I had changed careers.
results.tgt_text:
TIM RICE

Ik werd de salon van de jongeman binnengeleid, een oase van gecultiveerde rust, omgeven door wat een nogal rommelige verzameling kamers leek te zijn waar de minder ondernemende leden van de familie hun gang gingen. Van de keuken naar zijn salon gaan was een upgrade van economy naar business class.

Hier stond de grootste platencollectie die ik ooit had gezien, de eerste stereo-platenspeler met tuner die ik ooit was tegengekomen en het verbazingwekkende bewijs dat er ooit een tiener was geweest die geld had uitgegeven aan Georgische wijnglazen, schilderijen en meubels.

Zijn naam was Andrew Lloyd Webber. Hij had een beurs gewonnen voor Magdalen College in Oxford om geschiedenis te studeren, en hij had nog negen maanden te overbruggen voordat hij erheen ging. In die tijd wilde hij de Engelse tegenhanger van componist Richard Rodgers worden.

Mijn eigen ambities waren net zo waanzinnig als die van hem. Ik wilde popster worden, om alle gezonde redenen: vrouwen, geld en roem. Het verschil tussen Andrew en mij was dat mijn dromen voor mij nooit een kwestie van leven of dood waren, hoewel dat nu makkelijk gezegd kan worden. Dat hadden ze misschien wel kunnen worden als ik gefaald had.

Toen Andrew me daarom een ​​compleet nieuwe, waanzinnige ambitie voorstelde – namelijk om net zo'n beroemde tekstschrijver te worden als Oscar Hammerstein – aarzelde ik geen moment om het te proberen. Dat kwam mede doordat hij binnen tien minuten na onze kennismaking al achter de piano zat en me drie door hem gecomponeerde nummers had laten horen – ik wist meteen dat hij goed was. Heel goed.

Terwijl hij vol zelfvertrouwen fragmenten speelde uit de vele musicals die hij op school had geschreven en geproduceerd, moest ik denken aan veel van de beste musicalalbums uit de lp-collectie van mijn ouders. Hij had een nieuwe tekstschrijver nodig voor de buitenwereld.

Ik had weinig om hem mee te imponeren, behalve onmiddellijke lof voor zijn muziek en een echte, daadwerkelijk uitgebrachte 7-inch single van een nummer dat ik had geschreven (zowel tekst als muziek), waarmee een onbekende popgroep drie maanden eerder de genadeslag aan hun tanende carrière had gegeven door het op te nemen. We namen afscheid met de belofte elkaar weer te zien en samen iets te schrijven. Ik was nog steeds meer geïnteresseerd in de hitlijsten dan in het West End-theater, maar op de bus terug naar mijn appartement zei ik tegen mezelf dat ik net iemand met een zeldzaam talent en een enorme vastberadenheid had ontmoet, en dat ik gek zou zijn om de kans te missen om rechterhand te zijn van een kerel die de musicalwereld ongetwijfeld stormenderhand zou veroveren, waarschijnlijk al volgende week.

En zelfs als we er samen niet in zouden slagen de topcomponisten te verslaan, konden we later in de zomer proberen de Beatles en de Rolling Stones van hun troon te stoten. De Everly Brothers hadden net een comeback gemaakt en zouden ongetwijfeld nieuw materiaal nodig hebben.

De volgende dag, terug aan mijn bureau op kantoor, waar ik een opleiding tot advocaat volgde, was de korte zekerheid die ik had gehad over een leven in de showbusiness met Andrew Lloyd Webber enigszins vervaagd. Natuurlijk bleef ik de kleine advertenties in Melody Maker in de gaten houden voor groepen die een zanger zochten, en schreef ik nog een paar liedjes met drie akkoorden die de beperkingen van mijn stem niet zouden blootleggen. Maar de kans was groot dat ik uiteindelijk mijn examens zou halen en tegen de tijd dat ik vijfentwintig was een respectabel advocaat zou zijn.

Tegen die tijd zou ik vast en zeker te oud zijn voor popmuziek, zoals mijn vader vol vertrouwen had voorspeld dat ik tegen mijn eenentwintigste zou zijn. Dat baarde me zorgen – als hij gelijk had, kon ik er nog maar een paar maanden van genieten.

Maar ondertussen had ik het gevoel dat ik niets te verliezen had door Andrew weer te zien. Het zou leuk zijn om met hem naar een musical te gaan, om teksten te schrijven die meer op die van musicaltekstschrijvers leken dan op die van popsterren. En Andrew was een fascinerende man die het had over culinaire gidsen en Victoriaanse architectuur, en bovendien supporter was van voetbalclub Leyton Orient.

Ik was niet overtuigd van het idee voor een musical waar hij het afgelopen jaar aan had gewerkt, maar in 1965 was ik zelden ergens van overtuigd. Zijn talent stond buiten kijf en hij beweerde alle contacten te hebben. Ik zat al snel weer in zijn salon.

Het idee was het leven van Dr. Thomas Barnardo, de negentiende-eeuwse filantroop die de weeshuizen stichtte die zijn naam dragen. Zijn verhaal was zeker de moeite waard, maar het sprak me niet echt aan. De held was te braaf, tenminste in Andrews versie van zijn leven, en het project was zowel qua concept als uitvoering onorigineel, en leunde veel te veel op Lionel Barts hitshow Oliver.

Aan de andere kant was Andrews overtuiging van de vroegrijpe genialiteit van zijn muziek aanstekelijk en niet geheel onterecht. Wat wist ik nou van musicals? Zoals David Land, die later meer dan een kwart eeuw mijn agent zou zijn, op memorabele (en herhaaldelijke) wijze zei: als er vraag is naar één hamburgerzaak in de straat, is er ruimte voor twee. Wij zouden de tweede hamburgerzaak kunnen zijn.

Ik ging met enorm veel enthousiasme aan de slag, vooral met de liedjes die grappig moesten zijn. Andrew schetste de plot, speelde de melodieën voor me en gaf me in veel gevallen ook de titel, waarvan de meeste vermoedelijk bedacht waren door zijn ex-schoolvriend, die al eens een poging had gewaagd. Ik spijbelde een dag van het advocatenkantoor, deed alsof ik ziek was, om mijn eerste reeks toneelteksten te schrijven. Ik wist het die dag nog niet, maar ik had een carrièreswitch gemaakt.
results.back_text:
TIM RICE

I was led into the young man's drawing room, an oasis of cultivated calm, surrounded by what appeared to be a rather messy collection of rooms where the less enterprising members of the family went about their business. Going from the kitchen to his drawing room was an upgrade from economy to business class.

Here stood the largest record collection I had ever seen, the first stereo record player with a tuner I had ever encountered, and the astonishing proof that there had once been a teenager who had spent money on Georgian wine glasses, paintings, and furniture.

His name was Andrew Lloyd Webber. He had won a scholarship to Magdalen College in Oxford to study history, and he had nine months to bridge before he went there. During that time, he wanted to become the English counterpart to composer Richard Rodgers.

My own ambitions were just as insane as his. I wanted to become a pop star, for all sound reasons: women, money, and fame. The difference between Andrew and me was that my dreams were never a matter of life or death for me, although that is easy to say now. That is perhaps what they could have become if I had failed.

So when Andrew proposed a completely new, insane ambition to me—namely, to become just as famous a lyricist as Oscar Hammerstein—I didn't hesitate for a moment to give it a try. This was partly because, within ten minutes of meeting, he was already sitting at the piano and had played me three songs he had composed—I knew immediately that he was good. Very good.

As he confidently played excerpts from the many musicals he had written and produced at school, I was reminded of many of the best musical albums in my parents' LP collection. He needed a new lyricist for the outside world.

I had little to impress him with, except for immediate praise for his music and a real, actually released 7-inch single of a song I had written (both lyrics and music), which an unknown pop group had dealt the death blow to their fading career three months earlier by recording. We parted ways with the promise to see each other again and write something together. I was still more interested in the charts than in the West End theatre, but on the bus back to my apartment I told myself that I had just met someone with a rare talent and enormous determination, and that I would be crazy to miss the chance to be the right-hand man of a guy who would undoubtedly take the musical world by storm, probably as early as next week.

And even if we didn't manage to beat the top composers together, we could try to dethrone the Beatles and the Rolling Stones later in the summer. The Everly Brothers had just made a comeback and would undoubtedly need new material.

The next day, back at my desk at the office, where I was training to become a lawyer, the brief certainty I had had about a life in show business with Andrew Lloyd Webber had faded somewhat. Of course, I kept an eye on the small ads in Melody Maker for groups looking for a singer, and I wrote a few more three-chord songs that wouldn't expose the limitations of my voice. But chances were high that I would eventually pass my exams and be a respectable lawyer by the time I was twenty-five.

By then, I would surely be too old for pop music, just as my father had confidently predicted I would be by my twenty-first birthday. That worried me—if he was right, I would only have a few months left to enjoy it.

But in the meantime, I felt I had nothing to lose by seeing Andrew again. It would be fun to go to a musical with him, to write lyrics that resembled those of musical lyricists more than those of pop stars. And Andrew was a fascinating man who talked about culinary guides and Victorian architecture, and was, moreover, a supporter of football club Leyton Orient.

I was not convinced by the idea for a musical he had been working on over the past year, but in 1965 I was rarely convinced of anything. His talent was beyond question and he claimed to have all the contacts. I was soon back in his salon.

The idea was the life of Dr. Thomas Barnardo, the nineteenth-century philanthropist who founded the orphanages that bear his name. His story was certainly worthwhile, but it didn't really appeal to me. The hero was too tame, at least in Andrew's version of his life, and the project was unoriginal in both concept and execution, relying far too heavily on Lionel Bart's hit show Oliver.

On the other hand, Andrew's conviction regarding the precocious genius of his music was infectious and not entirely unfounded. What did I know about musicals anyway? As David Land, who would later be my agent for more than a quarter of a century, memorably (and repeatedly) said: if there is demand for one hamburger joint on the street, there is room for two. We could be the second hamburger joint.

I set to work with enormous enthusiasm, especially on the songs that had to be funny. Andrew sketched out the plot, played the melodies for me, and in many cases also gave me the title, most of which were presumably conceived by his ex-school friend, who had already made an attempt. I played truant for a day at the law firm, pretended to be sick, to write my first series of plays. I didn't know it that day yet, but I had made a career switch.

Clutter

Sometimes it seems that no matter how many possessions you have, you never feel secure. While it is reasonable to have a basic nesting instinct and create a home which meets your needs, there is a point where the motivation for acquiring things gets out of control. Modern advertising is moreover deliberately designed to play on our insecurities.If you don’t have one of these you will be a lesser human being is one of the consistent underlying messages we receive. To discover just how much you are influenced, I challenge you to try not to read any advertising billboards next time you go down the street. These multi-million dollar messages relentlessly condition us in very persuasive ways without our ever realising it. We are bombarded by them - television, radio, newspapers, magazines, posters, tee shirts, the internet, you name it - all encouraging us to buy, buy, buy.

Caves

Research establishments and university departments around the world have invested years of research time in all aspects of caves, mainly their origins, their hydrology and their biology. Caves constitute a small but rather mysterious component of the natural environment - as such they arouse our curiosity and challenge our desire for knowledge, and consequently have had a considerable amount of research effort devoted to them. Furthermore, because of their presence as natural phenomena, they have had a long history of study, which has been intensified in those parts of the world where caves have had a direct effect on our way of life. However, the physical agility required to visit many caves means that cave research has been less in the hands of the learned professors than in most other scientific fields. Indeed there is a considerable, perhaps unique, overlap between the professional, scientific study of caves and the amateur studies carried out by those who mainly visit caves for sport.

Weather Watch

Countless observant people without any instruments other than their own senses originally laid the foundations of meteorology, which has progressed since the 17th century into the highly technical science of today. Satellites and electronic instruments relay endless weather information to us with the minimum of delay, computers solve in minutes abstruse mathematical sums at a speed beyond the capability of the human brain. Meteorological theory is peppered with long words which have little meaning to the non-professional. It sometimes seems there is no room left for simple weather wisdom, but nothing could be further from the truth. Human experience is still the vital ingredient which translates computed data into weather forecasts. Human observations can still provide unusual evidence which is of great help to professionals who are trying to unravel the mysteries of the atmosphere.

Soms lijkt het alsof je je, hoeveel bezittingen je ook hebt, nooit echt veilig voelt. Moderne reclame is bovendien bewust ontworpen om in te spelen op onze onzekerheden. "Als je er geen hebt, ben je een minderwaardig mens" is een van de terugkerende, onderliggende boodschappen die we te horen krijgen. Om te ontdekken hoeveel invloed je hierop hebt, daag ik je uit om de volgende keer dat je over straat loopt geen reclameborden te lezen. Deze miljoenen kostende boodschappen conditioneren ons onophoudelijk op zeer overtuigende wijze, zonder dat we het ons ooit realiseren. We worden erdoor gebombardeerd - televisie, radio, kranten, tijdschriften, posters, T-shirts, internet, noem maar op - allemaal moedigen ze ons aan om te kopen, kopen, kopen.

Grotten

Onderzoeksinstituten en universiteitsafdelingen over de hele wereld hebben jarenlang onderzoek gedaan naar alle aspecten van grotten, met name hun ontstaan, hun hydrologie en hun biologie. Grotten vormen een klein maar mysterieus onderdeel van de natuurlijke omgeving. Ze wekken onze nieuwsgierigheid en prikkelen onze drang naar kennis, waardoor er aanzienlijk veel onderzoek naar is verricht. Bovendien hebben ze, vanwege hun natuurlijke aard, een lange geschiedenis van onderzoek, die is geïntensiveerd in die delen van de wereld waar grotten een directe invloed hebben op onze manier van leven. De fysieke inspanning die nodig is om veel grotten te bezoeken, betekent echter dat grotonderzoek minder in handen is geweest van hoogopgeleide professoren dan in de meeste andere wetenschappelijke vakgebieden. Er is dan ook een aanzienlijke, misschien wel unieke, overlap tussen de professionele, wetenschappelijke studie van grotten en de amateurstudies van mensen die grotten voornamelijk bezoeken voor hun plezier.

Weerwaarneming

Talloze oplettende mensen, zonder andere instrumenten dan hun eigen zintuigen, legden oorspronkelijk de basis voor de meteorologie, die zich sinds de 17e eeuw heeft ontwikkeld tot de hoogtechnische wetenschap van vandaag. Satellieten en elektronische instrumenten geven ons met minimale vertraging eindeloze weersinformatie door, computers lossen in enkele minuten ingewikkelde wiskundige vraagstukken op met een snelheid die het menselijk brein niet aankan. Meteorologische theorieën zitten vol met moeilijke woorden die voor de leek weinig betekenis hebben. Soms lijkt er geen ruimte meer te zijn voor eenvoudige weerkennis, maar niets is minder waar. Menselijke ervaring is nog steeds het essentiële ingrediënt dat computergegevens vertaalt naar weersvoorspellingen. Menselijke observaties kunnen nog steeds ongebruikelijk bewijsmateriaal opleveren dat van grote waarde is voor professionals die de mysteries van de atmosfeer proberen te ontrafelen.

CRYING 

Charles Darwin thought that the human tendency to cry had no obvious evolving purpose. He was almost certainly wrong. More recently scientists have pointed to its social significance, with psychiatrist John Bowlby highlighting the role of crying in developing the attachment between mother and child. Many believe that tears, at least during childhood, are mainly an expression of helplessness. However, the persistence of crying into adulthood is harder to explain. It seems that the sound of crying becomes considerably less important than the visual signal it conveys. It may have been advantageous to early human communities as a means of promoting trust and social connectedness. 
Tears can undoubtedly have other causes too. We may cry to express sympathy for those suffering terrible injustice. Furthermore, tears can be shed involuntarily, rather to our embarrassment, when we hear inspiring music or moving speeches. We may cry when watching a sentimental film, but interestingly, this is more likely to occur in company than when we are alone. The social function of crying would seem to be undeniable, but research continues.

HUILEN

Charles Darwin dacht dat de menselijke neiging om te huilen geen duidelijk evolutionair doel had. Hij had het vrijwel zeker mis. Recenter hebben wetenschappers gewezen op de sociale betekenis ervan, waarbij psychiater John Bowlby de rol van huilen in de ontwikkeling van de band tussen moeder en kind benadrukte. Velen geloven dat tranen, in ieder geval tijdens de kindertijd, vooral een uiting van hulpeloosheid zijn. Het voortduren van huilen tot in de volwassenheid is echter moeilijker te verklaren. Het lijkt erop dat het geluid van huilen aanzienlijk minder belangrijk wordt dan het visuele signaal dat het overbrengt. Het kan in vroege menselijke gemeenschappen voordelig zijn geweest als middel om vertrouwen en sociale verbondenheid te bevorderen.

Tranen kunnen ongetwijfeld ook andere oorzaken hebben. We kunnen huilen om medeleven te betuigen aan mensen die vreselijk onrecht lijden. Bovendien kunnen tranen onvrijwillig, tot onze schaamte, vloeien bij het horen van inspirerende muziek of ontroerende toespraken. We kunnen huilen bij het kijken naar een sentimentele film, maar interessant genoeg gebeurt dit vaker in gezelschap dan wanneer we alleen zijn. De sociale functie van huilen lijkt onmiskenbaar, maar het onderzoek gaat door.

We are Talking Big Boots here. Really BIGTIME Boots.
I stood in my 800-dollar-each designer-label cowboy boots on the rocks of an old formation in the Arizona desert sand. Money no object. I wore the whole truly cowboy outfit and if you had the outfit you might be a cowboy. But I was not. It wasn’t working. I squinted info the morning sun looking out at the Arizona mountains and I had to admit, I was not at home on the range,
Flying in from Denver just after dawn, I had the feeling that I just might pass far an ol' cowhand coming in from the sky. The feeling didn’t last past the first real cowboy in the luggage hall of Phoenix airport. He was wearing a sweat-stained I-shirt, needed a shave, and was hoisting a dirty canvas bag off the conveyer belt when he caught sight of my brand new cowboy boots. He slowly raised one eyebrow and moved off out of the door without looking back.
There ought to be, somewhere, hanging in a closet, a suit of clothes an ex-racing driver can put on without feeling like he is from another planet. Something he could wear so that wherever he goes he doesn’t get the feeling that everybody is talking another language and doing whatever they do at half speed. I liked, no, not liked... I flatout loved being a racing driver, driving racing cars. I am addicted to it and it is all I know how to do. But I don’t do it any more. I couldn’t if I wanted to. Question is, I thought, looking into the mean, rust-coloured rock of the mountains in the distance, what do I do now?
A racing driver should have one or two fall-back identities lined up for when he climbs out of his car. I thought I did, but when I reached for them they just disappeared. How about: an ex-racing driver adds colour to the commentary direct from the trackside? 'We got fifteen guys, all of them former Indy and Formula One drivers, fifteen guys in front of you, Forrest, standing in line to be colour commentators. We’ll call you.'
Well then, how about: an ex-racing driver coins a partnership to sell classic cars? That lasted nearly all winter with phone calls, lunches, lawyers und meetings with bankers. But it was the year nobody was buying old Ferraris and Honda was 'reviewing' its dealer list. So in the end I gracefully withdrew before there was nothing to withdraw from. Being an 'ex' anything is depressing work. I mean you tell me, how badly do you want to hear about how I was almost the World Champion? Nobody wants to hear a story that ends in ‘almost'. And even if I had been world champion you could probably just about stand to listen to the story for five minutes before your ears turned to cement. Last year's champion was last year.
Not that I want sympathy. Which is just as well, since I don’t get any. Well, why should I? I had a good run, made money and hung on to enough. But oh, man, I miss the heat of slipping into that graceful, elegant, shrink-wrapped super-tech machine with seven hundred horsepower behind my neck. Zero to a hundred and fifty miles an hour in 4,9 seconds. And yes, I miss coming within an eyelash of killing myself every race or so. I miss the bright and gorgeous people and the reporters who acted as if what I said mattered. Being famous, even in a minor way, isn't all bad. Businessmen and politicians bragged to their friends that they knew me. Little boys slid under fences to get my autograph. And now that I don’t drive a racing car... Only last week the phone rang twice. I have time in the morning and I have time in the afternoon. And let me just check, but I think tomorrow is free, so much empty time.
I looked up into the soft blue morning sky. No buzzards overhead. Maybe Arizona doesn't have buzzards. But a couple of little brown birds in a saguaro cactus just in front of me were giving me advice, something like 'get away from our nest before we sing our hearts out’. It had never occurred to me that the desert had songbirds. It did occur to me that a bogus cowboy in designer boots had a lot to learn.

We hebben het hier over gigantische laarzen. Echt ENORME laarzen.

Ik stond in mijn designer cowboylaarzen van 800 dollar per stuk op de rotsen van een oude formatie in het woestijnzand van Arizona. Geld speelde geen rol. Ik droeg de complete cowboy-outfit en als je die outfit had, was je misschien wel een cowboy. Maar ik was het niet. Het werkte niet. Ik kneep mijn ogen samen tegen de ochtendzon terwijl ik naar de bergen van Arizona keek en ik moest toegeven dat ik me niet thuis voelde op de prairie.
Toen ik net na zonsopgang vanuit Denver aankwam, had ik het gevoel dat ik zo voor een oude cowboy uit de lucht zou kunnen doorgaan. Dat gevoel verdween echter snel toen ik de eerste echte cowboy in de bagagehal van de luchthaven van Phoenix zag. Hij droeg een doorweekt T-shirt, moest zich scheren en tilde een vieze canvas tas van de bagageband toen hij mijn gloednieuwe cowboylaarzen zag. Hij trok langzaam een ​​wenkbrauw op en liep de deur uit zonder om te kijken.

Ergens in een kast zou een pak moeten hangen dat een ex-coureur kan aantrekken zonder zich van een andere planeet te voelen. Iets wat hij kan dragen zodat hij, waar hij ook gaat, niet het gevoel krijgt dat iedereen een andere taal spreekt en alles op halve snelheid doet. Ik vond het leuk, nee, niet leuk... ik was er dol op om coureur te zijn, om in raceauto's te rijden. Ik ben eraan verslaafd en het is het enige wat ik kan. Maar ik doe het niet meer. Ik zou het niet kunnen, zelfs als ik het zou willen. De vraag is, dacht ik, terwijl ik naar de dreigende, roestkleurige rotsen van de bergen in de verte keek, wat moet ik nu doen?
Een coureur zou een of twee reserve-identiteiten achter de hand moeten hebben voor als hij uit zijn auto stapt. Ik dacht dat ik die had, maar toen ik ernaar greep, waren ze gewoon verdwenen. Wat dacht je van: een ex-coureur die kleur geeft aan het commentaar, rechtstreeks vanaf de baan? 'We hebben vijftien mannen, allemaal voormalige IndyCar- en Formule 1-coureurs, vijftien mannen voor je, Forrest, die in de rij staan ​​om als commentator op te treden. We bellen je wel.'

Nou, wat dacht je van: een ex-coureur die een partnerschap aangaat om klassieke auto's te verkopen? Dat duurde bijna de hele winter, met telefoontjes, lunches, advocaten en vergaderingen met bankiers. Maar het was het jaar dat niemand oude Ferrari's kocht en Honda zijn dealerlijst 'herzag'. Dus uiteindelijk trok ik me elegant terug voordat er niets meer was om me uit terug te trekken. 'Ex' zijn is deprimerend werk. Ik bedoel, zeg me eens, hoe graag wil je horen hoe ik bijna wereldkampioen was? Niemand wil een verhaal horen dat eindigt met 'bijna'. En zelfs als ik wereldkampioen was geweest, zou je het verhaal waarschijnlijk nog net vijf minuten kunnen aanhoren voordat je oren van cement zouden worden. De kampioen van vorig jaar was vorig jaar.

Niet dat ik medelijden wil. Wat maar goed ook is, want ik krijg het toch niet. Nou ja, waarom zou ik? Ik heb een mooie tijd gehad, geld verdiend en genoeg overgehouden. Maar oh man, wat mis ik de hitte van het instappen in die sierlijke, elegante, supertechnologische machine met zevenhonderd pk achter mijn nek. Van nul naar 280 kilometer per uur in 4,9 seconden. En ja, ik mis het om bij elke race op een haar na mezelf te doden. Ik mis de stralende en knappe mensen en de verslaggevers die deden alsof wat ik zei ertoe deed. Beroemd zijn, zelfs een beetje, is niet alleen maar slecht. Zakenlieden en politici schepten tegen hun vrienden op dat ze me kenden. Kleine jongens gleden onder hekken door om mijn handtekening te krijgen. En nu ik geen raceauto meer rijd... Vorige week ging de telefoon nog twee keer. Ik heb 's ochtends tijd en 's middags tijd. En laat me even checken, maar ik denk dat ik morgen vrij ben, zoveel vrije tijd.
Ik keek omhoog naar de zachtblauwe ochtendhemel. Geen gieren boven me. Misschien hebben ze in Arizona geen gieren. Maar een paar kleine bruine vogeltjes in een saguaro-cactus vlak voor me gaven me advies, zoiets als: 'Ga weg bij ons nest voordat we uit volle borst zingen'. Het was me nooit opgevallen dat er zangvogels in de woestijn leefden. Het was me wel opgevallen dat een nepcowboy in designlaarzen nog veel te leren had.
results.back_text:
We are talking about gigantic boots here. Really HUGE boots.

I stood in my designer cowboy boots, $800 apiece, on the rocks of an ancient formation in the desert sands of Arizona. Money was no object. I was wearing the complete cowboy outfit, and if you had that outfit, you might well be a cowboy. But I wasn't. It didn't work. I squinted my eyes against the morning sun as I looked at the mountains of Arizona, and I had to admit that I didn't feel at home on the prairie.
When I arrived from Denver just after sunrise, I felt like I could pass for an old cowboy out of the sky. However, that feeling vanished quickly when I saw the first real cowboy in the baggage claim area of ​​Phoenix airport. He was wearing a soaked T-shirt, needed to shave, and was lifting a dirty canvas bag off the conveyor belt when he saw my brand-new cowboy boots. He slowly raised an eyebrow and walked out the door without looking back. Somewhere in a closet, there should be a suit hanging that an ex-racer can put on without feeling like he's from another planet. Something he can wear so that, wherever he goes, he doesn't feel like everyone is speaking a different language and doing everything at half speed. I liked it, no, didn't like it... I loved being a racer, driving race cars. I am addicted to it and it is the only thing I can do. But I don't do it anymore. I couldn't, even if I wanted to. The question is, I thought, as I looked at the menacing, rust-colored rocks of the mountains in the distance, what should I do now?
A racer should have one or two backup identities up his sleeve for when he gets out of his car. I thought I had them, but when I reached for them, they had simply vanished. How about this: an ex-racer adding color to the commentary, straight from the track? 'We have fifteen men, all former IndyCar and Formula 1 drivers, fifteen men for you, Forrest, lining up to act as commentators. We’ll give you a call.'

Well, how about this: an ex-driver entering into a partnership to sell classic cars? That took almost the entire winter, with phone calls, lunches, lawyers, and meetings with bankers. But it was the year that no one was buying old Ferraris and Honda 'revised' its dealer list. So eventually, I withdrew elegantly before there was nothing left to withdraw from. Being an 'ex' is depressing work. I mean, tell me, how much do you want to hear how I was almost world champion? No one wants to hear a story that ends with 'almost'. And even if I had been world champion, you would probably only be able to listen to the story for five minutes before your ears would turn to cement. Last year's champion was last year.

Not that I want pity. Which is just as well, because I won't get it anyway. Well, why would I? I had a great time, made money, and had enough left over. But oh man, how I miss the heat of getting into that graceful, elegant, super-technological machine with seven hundred horsepower behind my neck. From zero to 280 kilometers per hour in 4.9 seconds. And yes, I miss killing myself by a hair's breadth at every race. I miss the radiant and handsome people and the reporters who acted like what I said mattered. Being famous, even a little bit, isn't all bad. Businessmen and politicians bragged to their friends that they knew me. Little boys slid under fences to get my autograph. And now that I don't drive a race car anymore... Last week the phone rang twice. I have time in the morning and time in the afternoon. And let me just check, but I think I'm off tomorrow, so much free time.
I looked up at the soft blue morning sky. No vultures above me. Maybe they don't have vultures in Arizona. But a few small brown birds in a saguaro cactus right in front of me gave me advice, something like: 'Get away from our nest before we sing at the top of our lungs'. It had never occurred to me that songbirds lived in the desert. It had occurred to me, however, that a fake cowboy in designer boots still had a lot to learn.

Running a business in the countryside 

Five women talk about their experiences setting up a business in the countryside. 

A.
‘My customers are friends,' says CHRISTINE HOGAN, who runs a computer-aided design business with a turnover of over £200,000 a year and four full-time employees. 'My husband and I moved out of London to the country when our children were small, and I wanted work I could do at home. I had worked with computers before I was married, so my husband suggested I set up a computer-aided design business. It needed a huge amount of money and things were difficult in the beginning. But I have been very careful, making sure that I told the bank manager if I was likely to overspend. Being in the house is a big saving, and I can carry on working in the evening if I want. It has remained a small business. We hardly ever deliver work - people from the area tend to collect it from us.' 

B.
’I enjoy being independent,' says MAGGY SASANOW, who works from home as a designer of greetings cards. 'I trained in art at university, and wanted to work in a museum. But when I married, we went to live in the countryside, where there wasn't that sort of work. So I decided to set up my own business and I produce a range of 50 greetings cards which I sell to museums. I work in a big room upstairs. The disadvantage of working from home is that there is always something that needs doing - like mowing the lawn. My business comes completely by word of mouth - I don't advertise at all. People send work down from London as I am cheaper than other artists. Working alone, I don't get to exchange ideas with other people any more, but generally there are more advantages than disadvantages.' 

C.
’It has been hard at times,' says DELIA TURNER, whose curtain-making business has seen good times and bad. 'I started my business eight years ago. Then this type of business was expanding, and in two years my turnover went from £24,000 to £80,000. I used to manage six full-time curtain-makers. But I had to sack them because of the decline in the economy, which was painful because it is not easy to find other jobs in this area. I am right back almost to where I started, making the curtains at home myself, with my husband's help, and using women who work from their homes. I have to be prepared to cut my prices when it's necessary and to look at different opportunities.' 

D.
TESSA STRICKLAND runs the editorial and production side of her children's book publishing business from her farmhouse. 'I moved to the countryside three years ago for two reasons. The first was financial, because London was so expensive, and the second was because I love the country. I enjoy being able to work when I want to. Eighty per cent of my income comes from deals with Australia, the Far East and North America, so I have to take calls at odd hours. The disadvantage is that it requires discipline to shut the office door. I publish children's books from cultures around the world, working with authors and artists. All my professional experience had been in London, so I used to feel very alone at first.' 

E.
MEG RIVERS runs a cakes-by-post business and a shop with a turnover of £250,000 a year and employs six people, some part-time. 'I started ten years ago at home. I am very interested in health, so I started making fruit cakes, using good quality flour and eggs. Then I started getting requests from friends and relatives, and soon I was sending cakes all over the country. Seven years ago I rented a small building and everything is made there - we have a baker and assistant, and a professional cake-icer. I don't cook at all now, as I run the commercial side. My greatest problem has been the financial side of the business, which has been difficult simply because we didn't have an enormous amount of money to set up with.'

Een bedrijf runnen op het platteland

Vijf vrouwen vertellen over hun ervaringen met het opzetten van een bedrijf op het platteland.

A.
'Mijn klanten zijn vrienden', zegt Christine Hogan, die een computergestuurd ontwerpbedrijf runt met een jaaromzet van meer dan £ 200.000 en vier vaste medewerkers. 'Mijn man en ik verhuisden van Londen naar het platteland toen onze kinderen klein waren, en ik wilde werk dat ik vanuit huis kon doen. Ik had al met computers gewerkt voordat ik trouwde, dus stelde mijn man voor dat ik een computergestuurd ontwerpbedrijf zou beginnen. Het vergde een enorm bedrag en het was in het begin moeilijk. Maar ik ben heel voorzichtig geweest en heb de bankmanager altijd op de hoogte gesteld als ik dreigde te veel uit te geven. Thuiswerken scheelt een hoop geld, en ik kan 's avonds doorwerken als ik dat wil. Het is een klein bedrijf gebleven. We bezorgen bijna nooit werk - mensen uit de buurt halen het meestal bij ons op.'

B.
'Ik geniet van mijn onafhankelijkheid', zegt Maggy Sasanow, die vanuit huis werkt als ontwerpster van wenskaarten. 'Ik heb kunst gestudeerd aan de universiteit en wilde graag in een museum werken. Maar toen ik trouwde, zijn we op het platteland gaan wonen, waar dat soort werk niet was. Dus besloot ik mijn eigen bedrijf op te zetten en ik maak een assortiment van 50 wenskaarten die ik aan musea verkoop. Ik werk in een grote kamer boven. Het nadeel van thuiswerken is dat er altijd wel iets te doen is, zoals het gazon maaien. Mijn klanten komen volledig via mond-tot-mondreclame – ik adverteer helemaal niet. Mensen sturen werk op vanuit Londen, omdat ik goedkoper ben dan andere kunstenaars. Doordat ik alleen werk, kan ik geen ideeën meer uitwisselen met anderen, maar over het algemeen wegen de voordelen zwaarder dan de nadelen.'

C.
'Het is soms moeilijk geweest', zegt Delia Turner, wiens gordijnenbedrijf goede en slechte tijden heeft gekend. 'Ik ben acht jaar geleden met mijn bedrijf begonnen.' Toen groeide dit soort bedrijven en in twee jaar tijd steeg mijn omzet van £24.000 naar £80.000. Ik had zes fulltime gordijnmakers in dienst. Maar ik moest ze ontslaan vanwege de economische neergang, wat pijnlijk was omdat het niet makkelijk is om ander werk te vinden in deze sector. Ik ben bijna weer terug bij af, ik maak de gordijnen zelf thuis, met de hulp van mijn man, en ik werk samen met vrouwen die vanuit huis werken. Ik moet bereid zijn mijn prijzen te verlagen wanneer dat nodig is en naar andere mogelijkheden te kijken.

D.
TESSA STRICKLAND runt de redactie en productie van haar kinderboekenuitgeverij vanuit haar boerderij. 'Ik ben drie jaar geleden naar het platteland verhuisd om twee redenen. De eerste was financieel, omdat Londen zo duur was, en de tweede was omdat ik van het platteland houd. Ik geniet ervan om te kunnen werken wanneer ik wil. Tachtig procent van mijn inkomen komt uit deals met Australië, het Verre Oosten en Noord-Amerika, dus ik moet op ongebruikelijke tijden telefoontjes aannemen.' Het nadeel is dat het discipline vereist om de kantoordeur dicht te doen. Ik publiceer kinderboeken uit culturen over de hele wereld en werk samen met auteurs en illustratoren. Al mijn professionele ervaring had ik in Londen opgedaan, dus ik voelde me in het begin erg alleen.

E.
MEG RIVERS runt een bedrijf dat gebak per post verstuurt en een winkel met een jaaromzet van £250.000 en zes medewerkers, waarvan sommigen parttime. 'Ik ben tien jaar geleden thuis begonnen. Ik ben erg geïnteresseerd in gezondheid, dus ik begon met het bakken van vruchtengebak met goede kwaliteit bloem en eieren. Toen kreeg ik steeds meer verzoeken van vrienden en familie, en al snel verstuurde ik gebak door het hele land. Zeven jaar geleden huurde ik een klein pand en alles wordt daar gemaakt - we hebben een bakker en een assistent, en een professionele taartdecorateur. Ik kook nu helemaal niet meer, omdat ik de commerciële kant run. Mijn grootste probleem is de financiële kant van het bedrijf geweest, wat lastig was omdat we niet enorm veel geld hadden om mee te beginnen.'

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi is known as Mahatma meaning ‘Great Soul’. He was an astute political campaigner who fought for Indian independence from British rule and for the rights of the Indian poor.
His example of non-violent protest is still revered throughout the world today. Find out how this man of peace and representative of India's poor came from a privileged background and spent his teenage years as a rebel.
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi is born in north-west India in the princely state of Porbandar on 2 October 1869.
His family comes from an elite background. His father works for the government as the chief minister of Porbandar. His mother is a deeply pious woman who spends a lot of her time at temple and on frequent fasts. She instils in him a strong Hindu ethic, with an emphasis on vegetarianism, religious tolerance, a simple lifestyle, and non-violence.
Gandhi’s father moves the family to the nearby city of Rajkot. Crucially schooling here is better and Gandhi is taught English.
At the age of 13 Gandhi marries Kasturba, a local girl who is 14. Gandhi is a rebellious teenager – drinking, eating meat and womanising. Yet he is interested in self-improvement and is repentant after each act of vice. When his father is on his death bed, Gandhi leaves to have sex with his wife and misses the moment of his death. When his wife becomes pregnant and the child dies shortly after birth, he sees this as divine retribution.

Our system of government, at both the national and state levels, is based on the principle of representation. People do not themselves govern, nor do they ordinarily vote to adopt laws and public policy. Rather, they govern indirectly by electing legislators who represent them. 
For the framers of the U.S. Constitution, the legitimacy of the government came from the consent of the governed. The House of Representatives, with its members elected by constituencies throughout the nation, was designed to reflect the views of the people. The Senate, with its members originally selected by state legislatures, was designed to reflect the sovereignty of the states. The will of the people would find its way through legislative chambers by means of lawmakers who would assess their constituencies’ preferences and interests and take them into account in deciding matters of public policy.  Legislators would lead, interpret and reflect public opinion as they assembled in Congress.
Today, members of both the U.S. House and U.S. Senate and the houses and senates of the 50 states (except Nebraska, which is unicameral and has a senate, but not a house) are elected by the people and are considered to be representatives of the people.
At the state level, for example, legislators represent their constituents in a number of ways. They help constituents in their district who may have problems with governmental regulation or the service provision, such as welfare benefits, unemployment compensation, driver’s licenses, insurance costs, taxes—almost anything under the sun. They try to secure funds for projects—such as construction of a court house or funding for travel by a high school band—for their districts. They also are constantly looking for as many state dollars as possible to be channeled to their districts as school, county and municipal aid.
results.tgt_text:
Ons regeringssysteem, zowel op nationaal als op staatsniveau, is gebaseerd op het principe van representatie. Het volk regeert niet zelf, noch stemt het doorgaans over wetten en overheidsbeleid. In plaats daarvan regeert het indirect door wetgevers te kiezen die hen vertegenwoordigen.

Voor de opstellers van de Amerikaanse Grondwet kwam de legitimiteit van de regering voort uit de instemming van de geregeerden. Het Huis van Afgevaardigden, waarvan de leden door kiesdistricten in het hele land werden gekozen, was bedoeld om de standpunten van het volk te weerspiegelen. De Senaat, waarvan de leden oorspronkelijk door de wetgevende machten van de staten werden gekozen, was bedoeld om de soevereiniteit van de staten te weerspiegelen. De wil van het volk zou via de wetgevende kamers tot uiting komen door middel van wetgevers die de voorkeuren en belangen van hun kiezers zouden peilen en daarmee rekening zouden houden bij het nemen van beslissingen over overheidsbeleid. Wetgevers zouden de publieke opinie leiden, interpreteren en weerspiegelen wanneer zij in het Congres bijeenkwamen.

Tegenwoordig worden leden van zowel het Amerikaanse Huis van Afgevaardigden als de Amerikaanse Senaat, en de huizen en senaten van de 50 staten (met uitzondering van Nebraska, dat een eenkamerstelsel heeft met een senaat maar geen Huis van Afgevaardigden) door het volk gekozen en beschouwd als vertegenwoordigers van het volk.

Op staatsniveau vertegenwoordigen wetgevers bijvoorbeeld hun kiezers op verschillende manieren. Ze helpen kiezers in hun district die problemen hebben met overheidsregulering of de dienstverlening, zoals uitkeringen, werkloosheidsuitkeringen, rijbewijzen, verzekeringskosten, belastingen – vrijwel alles wat je je kunt voorstellen. Ze proberen geld te verkrijgen voor projecten – zoals de bouw van een gerechtsgebouw of financiering voor reizen van een schoolorkest – voor hun districten. Ze zijn ook voortdurend op zoek naar zoveel mogelijk staatsgeld dat naar hun districten kan worden gesluisd als steun aan scholen, provincies en gemeenten.

results.src_text:
Climbing to the top of Britain

Each year thousands of people climb Ben Nevis in Scotland, and because of its northerly location, the climate can be bitterly cold. Climber Keith Hewitt describes his first time on Ben Nevis.

It was February, my first big winter climb. Our route was up the north face of the mountain to Tower Ridge. It's six hundred metres up - probably the longest climb in Britain. We planned to camp for three days in the 'Carries', which are like big bowls cut into the walls of the mountain half-way up.
We were carrying tents, sleeping bags, and metal spikes for our boots -you'd have trouble on Ben Nevis without them because you get snow so hard it's like walking on ice. Even though some of the group were very experienced, we packed all kinds of safety equipment, including lights for attracting attention, hard hats and extra clothing. Although the weather forecast was perfect, with no strong winds, there was still a general feeling of nervousness when we set out. Ben Nevis in winter is always a challenge.
The track soon climbed and my legs felt heavy. Being the weakest member of the group, I had to rest more frequently. The others sometimes stopped for a break to let me catch up, but as soon as I reached them they set off again. I promised myself that in future I would always train properly before a climb.
After 200 metre<;,we reached the beginning of Tower Ridge, the route that would take us to the top of Ben Nevis. It's only a metre and a half wide and the mountain drops away hundreds of metres on each side. We knew we had to keep calm and concentrate on every step as we moved slowly along it.
After seven hours of climbing, we reached the top. On a clear day, you can see the sea and right across it to the island of Skye, 48 kilometres away. However, we weren't so lucky, as a mist had come down.
On Ben Nevis, getting back down to camp can be as much of a challenge as going up. You need to be able to read a map properly a wrong turn could lead to slopes too dangerous to go down in winter. I was glad we had decided to take it in turns to do that job. That first time, it was only when I was safe in the tent that I could say I really enjoyed the experience. But at least I made it to the top.
results.tgt_text:
Naar de top van Groot-Brittannië

Elk jaar beklimmen duizenden mensen Ben Nevis in Schotland, en vanwege de noordelijke ligging kan het er bitter koud zijn. Klimmer Keith Hewitt beschrijft zijn eerste keer op Ben Nevis.

Het was februari, mijn eerste grote winterbeklimming. Onze route liep via de noordwand van de berg naar Tower Ridge. Dat is zeshonderd meter omhoog – waarschijnlijk de langste beklimming in Groot-Brittannië. We waren van plan om drie dagen te kamperen in de 'Carries', grote komvormige uithollingen in de bergwand halverwege de berg.

We hadden tenten, slaapzakken en metalen spikes voor onze schoenen bij ons – zonder die spullen zou je het moeilijk hebben op Ben Nevis, want de sneeuw is er zo hard dat het voelt alsof je over ijs loopt. Hoewel sommige leden van de groep zeer ervaren waren, pakten we allerlei veiligheidsuitrusting in, waaronder lampen om de aandacht te trekken, helmen en extra kleding. Hoewel de weersvoorspelling perfect was, zonder harde wind, hing er toch een algemene spanning in de lucht toen we vertrokken. Ben Nevis in de winter is altijd een uitdaging.

Het pad liep al snel omhoog en mijn benen voelden zwaar aan. Omdat ik de zwakste van de groep was, moest ik vaker rusten. De anderen stopten soms even om me bij te laten komen, maar zodra ik ze had ingehaald, gingen ze weer verder. Ik beloofde mezelf dat ik in de toekomst altijd goed zou trainen voor een klim.

Na 200 meter bereikten we het begin van Tower Ridge, de route die ons naar de top van Ben Nevis zou brengen. Het is slechts anderhalve meter breed en de berg loopt aan beide kanten honderden meters naar beneden. We wisten dat we kalm moesten blijven en ons op elke stap moesten concentreren terwijl we er langzaam overheen klommen.

Na zeven uur klimmen bereikten we de top. Op een heldere dag kun je de zee zien en aan de overkant het eiland Skye, 48 kilometer verderop. Wij hadden echter minder geluk, want er was mist opgetrokken.

Op Ben Nevis kan de afdaling naar het kamp net zo'n uitdaging zijn als de klim omhoog. Je moet een kaart goed kunnen lezen, want een verkeerde afslag kan leiden naar hellingen die in de winter te gevaarlijk zijn om af te dalen. Ik was blij dat we hadden afgesproken om die taak om de beurt uit te voeren. De eerste keer kon ik pas, toen ik veilig in de tent zat, zeggen dat ik er echt van genoten had. Maar ik ben tenminste boven gekomen.
results.back_text:
To the Top of Great Britain

Every year, thousands of people climb Ben Nevis in Scotland, and due to its northern location, it can be bitterly cold. Climber Keith Hewitt describes his first time on Ben Nevis.

It was February, my first major winter climb. Our route ran along the mountain's north face to Tower Ridge. That is six hundred meters uphill – probably the longest climb in Great Britain. We planned to camp for three days in the 'Carries', large bowl-shaped hollows in the mountain face halfway up the mountain.

We had tents, sleeping bags, and metal spikes for our shoes with us – without that gear, you would struggle on Ben Nevis, because the snow is so hard that it feels like walking on ice. Although some members of the group were very experienced, we packed all kinds of safety gear, including lights to attract attention, helmets, and extra clothing. Although the weather forecast was perfect, with no strong winds, there was still a general tension in the air when we set off. Ben Nevis in winter is always a challenge.

The path soon started climbing, and my legs felt heavy. Because I was the weakest in the group, I had to rest frequently. The others would stop for a moment to let me catch up, but as soon as I had caught up with them, they continued on their way. I promised myself that in the future, I would always train well for a climb.

After 200 meters, we reached the start of Tower Ridge, the route that would take us to the summit of Ben Nevis. It is only one and a half meters wide, and the mountain drops hundreds of meters down on both sides. We knew we had to stay calm and concentrate on every step as we slowly climbed over it.

After seven hours of climbing, we reached the summit. On a clear day, you can see the sea and, across the water, the Isle of Skye, 48 kilometers away. However, we were less fortunate, as the fog had lifted.

On Ben Nevis, the descent to the camp can be just as challenging as the climb up. You have to be able to read a map well, because a wrong turn can lead to slopes that are too dangerous to descend in winter. I was glad we had agreed to take turns performing that task. The first time, I could only say that I had really enjoyed it once I was safely inside the tent. But at least I made it to the top.
