Beweging is essentieel voor lichaam, geest en ziel. Het is een van de beste manieren om een ​​perfecte balans te behouden, terwijl alles om je heen steeds meer uit balans lijkt te raken en de wereld steeds sneller en hectischer wordt.

Zucht niet, want dit is alweer een artikel over fitness. De reden dat er zoveel zijn, is dat het echt goed voor je is. Er zijn talloze redenen waarom je zou moeten sporten en maar weinig – voor de meesten van ons – waarom je dat niet zou moeten doen. Sporten verbetert de spiertonus en zorgt voor snelle veranderingen in je lichaamsvorm. Het verbetert de spierkracht en bevordert een goede houding – de manier waarop je je lichaam houdt tijdens het zitten of staan. Het helpt spieronevenwichtigheden te voorkomen die tot blessures kunnen leiden. Het zorgt voor snelle verbetering in specifieke probleemgebieden zoals de dijen, buik en bovenarmen. Het verbetert de conditie van het hart en de longen en de bloedsomloop.

Waarschijnlijk zijn al deze redenen je al zo vaak voorgeschoteld dat je er misschien genoeg van hebt en bent afgehaakt. Oké, dit artikel zou je aandacht moeten trekken. Wist je dat bewegen helpt bij het verlichten van depressie en vermoeidheid, en dat het je slaapritme reguleert? En dat bewegen ook essentieel is voor het beheersen van stress? Bovendien kan bewegen bepaalde medische aandoeningen verlichten.

Deze argumenten zullen je hopelijk al een beetje overtuigen. Zo niet, dan zegt je gezond verstand je al dat bewegen goed voor je is.

Er zijn talloze soorten oefeningen die je kunt doen: aerobics, calisthenics, joggen, trainen met vrije gewichten, trainen met fitnessapparaten. Let wel op: te hard en met te veel gewicht trainen kan blessures veroorzaken, dus begin rustig en voorzichtig. Als je twijfelt, raadpleeg dan je arts over wat voor jou persoonlijk het beste is.

Geen enkele hoeveelheid beweging zal je figuur verbeteren als je geen goede houding hebt. Dit bepaalt in feite hoe je eruitziet en je voelt. Een stijf of ingevallen lichaam is niet alleen onaantrekkelijk, het mist ook energie en maakt je vatbaarder voor kleine gezondheidsklachten.

Als je de neiging hebt om voorover te buigen, stel je dan voor dat de bovenkant van je hoofd verbonden is met een heliumballon die je omhoog probeert te trekken. Dit helpt je om je borstkas te liften voor een vollere en gemakkelijkere ademhaling. Tegelijkertijd verlengt het je buik, waardoor je lichaam er veel slanker uitziet. Als je borstkas goed in balans is wanneer je staat, kun je je enkels zien.

Het rekken van de spieren verbetert de flexibiliteit en het bewegingsgemak, en helpt je om een ​​correcte houding te behouden en spierscheuren en blessures door overbelasting te voorkomen. Als je dit vier of vijf keer per week doet, garandeert het een flexibeler en fitter lichaam. Rekken zou dus een belangrijk onderdeel moeten zijn van je trainingsroutine, die zowel langzaam als gecontroleerd moet worden uitgevoerd.

De beste training bestaat daarom uit een goede warming-up, rekoefeningen, een energieke workout en zeker een cooling-down.

And certainly Catherine's education could not be described as appropriate for a heroine. In fact, she had an obvious dislike for the classroom and never could learn or understand anything before she was taught; occasionally she even seemed rather stupid. 
Her mother wanted her to learn music and Catherine was sure that she would like to play the piano, so at eight years old she began lessons. But she soon gave up, and the day on which the music teacher was dismissed was one of the happiest days of her young life. Her drawing ability was also disappointing; although she enjoyed drawing animals, all her pictures, from chickens to horses, looked very similar. 
What a strange, incomprehensible character! Incomprehensible because, in spite of such clear signs of a difficult nature, Catherine was seldom unpleasant; she rarely quarrelled and was very kind to her six younger brothers and sisters and quite friendly with the three older ones. But it still must be admitted that she was untidy, noisy and wild and loved nothing better than rolling down her favourite hill at the back of the house. 
At fifteen, Catherine's appearance began to improve; her skin was brighter, her hair was shinier and nicely styled, her eyes shone and her figure was pleasing. Her love of dirt was replaced by an interest in the latest fashions and in the possibility of going to a ball. She was quite thrilled one day to hear her father remark on her personal improvement: 'Catherine is almost pretty today.' To be almost pretty is a great prize to a girl who has been plain for fifteen years.

It was late autumn. The weather was wet and the wind had blown all the leaves from the trees. I was riding my horse across the wet, empty land. I was traveling alone. I was going toward a dark and strange house - the House of Usher.
Why had I come to this lonely place? I knew Roderick Usher - the owner of the house. We were old friends, but we had not met for many years. A few weeks ago, I had received a letter from Roderick.

I am ill - very ill. Please come and visit me. I am going mad! I want your help. We have been friends since we were boys. Please come!
Roderick Usher

I had been riding all day and it was now late. The pale sun was low in the sky when I arrived at the House of Usher.
A large lake of black water surrounded the house. I stopped by the lake and looked at the house. Roderick Usher's house was a large black building. Its many windows were like empty eyes. Suddenly, I felt cold...and a little afraid.
In front of me, a narrow road went across a bridge toward the house. I walked my horse along the narrow road until I reached the walls of the house.
I knocked on the front door and a servant opened it. He took my horse to a stable. Then he led me inside the house.
We climbed many stairs to his master's room. Lamps burned along the walls, but they gave little light. The long corridors and stairways were full of dark shadows.
The servant opened a big, wooden door and I looked inside a large room.

THE HISTORY OF THE LONDON POLICE

Today there are policemen everywhere, but in 1700 London had no policemen at all. A few old men used to protect the city streets at night and they were not paid very much.
About 300 years ago, London was starting to get bigger. The city was very dirty and many people were poor. There were so many thieves who stole money in the streets that people stayed in their homes as much as possible.
In 1750, Henry Fielding started to pay a group of people to stop thieves. They were like policemen and were called 'Bow Street Runners' because they worked near Bow Street.
Fifty years later, there were 120 Bow Street Runners, but London had become very big and needed more policemen. So, in 1829, the first Metropolitan (or London) Police Force was started with 3000 officers. Most of the men worked on foot, but a few rode horses. Until 1920 all the police in London were men.
Today, London police are quite well paid and for the few police officers who still ride horses, the pay is even better than for the others.

Once a select forum of the great and good, the Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) conference now has millions of avid online fans. How did an elite ideas-sharing gathering go mainstream?
Falling animals, misbehaving toddlers and footage of Justin Bieber may populate the bulk of any YouTube most-viewed list.
But amid the viral clips and pop music promos is a series of videos that seems to go against all received wisdom about what online audiences like to consume.
Their tone is sunnily optimistic, go-getting, Californian, with titles like Information Is Food, Crowdsource Your Health and Inventing Is the Easy Part.
They feature luminaries such as Stephen Hawking, JK Rowling and Bono delivering 18-minute lectures about big ideas - technology, culture, the environment, science, social trends.
Yet although there is nary a Lolcat in sight, the YouTube channel of the Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) conference has attracted nearly 112 million views.
The talks have a habit of catching on. TED attendees were given a preview of Al Gore's lecture on climate change lecture, later popularised in An Inconvenient Truth . Biologist Richard Dawkins' 2002 lecture on "militant atheism" laid the groundwork for the arguments set out in hishugely controversial book The God Delusion 
Others have entered the realms of the downright strange, such as whenMicrosoft founder Bill Gates unleashed live mosquitoes into the auditorium during a talk on malaria because "there's no reason why only poor people should have the experience" (the insects were not infected).
It's an impressive level of public interest in an event sneered at by detractors as an expensive talking-shop-cum-networking-event for latte-wielding, iPad clutching, West Coast blue-sky thinkers.

Almost everyone knows the story of “Peter Pan” which is why this is an easy read. Being familiar with a story already helps the reader to understand the text better. This book is aimed at children, but it continues to be enjoyed by adults around the world too.
Plot Summary
Every night Peter visits the Darling family house and listens to Mrs. Darling tell bedtime stories. He sits on the window listening. One evening, they see Peter trying to escape. As he tries to run away, he loses his shadow. He goes back to get his shadow. He wakes up the daughter of the house, Wendy Darling. Wendy helps him attach his shadow to his body again. Wendy tells him she knows a lot of bedtime stories too.
Peter invites Wendy to return to Neverland with him. He wants her to be the mother of the Lost Boys. Wendy agrees to the mission and asks for her brothers Michael and John to join them.
They have a magical flight as they travel to Neverland and have many adventures along the way. Wendy is nearly killed and the boys build her a house in the trees to recover. After Wendy is okay, she takes the role of the mother.
After all their adventures and fun, Wendy decides that her place is at home with their mother. Wendy helps all the Lost Boys return to London. But Peter doesn’t want her to go. Instead he tries to trick her. He tells her that their mother doesn’t want them anymore. However, he understands how sad their mother must be. In the end, he decides to let them go home.

The journey from our town to the capital was a journey of about five hours. When I arrived at Mr Jaggers's office the clerk told me that he was in court, and that he had left word I should wait in
his room. He led me to a dark room. After I had waited for a long time Mr Jaggers arrived.
Many people, men and women, who had been waiting for him outside the office, made a rush at him. He addressed himself to two of the men.
'Now, I have nothing to say to you,' said Mr Jaggers, pointing his finger at them. 'I want to know no more than I know. As to the result, it could go either way. I told you that from the start. Have you paid Wemmick?'
'Yes, sir,' said both the men together.
'Very well; then you may go. Now, I won't have it!' said Mr Jaggers, waving his hand at them to put them behind him. 'If you say a word to me, I'll throw up the case.'
'We thought, Mr Jaggers -' one of the men began, pulling off his hat.
'That's what I told you not to do,' said Mr Jaggers. 'You thought! I think for you; that's enough for you. If I want you, I know where to find you; I don't want you to find me. Now I won't have it. I won't hear a word.' 
The two men looked at one another as Mr Jaggers waved them behind him, and fell back and were heard no more.

Toen ik bij het kantoor van meneer Jaggers aankwam, vertelde de klerk me dat hij in de rechtbank was en dat hij had laten weten dat ik in zijn kamer moest wachten. Hij leidde me naar een donkere kamer. Nadat ik lang had gewacht, kwam meneer Jaggers aan.

Veel mensen, mannen en vrouwen, die buiten het kantoor op hem hadden gewacht, stormden op hem af. Hij sprak twee van de mannen aan.

'Nou, ik heb niets tegen jullie te zeggen,' zei meneer Jaggers, terwijl hij met zijn vinger naar hen wees. 'Ik wil niet meer weten dan ik al weet. Wat de uitkomst betreft, die kan alle kanten op. Dat heb ik jullie vanaf het begin gezegd. Hebben jullie Wemmick betaald?'

'Ja, meneer,' zeiden beide mannen tegelijk.

'Goed, dan kunnen jullie gaan. Maar nu pik ik het niet!' zei meneer Jaggers, terwijl hij met zijn hand gebaarde dat ze achter hem moesten blijven. 'Als jullie nog één woord tegen me zeggen, gooi ik de zaak overboord.'

'We dachten, meneer Jaggers -' begon een van de mannen, terwijl hij zijn hoed afzette.

'Dat is precies wat ik jullie had gezegd niet te doen,' zei meneer Jaggers. 'Jullie dachten! Ik denk voor jullie; dat is genoeg voor jullie. Als ik jullie nodig heb, weet ik waar ik jullie kan vinden; ik wil niet dat jullie mij vinden. Nu pik ik het niet meer. Ik wil geen woord meer horen.'

De twee mannen keken elkaar aan terwijl meneer Jaggers hen achter zich wenkte, waarna ze zich terugtrokken en niet meer gehoord werden.

The journey from our town to the capital took about five hours. When I arrived at Mr. Jaggers’ office, the clerk told me that he was in court and that he had let me know that I should wait in his room. He led me to a dark room. After I had waited for a long time, Mr. Jaggers arrived.

Many people, men and women, who had been waiting for him outside the office, rushed towards him. He spoke to two of the men.

"Well, I have nothing to say to you," said Mr. Jaggers, pointing his finger at them. "I don't want to know any more than I already know. As for the outcome, it could go either way. I told you that from the beginning. Have you paid Wemmick?"

"Yes, sir," said both men at the same time.

"Good, then you may go. But I won't take it now!" said Mr. Jaggers, gesturing with his hand for them to stay behind him. 'If you say one more word to me, I'll throw the whole thing overboard.'

'We thought, Mr. Jaggers—' one of the men began, taking off his hat.

'That is exactly what I told you not to do,' said Mr. Jaggers. 'You thought! I think for you; that is enough for you. If I need you, I know where to find you; I don't want you to find me. I won't take it anymore. I don't want to hear another word.'

The two men looked at each other while Mr. Jaggers beckoned them behind him, after which they withdrew and were not heard again.

Charles Darwin (1809-1882) developed a revolutionary theory of evolution that transformed the way we understand the world and we see ourselves. In On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, Darwin described the process of natural selection. 
The 'fittest' animals or plants - those with the characteristics best suited to their environment - are more likely to survive and reproduce. They pass on these desirable characteristics to their offspring. Gradually those features become more common, causing the species to change over time. If the changes are great enough, they can produce an entirely new species. 
The Descent of Man, published in 1871, suggested that humans descended from apes. When Darwin studied medicine, he witnessed an operation performed on a child without anaesthetic. That made him give up medical studies. 
He then studied theology but, instead of becoming a priest, in 1831 he set off on a five-year scientific expedition around the world. There he collected evidence for his future theory. One of the key arguments for natural selection came from the birds that Darwin collected from the Gal pagos Islands. The birds were clearly the same species but some had large strong beaks for eating nuts while others had long thin beaks for finding worms in the ground. 
Darwin realised that all came from a single ancestor but, as they dispersed to different islands, they had adapted to eat the various foods available. Darwin developed the theory of evolution in the 1830s but he didn't announce it then. He knew his ideas were radical so he delayed publishing the theory for about twenty years while he assembled more evidence.

The 'most suitable' animals or plants—those with the traits best adapted to their environment—have a greater chance of surviving and reproducing. They pass these desirable traits on to their offspring. Gradually, these traits become increasingly common, causing the species to change over time. If the changes are significant enough, they can produce an entirely new species.

'The Descent of Man', published in 1871, suggested that humans descended from apes. While studying medicine, Darwin witnessed an operation on a child without anesthesia. This led him to decide to abandon his medical studies.

He subsequently studied theology, but instead of becoming a priest, he embarked on a five-year scientific expedition around the world in 1831. There, he gathered evidence for his future theory. One of the most important arguments for natural selection came from the birds Darwin collected on the Galápagos Islands. The birds clearly belonged to the same species, but some had large, strong beaks for eating nuts, while others had long, thin beaks for searching for worms in the ground.

Darwin realized that they all descended from a single ancestor, but that by spreading across different islands, they had adapted to the diverse food supply. Darwin developed the theory of evolution in the 1830s, but did not make it public at that time. He knew that his ideas were radical, so he delayed the publication of the theory for about twenty years while he gathered more evidence.

Looking after the countryside 

THE NATIONAL TRUST 

The National Trust is an organisation whose aim is to conserve the British countryside. Gill Page visits the Lleyn Peninsula in North Wales and talks to one of the wardens employed by the Trust to look after the beautiful areas it owns. 

Common sense. That's what a National Trust Warden needs, according to Gareth Roberts. 'And you definitely need to be good at handling people, because you're continually dealing with farmers, visitors, conservationists and building firms.' 
Gareth was born and bred on the Lleyn Peninsula and worked on his parents' farm until he married. About 80 people applied for the post as National Trust Warden for the Lleyn Peninsula. In the end, Gareth's local knowledge and farming experience won him the job, despite his lack of formal training. 
'I find it particularly helpful that I still farm with my parents and that I can deal with farmers on the same level and be aware of their problems. Also, they can't take me in about anything!' he says. His farming life also means he is well able to cope with the physical demands of the job - erecting fences, planting trees, building walls. 
Since he has been with the Trust, Gareth says he has come to understand more about nature conservation. 'When I was a youngster,' he recalls, 'I used to pick and press flowers, collect butterfly larvae and old birds' nests. And I thought to myself recently, where would I find all those flowers, the birds' nests, the grasshoppers now? It's really become clear to me that farming has affected the countryside. It's not the farmers' fault - they were just doing what the government told them.' 
Gareth says that, when he started his job, farmers and conservationists were set against each other. Both sides wanted things done their way.Now they are talking and can see each other's point of view. 'We're at the crossroads and there's just a small step needed to join them together,' says Gareth. 
Conservation is one of the main aspects of Gareth's work, along with public entry to the Trust's land, tree planting and maintenance, and meeting the Trust's tenant farmers. 'My role is to make sure jobs get finished, with as little fuss and as economically as possible. What I enjoy most is seeing projects completed, although about half my time is spent on reports, signing bills and so on.' 
Gareth is certainly keen on his job and despite never being off duty, he obviously enjoys every minute of his work, especially talking to the public. Most of them, anyway. 'It's the attitude of some people I dislike,' he admits. 'They just walk into the area, demand everything, then walk out again as if it's their absolute right. Having to be nice to those people gets on my nerves!' 
But as Gareth says, it's all down to common sense really.So if you've got plenty of that, and you like the idea of an outdoor job, you might think of applying to become a warden like Gareth - but don't expect a job to be available on the Lleyn Peninsula for a good many years!

Zorg dragen voor het platteland

DE NATIONAL TRUST

De National Trust is een organisatie die zich ten doel stelt het Britse platteland te behouden. Gill Page bezoekt het schiereiland Lleyn in Noord-Wales en spreekt met een van de beheerders die door de Trust zijn aangesteld om de prachtige gebieden die zij beheert te onderhouden.

Gezond verstand. Dat is wat een beheerder van de National Trust nodig heeft, aldus Gareth Roberts. 'En je moet absoluut goed met mensen kunnen omgaan, want je hebt voortdurend te maken met boeren, bezoekers, natuurbeschermers en bouwbedrijven.'

Gareth is geboren en getogen op het schiereiland Lleyn en werkte op de boerderij van zijn ouders tot hij trouwde. Ongeveer 80 mensen solliciteerden naar de functie van beheerder van de National Trust voor het schiereiland Lleyn. Uiteindelijk won Gareth de baan dankzij zijn lokale kennis en ervaring in de landbouw, ondanks zijn gebrek aan formele opleiding.

'Ik vind het bijzonder nuttig dat ik nog steeds met mijn ouders samenwerk op de boerderij en dat ik op hetzelfde niveau met boeren kan praten en hun problemen begrijp. Bovendien kunnen ze me nergens over voor de gek houden!', zegt hij. Zijn achtergrond als boer zorgt er ook voor dat hij goed overweg kan met de fysieke eisen van het werk: hekken plaatsen, bomen planten, muren bouwen.

Sinds hij bij de stichting werkt, zegt Gareth dat hij meer inzicht heeft gekregen in natuurbehoud. 'Toen ik jong was,' herinnert hij zich, 'plukte en perste ik bloemen, verzamelde ik vlinderlarven en oude vogelnesten. En ik vroeg me onlangs af: waar vind ik al die bloemen, vogelnesten en sprinkhanen nu nog? Het is me echt duidelijk geworden dat de landbouw het platteland heeft beïnvloed. Het is niet de schuld van de boeren - ze deden gewoon wat de overheid hen opdroeg.'

Gareth zegt dat toen hij begon met zijn werk, boeren en natuurbeschermers lijnrecht tegenover elkaar stonden. Beide partijen wilden de zaken op hun eigen manier aanpakken. Nu praten ze met elkaar en kunnen ze elkaars standpunt begrijpen. 'We staan ​​op een kruispunt en er is maar een kleine stap nodig om ze samen te brengen,' zegt Gareth.

Natuurbehoud is een van de belangrijkste aspecten van Gareths werk, samen met de toegang voor het publiek tot het terrein van de stichting, het planten en onderhouden van bomen en het ontmoeten van de pachtboeren van de stichting. 'Mijn rol is ervoor te zorgen dat klussen zo snel en zo economisch mogelijk worden afgerond. Wat ik het leukst vind, is het zien van voltooide projecten, hoewel ik ongeveer de helft van mijn tijd besteed aan rapporten, het ondertekenen van facturen en dergelijke.'
Gareth is zeker enthousiast over zijn werk en hoewel hij nooit vrij is, geniet hij duidelijk van elke minuut, vooral van het contact met het publiek. Tenminste, met de meeste mensen. 'Het is de houding van sommige mensen die me stoort', geeft hij toe. 'Ze komen gewoon het gebied binnen, eisen alles en lopen dan weer weg alsof ze er absoluut recht op hebben. Het is echt irritant om aardig te moeten zijn tegen die mensen!'

Maar zoals Gareth al zegt, het komt eigenlijk allemaal neer op gezond verstand. Dus als je daar genoeg van hebt en een baan in de buitenlucht je wel aanspreekt, kun je overwegen om net als Gareth te solliciteren naar een functie als boswachter – maar verwacht niet dat er de komende jaren een baan beschikbaar zal zijn op het schiereiland Lleyn!

Monsieur Firmin was right. All Paris talked about the new Margarita in Faust, the girl with the beautiful voice, the girl with the voice of an angel. People loved her. They laughed and cried and called for more. Daae was wonderful, the best singer in the world!
Behind the stage Meg Giry looked at Annie Sorelli. 'Christine Daae never sang like that before,' she said to Annie. 'Why was she so good tonight?'
'Perhaps she's got a new music teacher,' Annie said.
The noise in the Opera House went on for a long time. In Box 14, Philippe, the Comte de Chagny, turned to his younger brother and smiled.
'Well, Raoul, what did you think of Daae tonight?'
Raoul, the Vicomte de Chagny, was twenty-one years old. He had blue eyes and black hair, and a wonderful smile. The Chagny family was old and rich, and many girls in Paris were in love with the young Vicomte. But Raoul was not interested in them.
He smiled back at his brother. 'What can I say? Christine is an angel, that's all. I'm going to her dressing-room to see her tonight.'
Philippe laughed. He was twenty years older than Raoul, and was more like a father than a brother.
'Ah, I understand,' he said. 'You are in love! But this is your first night in Paris, your first visit to the opera. How do you know Christine Daae?'
'You remember four years ago, when I was on holiday by the sea, in Brittany?' Raoul said. 'Well, I met Christine there. I was in love with her then, and I'm still in love with her today!'

Achter het podium keek Meg Giry naar Annie Sorelli. 'Christine Daae heeft nog nooit zo gezongen,' zei ze tegen Annie. 'Waarom was ze vanavond zo goed?'

'Misschien heeft ze een nieuwe muziekleraar,' zei Annie.

Raoul, de burggraaf van Chagny, was eenentwintig jaar oud. Hij had blauwe ogen en zwart haar, en een prachtige glimlach. De familie Chagny was oud en rijk, en veel meisjes in Parijs waren verliefd op de jonge burggraaf. Maar Raoul was niet in hen geïnteresseerd.

'Do you remember, four years ago, when I was on vacation by the sea, in Brittany?' said Raoul. 'Well, that is where I met Christine. I was already in love with her then, and I am still in love with her!'

The cop saw the car stop on the bridge but didn't think too much about it. People often stopped their cars on the bridge late at night, when there was not much traffic. The bridge was over the deep river that cut the city neatly in two, and the center of the bridge provided the best view of the city.
Suicides liked the bridge, too. The cop didn't think of that until he saw the man get out of the car, walk slowly along the footpath at the edge, and put a hand on the rail. There was something about that lonely figure, something about the grayness of the night, the fog coming off the river. The cop looked at him and swore, and wondered if he could get to him in time.
He didn't want to shout or blow his whistle because he knew what surprise could do to a probable suicide. Then the man lit a cigarette, and the cop knew he had time. They always smoked all of that last cigarette before they went over the edge.
When the cop was within ten yards of him, the man turned, gave a slight jump, then nodded as if accepting that the moment had passed. He appeared to be in his middle thirties, tall with a long narrow face and thick black eyebrows.
'Looking at the city?' said the cop. 'I saw you here, and thought I'd come and have a talk with you. It can get lonely at this hour of the night.' He patted his pockets, pretending to look for his cigarettes and not finding them. 'Got a spare cigarette on you?' he asked.
The man gave him a cigarette and lit it for him. The cop thanked the man and looked out at the city.

results.src_text:
Steve Jobs met engineering student Steve Wozniak through a mutual friend. Jobs was surprised to find Wozniak “knew more about electronics than I did.”
Their first joint venture was building devices that enabled people to make illegal free calls. Wozniak later said it was a “bad idea” to sell them, but it gave the duo “a taste of what we could do with my engineering skills and Jobs’ vision.” They then worked on a game for Atari, where Jobs convinced Wozniak to work round the clock to produce the game in four days – something Wozniak considered to be impossible. Jobs was paid a bonus for delivering on time that he kept secret from Wozniak.
Steve Jobs insisted on attending Reed College, Oregon, an expensive liberal arts university, despite his parents telling him they couldn’t afford it.
However, he soon dropped out. He had an on-off relationship with Chrisann Brennan and lived in a cabin in Los Gatos, California. His passion for good design led him to drop into a calligraphy class back at Reed which later inspired him to include a selection of fonts on his computers. He visited India, shaved his head and wore traditional Indian clothes. Eastern philosophy influenced him. He said: “I saw the craziness of the Western world as well as its capacity for rational thought.”
Jobs and Wozniak formed Apple Computer and built their first machine, the Apple I. It was sold without a case, screen, power supply or keyboard.

It's true - we're all getting too big for our boots

Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers teacher he wanted to join the navy when he left school. 'What do you want to be?' asked the teacher. 'The flagpole on a ship?' The teacher had a point - because Chris, though still only fourteen, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is Britain's tallest man.
Every decade, the average height of people in Europe grows another centimetre. Every year, more and more truly big people are born. Intriguingly, this does not mean humanity is producing a new super race. In fact, we are returning to what we were like as cavemen. Only now are we losing the effects of generations of poor diet - with dramatic effects. 'We are only now beginning to fulfil our proper potential,' says palaeontologist Professor Chris Stringer. 'We are becoming Cro-Magnons again - the people who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.'
For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a wide variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruits and berries, while men supplemented these with occasional kills of animals (a way of life still adopted by the world's few remaining tribes of hunter- gatherers). One research study found that they based their diet on 85 different wild plants, for example. Then about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented - with devastating consequences. Most of the planet's green places have been gradually taken over by farmers, with the result that just three carbohydrate-rich plants - wheat, rice and maize - provide more than half of the calories consumed by the human race today.
This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries we have lived on soups, porridges and breads that have left us underfed and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when they began to grow corn, healthy hunter-gatherers were turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did diseases. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, corn was a public health disaster, according to some anthropologists.
Nevertheless, from then on agriculture spread because a piece of farmed land could support ten times the number of people who had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people relying on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been tackled, even by the world's wealthier nations. Only in Europe, the US and Japan are diets again reflecting the richness of our ancestors' diets.
As a result, the average man in the US is now 179cm, in Holland 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, though not without its own problems. Heights may have risen, but the world has not moved on, it seems. A standard bed-length has remained at 190cm since 1860. Even worse, leg-room in planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than grown, while clothes manufacturers are constantly having to revise their range of products.
The question is: where will it all end? We cannot grow for ever. We must have some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of University, it could be as much as 193 cm - and we are likely to reach it some time this century.
However, scientists add one note of qualification. Individuals may be growing taller because of improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly rounder and taller - an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies are best at keeping in heat.) Since the climate warmed, we appear to have got slightly thinner and smaller, even when properly fed. And as the planet continues to heat up, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.

Eeuwenlang hebben we geleefd op soepen, pap en brood, waardoor we ondervoed en onderontwikkeld zijn gebleven. Desalniettemin verspreidde de landbouw zich vanaf dat moment, omdat een stuk landbouwgrond tien keer zoveel mensen kon onderhouden als voorheen, toen ze er als jagers-verzamelaars van leefden. Het feit dat de meeste mensen die van dit systeem afhankelijk zijn, slecht gevoed en in hun groei belemmerd worden, is pas recentelijk aangepakt, zelfs door de rijkere landen van de wereld. Alleen in Europa, de VS en Japan weerspiegelt het voedingspatroon weer de rijkdom van het dieet van onze voorouders.

Als gevolg hiervan is de gemiddelde man in de VS nu 179 cm, in Nederland 180 cm en in Japan 177 cm. Het is een welkome trend, hoewel niet zonder problemen. De lengte is dan wel toegenomen, maar de wereld lijkt niet vooruit te zijn gegaan. De standaard bedlengte is sinds 1860 onveranderd gebleven op 190 cm. Erger nog, de beenruimte in vliegtuigen en treinen lijkt eerder te zijn gekrompen dan gegroeid, terwijl kledingfabrikanten hun productassortiment voortdurend moeten aanpassen.

De vraag is: waar houdt dit allemaal op? We kunnen niet eeuwig blijven groeien. We moeten een geprogrammeerde bovengrens hebben. Maar wat is die? Volgens Robert Fogel van de universiteit zou die wel eens 193 cm kunnen zijn - en we zullen die waarschijnlijk ergens in deze eeuw bereiken.

Wetenschappers voegen hier echter een kanttekening bij. Individuen worden misschien langer door verbeterde voeding, maar als soort krimpen we juist. Tijdens de laatste ijstijd, 10.000 jaar geleden, waren mensen iets ronder en langer - een evolutionaire reactie op de kou. (Grote, ronde lichamen houden warmte het beste vast.) Sinds het klimaat warmer is geworden, lijken we iets dunner en kleiner te zijn geworden, zelfs met voldoende voeding. En naarmate de planeet verder opwarmt, zullen we misschien nog verder krimpen. Met andere woorden: de groei van de mensheid zou door de opwarming van de aarde tenietgedaan kunnen worden.

The Cabinet-Maker
Charles Hurst makes a living from perfectly crafted furniture Joanna Watt meets him
Charles Hurst gives the impression of being a man in a hurry. I arrive at his workshop, tucked under a railway arch in East London, and am greeted with a quick handshake and the words: 'Well, fire away then!' Whether this brusqueness is real or a front hiding a shy streak is not immediately apparent. But a glance around the workshop reveals that Hurst is obviously busy, with good reason not to waste a minute of his time.
The arched space is full of half-made pieces of furniture and planks of wood in an amazing array of natural colours. Hurst has been a cabinet-maker for ten years and has built up a very nice reputation for himself. His order book is always full for several months in advance, despite the fact that he does not really promote himself. Word has spread that if you want a decent cupboard or table, bookcase or kitchen units, Hurst is your man.
Of course, finding a furniture-maker is not that taxing a task. Wherever you live in the countryside, the craft is alive and well. But finding a cabinet- maker who prides himself on making beautifully crafted furniture with clean, simple lines is less easy. 'There are few real cabinet-makers now. People call themselves furniture-makers,' Hurst says wearily. As a craftsman who sets himself exacting standards, he is continually disappointed by some contemporary furniture. 'I am amazed by what some furniture-makers get away with, and saddened by what people will put up with.' He rails against shoddy, mass-produced furniture, and craftsmen who churn out second-rate pieces.
Such a quest for perfection is obviously a key to Hurst's success. That and his talent. This man is not coy about his ability. Indeed, his blatant self- confidence is as surprising as his initial brusque manner. 'I have a huge natural ability,' he says, with a deadpan expression. 'I have always been good at making things.' If it were not for the self-deprecating mood into which he slipped towards the end of our interview, I would have believed his conceit to be wholly genuine.
Hurst is self-taught. So how did he learn his craft? 'I asked the right questions and picked it all up,' he says nonchalantly. Almost all of his commissions come from private individuals ('l used to do some commercial work for companies but it was soul-destroying'). Some clients have returned time and again. 'You end up doing the whole of their house. That is very satisfying.' But he is honest enough to admit that relationships with clients do not always run smoothly. 'The most infuriating clients are those who don't know what they want, and then decide they do when it's too late ... my favourite clients are the exacting ones.'
If Hurst has every reason to be pleased with himself, he is also gracious in his praise for others - where it is due. With a sudden shot of modesty, he says: 'There are people far better than me. I can admire other people. After all, I wasn't trained at Parnham' (the leading college of furniture design). However, he is also unremittingly critical of those craftsmen who 'are trying to be artists and take a year to make one piece.' He also has little time for degree shows, in which students exhibit their work but at the same time are 'trying to make fashion statements. That can be pretentious. A piece of furniture is not about making a statement. It has to be something that people really can use.'
Confident Hurst may be, even brusque, but you could never call him or his work pretentious. Indeed, his parting shot displays a welcome down- to-earth approach to his craft and a streak of humility strangely at odds with his earlier self- confidence. 'After all, I am only making furniture,' he says as I make my exit.

De meubelmaker
Charles Hurst verdient de kost met perfect vervaardigde meubels. Joanna Watt ontmoet hem.
Charles Hurst maakt de indruk een man met haast te zijn. Ik kom aan bij zijn werkplaats, verscholen onder een spoorbrug in Oost-Londen, en word begroet met een snelle handdruk en de woorden: 'Nou, ga je gang dan!' Of deze botheid echt is of een façade die een verlegen kant verbergt, is niet meteen duidelijk. Maar een blik in de werkplaats onthult dat Hurst het duidelijk druk heeft, en terecht, hij wil geen minuut van zijn tijd verspillen.

De ruimte onder de spoorbrug is gevuld met half afgemaakte meubelstukken en houten planken in een verbazingwekkende reeks natuurlijke kleuren. Hurst is al tien jaar meubelmaker en heeft een uitstekende reputatie opgebouwd. Zijn orderboek is altijd maanden van tevoren vol, ondanks het feit dat hij zichzelf niet echt promoot. Het gerucht gaat dat als je een degelijke kast of tafel, boekenkast of keukenmeubels wilt, je bij Hurst moet zijn.

Natuurlijk is het vinden van een meubelmaker geen moeilijke opgave. Waar je ook woont op het platteland, het ambacht is er nog steeds springlevend. Maar een meubelmaker vinden die er trots op is prachtig vervaardigde meubels met strakke, eenvoudige lijnen te maken, is minder makkelijk. 'Er zijn tegenwoordig nog maar weinig echte meubelmakers. Mensen noemen zichzelf meubelmakers,' zegt Hurst vermoeid. Als vakman die zichzelf hoge eisen stelt, is hij voortdurend teleurgesteld in sommige hedendaagse meubels. 'Ik sta versteld van wat sommige meubelmakers allemaal voor elkaar krijgen, en ik vind het triest wat mensen allemaal accepteren.' Hij fulmineert tegen slordige, massaal geproduceerde meubels en ambachtslieden die tweederangs stukken afleveren.
Zo'n streven naar perfectie is duidelijk de sleutel tot Hursts succes. Dat, en zijn talent. Deze man is niet bescheiden over zijn vaardigheden. Zijn openlijke zelfvertrouwen is zelfs net zo verrassend als zijn aanvankelijk wat botte manier van doen. 'Ik heb een enorm natuurlijk talent,' zegt hij met een uitdrukkingloos gezicht. 'Ik ben altijd al goed geweest in dingen maken.' Als hij aan het einde van ons interview niet zo'n zelfspotvolle bui had gehad, zou ik zijn arrogantie volkomen oprecht hebben gevonden.
Hurst is autodidact. Hoe heeft hij zijn vak geleerd? 'Ik stelde de juiste vragen en pikte het allemaal op,' zegt hij nonchalant. Bijna al zijn opdrachten komen van particulieren ('ik deed vroeger wel eens commercieel werk voor bedrijven, maar dat was geestdodend'). Sommige klanten komen steeds weer terug. 'Uiteindelijk doe je hun hele huis. Dat is erg bevredigend.' Maar hij is eerlijk genoeg om toe te geven dat de relaties met klanten niet altijd even soepel verlopen. 'De meest irritante klanten zijn degenen die niet weten wat ze willen, en dan pas besluiten dat ze het wel weten als het te laat is... mijn favoriete klanten zijn de veeleisende.'

Hoewel Hurst alle reden heeft om tevreden met zichzelf te zijn, is hij ook gul in zijn lof voor anderen - waar dat terecht is. Met een plotselinge vlaag van bescheidenheid zegt hij: 'Er zijn mensen die veel beter zijn dan ik.' Ik kan andere mensen bewonderen. Ik ben tenslotte niet opgeleid aan Parnham (de toonaangevende hogeschool voor meubelontwerp). Hij is echter ook onophoudelijk kritisch over ambachtslieden die 'proberen kunstenaar te zijn en een jaar nodig hebben om één stuk te maken'. Hij heeft ook weinig op met afstudeertentoonstellingen, waar studenten hun werk tentoonstellen maar tegelijkertijd 'mode-statements proberen te maken. Dat kan pretentieus zijn. Een meubelstuk gaat niet over het maken van een statement. Het moet iets zijn dat mensen echt kunnen gebruiken.'
Zelfverzekerd, misschien zelfs bot, is Hurst, maar je zou hem of zijn werk nooit pretentieus kunnen noemen. Zijn laatste opmerking getuigt van een welkome nuchtere benadering van zijn vak en een vleugje nederigheid dat vreemd genoeg haaks staat op zijn eerdere zelfvertrouwen. The Furniture Maker
Charles Hurst earns his living making perfectly crafted furniture. Joanna Watt meets him.
Charles Hurst gives the impression of being a man in a hurry. I arrive at his workshop, tucked away under a railway bridge in East London, and am greeted with a quick handshake and the words: 'Well, go ahead then!' Whether this bluntness is genuine or a facade hiding a shy side is not immediately clear. But a glance inside the workshop reveals that Hurst is clearly busy, and rightly so; he does not want to waste a minute of his time.

The space under the railway bridge is filled with half-finished pieces of furniture and wooden shelves in an astonishing array of natural colors. Hurst has been a furniture maker for ten years and has built up an excellent reputation. His order book is always full months in advance, despite the fact that he does not really promote himself. Rumor has it that if you want a solid cupboard or table, bookcase, or kitchen furniture, Hurst is the place to go.

Of course, finding a furniture maker is not a difficult task. No matter where you live in the countryside, the craft is still very much alive. But finding a furniture maker who takes pride in creating beautifully crafted furniture with clean, simple lines is less easy. "There are very few real furniture makers left these days. People call themselves furniture makers," says Hurst wearily. As a craftsman who sets high standards for himself, he is constantly disappointed by some contemporary furniture. "I am amazed at what some furniture makers manage to accomplish, and I find it sad what people accept." He rails against sloppy, mass-produced furniture and artisans who deliver second-rate pieces.
Such a pursuit of perfection is clearly the key to Hurst's success. That, and his talent. This man is not modest about his skills. His open self-confidence is just as surprising as his initially somewhat blunt demeanor. "I have an enormous natural talent," he says with an expressionless face. "I have always been good at making things." If he hadn't been in such a self-deprecating mood at the end of our interview, I would have found his arrogance completely sincere.

Hurst is self-taught. How did he learn his trade? 'I asked the right questions and picked it all up,' he says nonchalantly. Almost all of his commissions come from private individuals ('I used to do commercial work for companies, but that was soul-numbing'). Some clients keep coming back. 'Eventually, you do their whole house. That is very satisfying.' But he is honest enough to admit that relationships with clients do not always run smoothly. 'The most annoying clients are the ones who don't know what they want, and only decide they do know when it is too late... my favorite clients are the demanding ones.'

Although Hurst has every reason to be satisfied with himself, he is also generous in his praise for others—where appropriate. With a sudden flash of modesty, he says: 'There are people who are much better than me.' I can admire other people. After all, I wasn't trained at Parnham (the leading college for furniture design). However, he is also incessantly critical of craftsmen who 'try to be artists and need a year to make a single piece'. He also has little regard for graduation exhibitions, where students display their work but at the same time 'try to make fashion statements. That can be pretentious. A piece of furniture isn't about making a statement. It has to be something that people can actually use.'

Hurst is self-assured, perhaps even blunt, but you could never call him or his work pretentious. His final remark testifies to a welcome down-to-earth approach to his craft and a touch of humility that, strangely enough, stands in stark contrast to his earlier self-confidence. 'After all, I just make furniture,' he says as I leave.

The Elephant Show 

by Daniel Allsop, age 14 

Last summer, I went to Thailand for a beach holiday with my family. One day, we took a trip to a park not far from our hotel. It had beautiful flower gardens but we were only interested in the elephant show. 
We went straight to a large square with seats on three sides. Three elephants came in with their keepers and stood in front of a large piece of white card. Each elephant was given a paintbrush and started to paint on its own card. From time to time, the keepers put a new brush full of paint into each elephant's trunk and took the old one away. Slowly, following their keepers' instructions, the elephants drew pictures on the cards. I couldn't believe what I was seeing! One picture showed a river, one a tree and the third a bunch of flowers. When the keepers held up the paintings, everyone wanted to buy one. We gave the elephants the bananas we brought for our lunch. 
Twenty years ago, elephants worked in the forest. Now, they no longer work there, but the cleverest of these animals live in special centres where visitors can watch them.

De Olifantenshow

Door Daniel Allsop, 14 jaar

Afgelopen zomer ging ik met mijn familie naar Thailand voor een strandvakantie. Op een dag gingen we naar een park vlakbij ons hotel. Het had prachtige bloementuinen, maar we waren alleen geïnteresseerd in de olifantenshow.

We liepen meteen naar een groot plein met zitplaatsen aan drie kanten. Drie olifanten kwamen binnen met hun verzorgers en gingen voor een groot wit karton staan. Elke olifant kreeg een penseel en begon te schilderen op zijn eigen kaartje. Van tijd tot tijd stopten de verzorgers een nieuw penseel met verf in de slurf van elke olifant en namen het oude penseel weer mee. Langzaam, de aanwijzingen van hun verzorgers volgend, tekenden de olifanten plaatjes op de kaartjes. Ik kon mijn ogen niet geloven! Op één plaatje stond een rivier, op een ander een boom en op het derde een bos bloemen. Toen de verzorgers de schilderijen omhoog hielden, wilde iedereen er een kopen. We gaven de olifanten de bananen die we voor onze lunch hadden meegenomen.

Twintig jaar geleden werkten olifanten in het bos. Ze werken daar nu niet meer, maar de slimste van deze dieren leven in speciale centra waar bezoekers ze kunnen bekijken.

results.src_text:
Paul Simon

Rock and roll in the 1950s was primarily a youth cult, but its lasting importance lay in the seismic impact it had on the middle class and the middle-aged. It also paved the way for the next generation of rock idols, who listened to it awestruck and aware that this strange, unsettling sound would somehow, irrevocably, be linked with their destinies.
For Paul Simon, as for other youngsters in the US, the chief opportunity for hearing this new and invigorating type of music that was sweeping the country was courtesy of Alan Freed's radio show, Moondog Rock'n'Roll Party. Freed's show was required listening for a whole generation of fledgling rock idols. Like the young John Lennon, 3,000 miles away in Liverpool, with his ear glued to Radio Luxembourg - the only European outlet for the new rock and roll - Paul Simon was fascinated by the sounds pouring from Freed's show, and prepared himself for the next big step for a rock and roll obsessed teenager, the switch from listening to others' music to making his own.

Snow

No path was visible, but I thought that I would be all right if I walked with due caution. The wind hammered down from the heights, knocking me over as I slid and slithered on the slippery ice. Suddenly the innocent-looking snow gave way beneath me. I dropped, startled, into a hole some four feet deep. The snow had formed a roof over the gap between two rocks, melting away to leave nothing but a thin crust through which I had plunged. I hauled myself out, shaken and unnerved, wondering what I would have done if the hole had been thirty feet deep. I sat back against the top of a pine tree that protruded from the snow to take stock of the situation. In an hour I had covered about half a mile. It was perfectly clear that I would have to abandon my plan.

Qualitative Research

There are now numerous books which attempt to give guidance to researchers about qualitative research. While much has been written about the collection of data, the books are often silent about the processes and procedures associated with data analysis. Indeed, much mystery surrounds the way researchers analyse their data. Accordingly, we invited a range of social scientists who have engaged in qualitative projects to discuss the approaches that they used. The idea was to share insight and understanding of the process of qualitative data analysis rather than to produce a guidebook for the intending researcher. Such a task involves a process of demystification, of making implicit procedures more explicit. While this may sound straightforward, we have found it far from simple. We have therefore given our contributors the opportunity to present their work in a range of styles, which include autobiographical narratives and more impersonal forms.

We hebben onze bijdragers daarom de gelegenheid gegeven om hun werk in verschillende stijlen te presenteren, waaronder autobiografische verhalen en meer onpersoonlijke vormen.

It's true - we're all getting too big for our boots
Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers teacher he wanted to join the navy when he left school. 'What do you want to be?' asked the teacher. 'The flagpole on a ship?' The teacher had a point - because Chris, though still only fourteen, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is Britain's tallest man.
Every decade, the average height of people in Europe grows another centimetre. Every year, more and more truly big people are born. Intriguingly, this does not mean humanity is producing a new super race. In fact, we are returning to what we were like as cavemen. Only now are we losing the effects of generations of poor diet - with dramatic effects. 'We are only now beginning to fulfil our proper potential,' says palaeontologist Professor Chris Stringer. 'We are becoming Cro-Magnons again - the people who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.'
For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a wide variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruits and berries, while men supplemented these with occasional kills of animals (a way of life still adopted by the world's few remaining tribes of hunter- gatherers). One research study found that they based their diet on 85 different wild plants, for example. Then about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented - with devastating consequences. Most of the planet's green places have been gradually taken over by farmers, with the result that just three carbohydrate-rich plants - wheat, rice and maize - provide more than half of the calories consumed by the human race today.
This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries we have lived on soups, porridges and breads that have left us underfed and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when they began to grow corn, healthy hunter-gatherers were turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did diseases. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, corn was a public health disaster, according to some anthropologists.
Nevertheless, from then on agriculture spread because a piece of farmed land could support ten times the number of people who had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people relying on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been tackled, even by the world's wealthier nations. Only in Europe, the US and Japan are diets again reflecting the richness of our ancestors' diets.
As a result, the average man in the US is now 179cm, in Holland 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, though not without its own problems. Heights may have risen, but the world has not moved on, it seems. A standard bed-length has remained at 190cm since 1860. Even worse, leg-room in planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than grown, while clothes manufacturers are constantly having to revise their range of products.
The question is: where will it all end? We cannot grow for ever. We must have some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of University, it could be as much as 193 cm - and we are likely to reach it some time this century.
However, scientists add one note of qualification. Individuals may be growing taller because of improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly rounder and taller - an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies are best at keeping in heat.) Since the climate warmed, we appear to have got slightly thinner and smaller, even when properly fed. And as the planet continues to heat up, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.

De lengte is dan wel toegenomen, maar de wereld lijkt niet vooruit te zijn gegaan. De standaard bedlengte is sinds 1860 onveranderd gebleven op 190 cm. Erger nog, de beenruimte in vliegtuigen en treinen lijkt eerder te zijn gekrompen dan gegroeid, terwijl kledingfabrikanten hun productassortiment voortdurend moeten aanpassen.

De vraag is: waar houdt dit allemaal op? We kunnen niet eeuwig blijven groeien. We moeten een geprogrammeerde bovengrens hebben. Maar wat is die? Volgens Robert Fogel van de universiteit zou die wel eens 193 cm kunnen zijn - en we zullen die waarschijnlijk ergens in deze eeuw bereiken.

Wetenschappers voegen hier echter een kanttekening bij. Individuen worden misschien langer door verbeterde voeding, maar als soort krimpen we juist. Tijdens de laatste ijstijd, 10.000 jaar geleden, waren mensen iets ronder en langer - een evolutionaire reactie op de kou. (Grote, ronde lichamen houden warmte het beste vast.) Sinds het klimaat warmer is geworden, lijken we iets dunner en kleiner te zijn geworden, zelfs met voldoende voeding. En naarmate de planeet verder opwarmt, zullen we misschien nog verder krimpen. Met andere woorden: de groei van de mensheid zou door de opwarming van de aarde tenietgedaan kunnen worden.

results.src_text:
The Young Achiever of the Year

Kal Kaur Rai has always been interested in fashion and has just won the title of Young Achiever of the Year at the Asian Business Awards. Ever since she was a child, she has drawn clothes and designed patterns. She never told her hard-working parents, who own a supermarket, that she wanted to turn her hobby into a career. She thought they expected her to go into a more established business, so she went to university to do a management degree.

After university, she moved to London and worked in an advertising agency. She had to attend industry events but couldn't afford the designer clothes she liked. She started making skirts and tops for herself. When her friends saw her clothes, they asked her to make things for them. She then found a small shop in London willing to take her designs on a sale-or- return basis. They were very popular and nothing came back. This encouraged her to leave her advertising job, take out a PS20,000 loan and begin her own womenswear label.

Kal's parents were not angry about her career change and said they would support her, which really pleased her. Her clothes are now on sale in over 70 stores and her business has an income of over PS500,000. Her clothes appear in fashion magazines, she designs for pop stars and she has just gained public recognition by winning this award. Her business has come a long way and she knows she is extremely lucky. 'What I do is my hobby - and I get paid for it! But remember, I've worked hard for this.'
results.tgt_text:
Jonge Talent van het Jaar

Kal Kaur Rai is altijd al geïnteresseerd geweest in mode en heeft zojuist de titel 'Jonge Talent van het Jaar' gewonnen bij de Asian Business Awards. Al sinds haar kindertijd tekent ze kleding en ontwerpt ze patronen. Ze heeft haar hardwerkende ouders, die een supermarkt bezitten, nooit verteld dat ze van haar hobby haar carrière wilde maken. Ze dacht dat ze verwachtten dat ze in een meer gevestigde branche zou gaan werken, dus ging ze naar de universiteit om management te studeren.

Na haar studie verhuisde ze naar Londen en werkte ze bij een reclamebureau. Ze moest branche-evenementen bijwonen, maar kon zich de designerkleding die ze mooi vond niet veroorloven. Ze begon rokken en topjes voor zichzelf te maken. Toen haar vriendinnen haar kleding zagen, vroegen ze haar om ook iets voor hen te maken. Young Talent of the Year

Kal Kaur Rai has always been interested in fashion and has just won the title 'Young Talent of the Year' at the Asian Business Awards. She has been drawing clothes and designing patterns since childhood. She never told her hardworking parents, who own a supermarket, that she wanted to turn her hobby into a career. She thought they expected her to work in a more established industry, so she went to university to study management.

After her studies, she moved to London and worked at an advertising agency. She had to attend industry events but could not afford the designer clothes she liked. She started making skirts and tops for herself. When her friends saw her clothes, they asked her to make something for them as well. Subsequently, she found a small shop in London that was willing to sell her designs on installment. The clothes were very popular, and there was no return. This encouraged her to quit her job in advertising, take out a loan of £20,000, and start her own women's clothing brand. Kal's parents were not angry about her career switch and said they would support her, which made her very happy. Her clothing is now for sale in more than 70 stores and her company has a turnover of over £500,000. Her clothing appears in fashion magazines, she designs for pop stars, and she recently gained public recognition by winning this award. Her company has come a long way and she knows she is incredibly lucky. 'What I do is my hobby – and I even get paid for it! But don't forget, I worked hard for this.'

BURGLARS LOVE THE AFTERNOON

Most house burglaries happen between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m.,say the police.
Inspector Ian Saunders told our newspaper that the number of house burglaries has gone up by more than 30% compared with last year. He also said that 67% of burglaries happen when people have gone out and forgotten to dose a door or a window.
He went on to report that night-time burglaries are unusual because families are usually at home at that time. But he said that winter afternoons are the best time for burglars because it is dark and they can't be seen easily. Also many houses are empty at that time, because people are often still at work.
Inspector Saunders said that it is a good idea to leave lights on in living rooms and bedrooms when you go on holiday. This will help to keep burglars away. He also asked neighbours to watch the other houses in the street when people are not at home. They should call the police if they see anything strange. 'We will also tell you how to make your house safe,' Inspector Saunders said. 'This kind of help costs nothing.'

results.src_text:
Life was getting out of hand

Susan Harr unplugs her gadgets and rediscovers the joys of manual labour.

Everyone is in love with technology. It gives us all those marvellous gadgets that make life easier and leave us so much more time to do other things. A gradual, though not particularly subtle, form of brainwashing has persuaded us that technology rules, and that it is OK.
These implications are obvious. The movement of my fingers uses nothing from the previous power supply being eaten up by our greedy race. A craft executed by hand does not pollute the environment.
However, a recent unhappy experience with my malfunctioning word processor -
a PS48 call-out fee, a labour charge of PS15 per quarter of an hour, plus parts and replacements costs - has confirmed a suspicion that gadgets are often not worth the expense or the trouble. Are we as dependent on technology as we imagine? Bit by bit, I have been letting the household technology fall by the wayside as its natural and often short life expires.
This makes me wonder just what 'time' technology gives us. The time to take up more activities for which we must buy more gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts: but I think they are conning us.
So when the thing started making curious noises, which continued even when it was disconnected by a puzzled service agent, I abandoned it to the backyard, where it whispers damply to itself like some robot ghost.
I am not tied to a noisy, whirring machine, with my head bent and my back turned on the world, and I can take my time over the garment. In any case, I was always slightly alarmed by those electric machines that dash across the fabric towards your fingers. Best of all, I can pop the whole lot into a carrier bag and take it with me wherever I go.
Of course, there are some gadgets I would not like to be without. A year living without a washing machine convinced me of the value of the electric washtub. But there are others whose loss has brought unexpected delight. Feeling that we were becoming too apt to collapse in front of the television, or slot in a video, I sent back the rented colour equipment and we returned to the small black-and-white portable.
It is a real strain on the eyes and concentrates the mind on what is really worth watching. We now spend a lot more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, talking or pursuing other hobbies.
One of these, in my own case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that went by the board. My old Singer sewing machine is now an ornamental plant table, and as l cannot afford to replace it, I have taken to sewing by hand.
We have come to believe that we could not do without it, and if we do resist the notion that our lives would be unmanageable without the appliances of science we certainly do not want to relinquish them. Pity the generations whose lives were blighted by tedious and blister inducing toil. Even our brains are relieved of exertion by computers that not only perform miraculous calculations with amazing speed but now provide entertainment.
In fact, the time I now spend placidly stitching is anything but tedious, and the advantages are numerous. For a start, I can sew and listen to the radio - another rediscovered pleasure - or I can talk with family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch the programmes I do want to see on television, and alleviate my puritanical guilt at sitting in front of the box by doing something useful at the same time. And what a lovely, cosy feeling it is to sit by the fire and sew with a pot of tea for company.
Quite wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of the women who sewed elaborate garments, robes, linen and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the strain on the eyes and so on. 
There is a wonderfully soothing quality about executing a craft by hand, a great satisfaction in watching one's work become neater, more assured. I find things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows down to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th century life the need to rush to finish an activity so that I can rush to the next.
Meanwhile I have regained control of my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and daydream while doing the washing up agreeable, if temporarily forgotten, activity.
The result of all this brooding is that I now prowl the house with a speculative eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, that powered lawnmower? Come to think of it, we could save an awful lot of money by doing without electric lights!

Het leven liep uit de hand

Susan Harr koppelt haar gadgets los en herontdekt de geneugten van handarbeid.

Iedereen is dol op technologie. Het geeft ons al die fantastische gadgets die het leven makkelijker maken en ons zoveel meer tijd geven voor andere dingen. Een geleidelijke, zij het niet bepaald subtiele, vorm van hersenspoeling heeft ons ervan overtuigd dat technologie de baas is en dat het oké is.

De implicaties zijn duidelijk. De beweging van mijn vingers verbruikt niets van de energie die onze hebzuchtige soort opslokt. Handwerk vervuilt het milieu niet.

Een recente, vervelende ervaring met mijn defecte tekstverwerker -
48 pond voorrijkosten, 15 pond per kwartier, plus kosten voor onderdelen en vervanging - heeft echter mijn vermoeden bevestigd dat gadgets vaak de kosten en moeite niet waard zijn. Zijn we zo afhankelijk van technologie als we denken? Beetje bij beetje heb ik de huishoudelijke technologie aan de kant geschoven, omdat de natuurlijke en vaak korte levensduur ervan ten einde loopt.

Dit doet me afvragen welke 'tijd' technologie ons nu eigenlijk geeft. Tijd om meer activiteiten te ondernemen waarvoor we nog meer gadgets moeten kopen? Zo ja, petje af voor de marketingexperts: maar ik denk dat ze ons voor de gek houden.

Dus toen het ding vreemde geluiden begon te maken, die zelfs aanhielden nadat een verbaasde servicemedewerker het had losgekoppeld, heb ik het in de achtertuin achtergelaten, waar het vochtig voor zichzelf fluistert als een soort robotgeest.

Ik ben niet gebonden aan een lawaaierige, zoemende machine, met mijn hoofd gebogen en mijn rug naar de wereld gekeerd, en ik kan rustig de tijd nemen voor mijn kledingstuk. Ik was sowieso altijd al een beetje bang voor die elektrische machines die zo snel over de stof naar je vingers schieten. Het mooiste is dat ik alles in een draagtas kan stoppen en overal mee naartoe kan nemen.

Natuurlijk zijn er gadgets die ik niet zou willen missen. Een jaar zonder wasmachine heeft me overtuigd van de waarde van de elektrische wastobbe. Maar er zijn er ook waarvan het gemis onverwachte vreugde heeft gebracht. Omdat ik merkte dat we te vaak voor de televisie in elkaar zakten of een video opzetten, heb ik de gehuurde kleurentelevisie teruggestuurd en zijn we weer overgestapt op de kleine zwart-wit draagbare tv.

Het is echt een belasting voor de ogen en het concentreert je op wat echt de moeite waard is om te kijken. We besteden nu veel meer tijd aan het uitlaten van de hond (die sowieso nooit van televisie hield), lezen, praten of andere hobby's.

Een daarvan is naaien; en dit is weer zo'n gadget dat ik heb laten varen. Mijn oude Singer naaimachine is nu een sierlijke plantentafel, en omdat ik het me niet kan veroorloven om hem te vervangen, ben ik met de hand gaan naaien.

We zijn gaan geloven dat we er niet zonder kunnen, en hoewel we ons verzetten tegen het idee dat ons leven onhoudbaar zou zijn zonder de hulpmiddelen van de wetenschap, willen we ze zeker niet opgeven. Het is te doen met de generaties wier leven werd geteisterd door saaie en blaarvormende arbeid. Zelfs onze hersenen worden ontlast door computers die niet alleen wonderbaarlijke berekeningen met verbazingwekkende snelheid uitvoeren, maar nu ook entertainment bieden.

De tijd die ik nu rustig naai, is allesbehalve saai, en de voordelen zijn talrijk. Om te beginnen kan ik naaien en naar de radio luisteren – nog een herontdekt plezier – of ik kan met familie en vrienden praten. Als het een eenvoudige taak is, kan ik de programma's kijken die ik wél wil zien op televisie en mijn puriteinse schuldgevoel over het zitten voor de tv verlichten door tegelijkertijd iets nuttigs te doen. En wat een heerlijk, gezellig gevoel is het om bij de open haard te zitten en te naaien met een pot thee erbij.

Ten onrechte had ik de neiging om met afschuw te denken aan de vrouwen die ingewikkelde kledingstukken, gewaden, linnen en huishoudelijke artikelen met de hand naaiden. Ik dacht aan die lange uren, de belasting voor de ogen, enzovoort.

Er is iets heerlijk rustgevends aan het met de hand uitvoeren van een ambacht, een grote voldoening in het zien hoe je werk netter en zekerder wordt. Ik merk dat dingen verrassend snel gedaan worden en dat het tempo van het leven plotseling vertraagt ​​tot het ritme van mijn eigen handen. Ik ben ook bevrijd van een van de meest verachtelijke aspecten van het leven aan het einde van de 20e eeuw: de noodzaak om me te haasten om een ​​activiteit af te ronden, zodat ik me naar de volgende kan haasten.

Ondertussen heb ik de controle over mijn gootsteen teruggevonden, waar ik mijn handen in het zeepsop dompel en dagdroom terwijl ik de afwas doe – een aangename, zij het tijdelijk vergeten, bezigheid.

Het resultaat van al dat gepeins is dat ik nu met een onderzoekende blik door het huis dwaal. Hebben we die vriezer, die magnetron, die elektrische grasmaaier echt nodig? Nu ik erover nadenk, zouden we een hoop geld kunnen besparen door het zonder elektrische verlichting te stellen!
